[SECTION] title
Noninvasive individual and species identification of jaguars (Panthera onca), pumas (Puma concolor) and ocelots (Leopardus pardalis) in Belize, Central America using cross-species microsatellites and faecal DNA

[SECTION] abstract
There is a great need to develop efficient, noninvasive genetic sampling methods to study wild populations of multiple, co-occurring, threatened felids. This is especially important for molecular scatology studies occurring in challenging tropical environments where DNA degrades quickly and the quality of faecal samples varies greatly. We optimized 14 polymorphic microsatellite loci for jaguars (Panthera onca), pumas (Puma concolor) and ocelots (Leopardus pardalis) and assessed their utility for cross-species amplification. Additionally, we tested their reliability for species and individual identification using DNA from faeces of wild felids detected by a scat detector dog across Belize in Central America. All microsatellite loci were successfully amplified in the three target species, were polymorphic with average expected heterozygosities of H E = 0.60 AE 0.18 (SD) for jaguars, H E = 0.65 AE 0.21 (SD) for pumas and H E = 0.70 AE 0.13 (SD) for ocelots and had an overall PCR amplification success of 61%. We used this nuclear DNA primer set to successfully identify species and individuals from 49% of 1053 field-collected scat samples. This set of optimized microsatellite multiplexes represents a powerful tool for future efforts to conduct noninvasive studies on multiple, wild Neotropical felids.

[SECTION] introduction
Jaguars (Panthera onca) and co-occurring Neotropical felids, such as pumas (Puma concolor) and ocelots (Leopardus pardalis), are extremely difficult to study in the wild due to their elusive nature. As landscapes change and human impacts increase, felid populations become increasingly fragmented and ecological processes such as dispersal, intraguild competition and top-down trophic impacts (Linnell & Strand 2000) are affected, but remain understudied. Consequently, there is a great need for efficient survey methods that can be applied to multiple co-occurring species instead of focusing research efforts on a single species. Noninvasive genetic monitoring has been of increasing importance in the field of wildlife management and conservation in recent years (e.g. Waits & Paetkau 2005;Beja-Pereira et al. 2009), providing the potential to gain valuable information on multiple species existing across a fragmented landscape. Molecular scatology, in which individuals are genotyped using DNA isolated from sloughed intestinal epithelial cells in field-collected faecal samples (Hoss et al. 1992;Kohn & Wayne 1997), is especially suitable for wild felids, which often deposit scat at prominent sites for intraand interspecific communication (Sunquist & Sunquist 2002). Additionally, DNA extracted from faeces can be obtained without physically capturing or disturbing animals of interest (Taberlet et al. 1999). Noninvasive genetic sampling also holds great promise for providing large sample sizes for multiple species simultaneously and identification of species, gender and individuals, which is beneficial for a wide array of analyses (e.g. Waits & Paetkau 2005;Kelly et al. 2012;Rodgers & Janecka 2013).
To efficiently monitor threatened species, robust identification of individuals is crucial for various types of studies (e.g. capture-recapture analysis). However, individual-based molecular scatology studies of single and especially of multiple wild felid species are rare, particularly in tropical regions. Multispecies felid studies often do not go beyond the species level (e.g. Zuercher et al. 2003;Cossios & Angers 2006;Haag et al. 2009;Michalski et al. 2011;Roques et al. 2011), with a few exceptions (e.g. Singh et al. 2004;Trigo et al. 2008;Mondol et al. 2012). One of the challenges to conducting individual-based genetic population monitoring using faecal DNA collected in tropical environments is the rapid removal of faecal samples by insects and rain and the rapid degradation of DNA. DNA degradation is affected by various environmental factors (high temperatures, precipitation and UV radiation) (e.g. Brinkman et al. 2010;Vynne et al. 2012), which are particularly problematic in tropical climates where excessive heat and humidity cause DNA to deteriorate rapidly. Generally, low DNA quantity and quality are major concerns for molecular scatology studies in the tropics (e.g. Michalski et al. 2011;Vynne et al. 2012), as they decrease polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification success and cause genotyping errors (Taberlet et al. 1996). Genotyping errors increase the chance of misidentification of individuals and potentially bias population estimates (Taberlet & Luikart 1999;Taberlet et al. 1999;Mills et al. 2000;Waits & Leberg 2000).
To conduct a noninvasive genetic study of multiple Neotropical felid species simultaneously, a set of highly polymorphic microsatellite markers, also known as simple sequence repeats (SSRs), are needed that amplify multiple target species and have the potential to identify species and individuals from faecal DNA. Cross-species amplification of microsatellites depends on the conservation of primer sequences, which has been described for several mammalian taxa (e.g. Moore et al. 1991). Crossspecies microsatellites are transferrable between closely related species (e.g. Barbara et al. 2007), which makes them a cost-effective and efficient approach for conservation genetic studies of multiple target species. Menotti-Raymond and O'Brien (1995) and Menotti-Raymond et al. (1999) characterized microsatellite loci for the domestic cat (Felis catus) and described their utility for cross-species amplification due to conserved flanking primer sequences across the family Felidae. Cross-species microsatellites subsequently were used for several felid studies (e.g. Menotti-Raymond & O'Brien 1995;Johnson et al. 1999;Carmichael et al. 2000;Williamson et al. 2002;Singh et al. 2004;Buckley-Beason et al. 2006;Moreno et al. 2006;Grisolia et al. 2007;Trigo et al. 2008). Their application is diverse and has helped facilitate comparisons among closely related feline species for assessing levels of genetic diversity and phylogeographic patterns (Johnson et al. 1999;Moreno et al. 2006;Grisolia et al. 2007), to recognize new feline species (Wilting et al. 2007), to assess hybridization between wild and domestic cats (e.g. Oliveira et al. 2008;Trigo et al. 2008) and to detect illegal hunting and trafficking of threatened felids (Maudet et al. 2004;Singh et al. 2004). Nevertheless, cross-species amplification of microsatellites has not often been used for demographic and genetic monitoring of multiple felids in the wild, which could ultimately improve conservation and management activities for these elusive species. Besides the comparison of population genetic parameters among multiple closely related species, cross-species microsatellites can also be applied for species identification based on species-specific allele sizes at multiple loci, a technique that has rarely been used for noninvasive studies of wild carnivores (e.g. Pilot et al. 2007;Wilting et al. 2007).
We conducted a 4-year noninvasive genetic study of three co-occurring felids (jaguar, puma and ocelot) across several study sites in tropical Belize, Central America. We initially screened 20 microsatellite loci developed in earlier feline studies (Menotti-Raymond et al. 1999) and identified 14 microsatellite markers for a molecular scatology study of three Neotropical felids suitable for answering a variety of questions relevant to conservation and management. Specifically, our objective was to define a set of highly polymorphic microsatellite loci applicable for reliable and cost-effective species and individual identification across three target species. Furthermore, we evaluated the reliability of genotypes from faecal samples of highly variable DNA quality and quantity as a primary DNA source by determining PCR amplification success, genotyping accuracy and error rates.

[SECTION] methods

[SECTION] study area
We conducted 2-to 3-month long scat surveys across five main study sites (Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve -MPR, Rio Bravo Conservation and Management Area -RB, Cockscomb Basin Wildlife Sanctuary -CBWS, Chiquibul Forest Reserve and National Park -CFRNP and Fireburn/Balam Na Nature Reserve -FB) and 2-to 10-day surveys at several other sites (Big Falls -BF, Bladen Nature Reserve -BNR, Boden Creek Ecological Preserve -BC, Bull Run Farm -BRF, Golden Stream Corridor Preserve -GS, Hidden Valley Reserve -HVR, Machaca Hills -MH, Manatee Forest Reserve -MFR, Sarstoon-Temash National Park -STNP, Shipstern Nature Preserve -SNP, Tiger Sandy Bay -TSB) from 2007 to 2010 across Belize, Central America (17°15 0 N, 88°45 0 W; Fig. 1). All sites except BF, BRF, MH and TSB are part of the national system of protected areas in Belize. The study sites also fall within the forests of La Selva Maya (The Mayan Forest), a recognized biodiversity hot spot that forms part of the northern section of the Mesoamerican Biological Corridor. Across study sites, elevation ranges from 0 to 1120 m. Mean annual rainfall varies from 1524 mm in the north to 4064 mm in the south, with a pronounced wet season from June to December. Average annual temperatures fluctuate between 17.7 and 31.3 °C. A high diversity of native habitat types is represented within the study sites, including lowland and submontane broad-leaved moist and wet forests, lowland and submontane pine forests, mangrove and littoral forests, lowland savannah, shrub land and wetland.

[SECTION] sample detection
Faecal samples were detected using a professionally trained scat detector dog (PackLeader LLC, Gig Harbor, WA, USA). Opportunistic searches with the dog off-leash were conducted within all study sites (Wasser et al. 2004) to detect scat samples along roads, trails, game trails, offtrail, and across various landscape features (e.g. streams) and habitat types. The scat detector dog was trained to locate scat samples of all five native feline species (jaguars, pumas, ocelots, margays, Leopardus wiedii; jaguarundis, Puma yaguarondi). All scat samples located by the scat detector dog, regardless of their appearance or suspected age, were collected and genotyped.

[SECTION] faecal dna storage and extraction
From each scat, approximately 0.5 mL sample was collected and stored at room temperature in sterile 2-mL screw-top tubes filled with dimethyl sulphoxide saline solution (DETs buffer, Seutin et al. 1991) at 1: ≥4 volume scat-to-solution ratio. Scat samples were collected using disposable gloves and wooden sampling sticks. Faecal DNA extractions were conducted in a separate room at the Laboratory for Ecological, Evolutionary and Conservation Genetics (LEECG) at the University of Idaho (Moscow, ID, US), dedicated to noninvasive genetic studies, in order to avoid contamination while working with low-concentration DNA samples. The QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit protocol (Qiagen, Inc.) was used to extract DNA from all faecal samples. An extraction negative was added to each extraction run to control for contamination.

[SECTION] microsatellite screening and selection
A total of 20 microsatellite loci (F53, F85, F98, F124, FCA008, FCA032, FCA043, FCA090, FCA096, FCA100, FCA124, FCA126, FCA132, FCA212, FCA225, FCA229, FCA275, FCA391, FCA441 and FCA741) originally identified for the domestic cat (Menotti- Raymond et al. 1999Raymond et al. , 2005) ) were tested on faecal samples from wild Neotropical felids (19 jaguars, 18 pumas and 12 ocelots) collected in the first two study sites (MPR and RB). Microsatellite performance was evaluated by assessing allelic variation, probabilities of identity for unrelated individuals and siblings (Waits et al. 2001), PCR amplification success, genotyping accuracy and genotyping error rates.

[SECTION] microsatellite amplification and genotyping
Following microsatellite screening, 14 highly polymorphic loci were selected, labelled with fluorescent dyes and arranged in three PCR multiplex reactions (multiplex 1 -F124-PET, FCA391-NED, FCA043-NED, FCA275-VIC, FCA096-6-FAM, FCA126-PET, FCA090-6-FAM; multiplex 2 -F85-VIC, F98-6-FAM, FCA741-PET, FCA225-PET, FCA008-6-FAM; and multiplex 3 -F53-NED and FCA441-6-FAM) to enhance performance and efficiency. The three multiplexes each contained 5.2 lL PCR mixture and 1.8 lL of DNA. Multiplex 1 included 3.5 lL 19 concentrated Qiagen Master Mix (Qiagen, Inc.), 0.7 lL of 0.59 concentrated Qiagen Q solution (Qiagen, Inc.), 0.88 lL of primers (0.10 lM F124, 0.34 lM FCA391, 0.07 lM FCA043, 0.13 lM FCA275, 0.21 lM FCA096, 0.20 lM FCA126, 0.20 lM FCA090), 0.12 lL H 2 O and 1.8 lL DNA extract. Multiplex 2 consisted of 3.5 lL 19 concentrated Qiagen Master Mix, 0.7 lL of 0.59 concentrated Qiagen Q solution, 0.65 lL of primers (0.20 lM for F85, 0.09 lM for F98, 0.11 lM for FCA741, 0.43 lM for FCA225, 0.10 lM for FCA008), 0.35 lL H 2 O and 1.8 lL DNA extract. Multiplex 3 only differed in the amount of water (0.76 lL) and primers (0.24 lL; 0.20 lM for F53, 0.14 lM for FCA441) added. Microsatellite PCR amplifications were conducted using a DNA Engine Tetrad 2 Peltier Thermal Cycler (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc.) starting with an initial denaturation step of 15 min at 95 °C; followed by 13 cycles of 30 s at 94 °C for denaturation, 1.5 min at 60 °C with a decrease in annealing temperature of 0.8 °C in each cycle and 1-min elongation at 72 °C; followed by 30 cycles of 30 s at 94 °C for denaturation, 1.5 min at 50 °C for annealing and 1 min elongation at 72 °C; and 30 min at 60 °C for final elongation. A polymerase chain reaction negative was included in each group of PCRs to indicate the presence/absence of contamination. We visualized PCR products using an ABI PRISM â 377 automated DNA sequencer (Applied Biosystems TM ), and genotypes were identified using the software GENEMAPPER, version 3.7 (Applied Biosystems TM ).
Initially, we performed a minimum of two PCRs for all scat samples using the screening multiplex 1 (seven loci). Depending on the number of successfully amplified loci within multiplex 1, we placed the scat samples in three categories describing amplification success: (i) bad (0-2 loci amplified), (ii) medium (3-5 loci amplified) and (iii) good (6-7 loci amplified). We conducted 1-4 additional PCR runs for scat samples placed into the medium and good quality categories. Scat samples with ≤2 loci amplified were discarded from the study. The total number of PCRs ranged from 2 to 6 replicates per locus and averaged 4.29 AE 1.84 (SD) per locus for samples with finalized genotypes. To finalize the consensus genotypes, a multitube approach was used where at least three identical homozygote PCR results were required for homozygote genotypes, and each allele had to be observed in two independent PCRs to record a heterozygous genotype.

[SECTION] species and individual identification
Scat samples were assigned to feline species based on species-specific alleles and allelic ranges initially identified across several loci from known faecal DNA samples of 12 jaguars, four pumas, 12 ocelots, 30 margays and four jaguarundis obtained from captive facilities (Belize Zoo, Belize; Feline Conservation Center, CA, US; Naples Zoo, FL, US, Profelis, Costa Rica). Additionally, to verify species assignment of all unique jaguar, puma and ocelot individuals, we conducted assignment tests with the Bayesian clustering software STRUCTURE, version 2.3.3 (Pritchard et al. 2000). Species assignment for all individual genotypes detected was verified by analysing clustering patterns based on distinctive allele frequencies and the most likely number of genetic clusters (K). The admixture model was used (predefined K = 1-5 corresponding to the five native feline species; 10 runs per K value; length of burn-in period: 10 5 iterations; number of MCMC iterations after burn-in: 10 6 ). The optimal K value was chosen by calculating the posterior probability for each K value, which is based on estimated maximum log-likelihood values. After finding the optimal K, individuals were assigned to distinct genetic clusters using the % of the genotype's ancestry (Q) attributed to each genetic cluster. For successful species identification, Q values had to be ≥95%. Also, mitochondrial sequencing was conducted for four DNA samples per species cluster to confirm species assignment. Four mitochondrial gene regions were amplified including cytochrome b (H15149, Kocher et al. 1989;Farrell-R, Farrell et al. 2000), 12S (L1085, H1259, Kitano et al. 2007), 16S (L2513, H2714, Kitano et al. 2007), 16Scp (16Scp-F, 16Scp-F, Kitano et al. 2007) and adenosine triphosphate-6 (ATP6-DF3, ATP6-DR2, Chaves et al. 2012). DNA sequences were edited and matched with reference samples from the Global Felid Genetics Program at the American Museum of Natural History (New York, NY) using GENEIOUS, v. 6.1.5. (Biomatters Ltd., Auckland, New Zealand).
For individual identification, we estimated probabilities of identity (per locus and cumulative) for unrelated individuals (P (ID) ) and siblings (P (ID)sib ) per species as described by Waits et al. (2001) using GIMLET, version 1.3.3. (Valiere 2002). Cumulative P (ID) and P (ID)sib values were calculated per species for screening multiplex 1, and the minimum number of loci required for individual identification was estimated following a criterion of P (ID) sib < 0.010 as suggested by Mills et al. (2000) and Waits et al. (2001).
Once consensus genotypes were finalized for multiplex 1, we used GENALEX, version 6.41 (Peakall & Smouse 2006) to determine the minimum number of individuals per species by checking for repeated matching genotypes, which if detected, were classified as recaptures of individual felids. Near-matching genotypes, which differed at only one or two loci, were genotyped two more times. We selected the scat sample with the highest PCR product quality for each detected individual and screened these using multiplex 2 (five loci) and multiplex 3 (two loci). We obtained consensus genotypes for the final two multiplexes after performing an additional 2-6 PCR replicates per locus. Genotypes, which were only detected once, were further examined using the software RELIOTYPE (Miller et al. 2002) and maximum likelihood to assess their reliability. If the accuracy of multilocus scores was below 95%, additional PCR replicates were conducted.

[SECTION] data analysis
GENALEX, version 6.41 (Peakall & Smouse 2006) was used to assess genetic variation per species at single loci and across all loci by calculating the number of alleles (N A ) and estimating observed (H O ) and expected heterozygosities (H E ). Additionally, we determined allelic richness (A R ) using the rarefaction method with HP-RARE, version 1.0 (Kalinowski 2005) and polymorphic information content (PIC) with CERVUS, version 3.0 (Kalinowski et al. 2007).
To calculate PCR amplification success, genotyping accuracy and genotyping error rates, we selected the last two PCR runs for all loci across all scat samples. We used only the last two runs to standardize the number included per sample. PCR amplification success rates were assessed by calculating the percentage of successful PCRs across all samples tested and for all samples with finalized species identification. Genotyping accuracy rates were estimated by calculating the percentage of successful PCRs, which matched the finalized consensus genotype. Genotyping error was quantified by calculating the rate of false alleles (FA) and allelic dropouts (ADO) following the protocols of Broquet and Petit (2004). False allele rates were calculated for all consensus genotypes, and allelic dropout rates were estimated only for heterozygous genotypes.
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and linkage disequilibrium (LD) were tested for all three species with GENE- POP, version 4.1 (Raymond & Rousset 1995) using default settings for Markov chain parameters. The presence of null alleles was examined with MICRO-CHECKER (Van Oosterhout et al. 2004). Data were tested for normality and homoscedasticity. Statistical differences between groups were evaluated using nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis and post hoc Wilcoxon rank-sum tests in program R, version 3.0.1 (R Development Core Team 2009). All results for multiple significance tests were adjusted by applying sequential Bonferroni correction (Rice 1989).

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] sample detection
The total number of faecal DNA samples located by the scat detector dog across all study sites was 1053, with 110 collected in MPR, 203 in RB, 223 in CBWS, 111 in CFRNP, 217 in FB and 189 samples during several shortterm surveys across various sites (BF, BNR, BC, BRF, GS, HVR, MH, MFR, STNP, SNP and TSB) in Belize.

[SECTION] microsatellite selection
Microsatellite DNA from faecal samples of wild jaguars, pumas and ocelots collected in MPR and RB amplified across all 20 initially selected loci, confirming their crossspecies utility. Nonetheless, six microsatellite loci (FCA032, FCA100, FCA124, FCA132, FCA212 and FCA229) were omitted from the analysis due to low levels of genetic variation (N A ≤ 2 and H E ≤ 0.5 for FCA100, FCA132 and FCA212 in jaguars; N A = 1 and H E = 0 for FCA032 and FCA212 in pumas; H E ≤ 0.5 for FCA132 in ocelots) and overlapping allelic size ranges (FCA124 with FCA043, FCA229 with FCA275). Based on P (ID)sib estimates, loci FCA132 for jaguars, FCA032 and FCA212 for pumas and FCA132 for ocelots were the least powerful loci for individual identification among those tested. We also assessed primer performance across 74 faecal samples collected in MPR and RB in terms of PCR amplification success and genotyping error rates. Loci FCA032 and FCA100 had generally low PCR amplification success rates. Loci FCA100 and FCA132 showed high rates of allelic dropout, and loci FCA100 and FCA229 produced high rates of false alleles.

[SECTION] species and individual identification
After screening, 14 highly polymorphic microsatellite loci were selected and used for species and individual identification. Species-specific alleles and allelic ranges were described for all target species using faecal samples obtained from the wild in Belize (Table S1, Supporting information). Across all finalized loci, for pumas, 70.3% of the alleles described were species-specific followed by 64.1% for ocelots and 63.8% for jaguars. The most powerful loci for species assignment (100% of alleles were species specific) were F124, FCA391, FCA096, FCA126 and FCA741 for jaguars, F124, FCA096, F98 and FCA008 for pumas, and F124, FCA043, FCA096 and F85 for ocelots.
Species identification was additionally confirmed by sequencing four mitochondrial gene regions for a subset of samples and by applying Bayesian assignment methods for all samples identified down to individual level, which estimated the number of K clusters with an increase of likelihood values, peaking at K = 3. At K = 3, all individuals tested were successfully assigned to one species cluster with an average proportion of membership or Q of 0.997 AE 0.005 (SD) for jaguars, 0.995 AE 0.007 (SD) for pumas and 0.997 AE 0.001 (SD) for ocelots (Fig. 2).
For individual identification, cumulative P (ID) and P (ID)sib values were calculated per species for the screening multiplex 1 (seven loci), which helped to assess the minimum number of loci required for individual identification. With the criterion of P (ID)sib < 0.010, a minimum of six finalized loci for jaguars and ocelots and 5 loci for pumas were needed to identify individuals with high statistical confidence (Fig. 3). The cumulative P (ID) and P (ID)sib values for seven loci of multiplex 1 were 2.5E-06 and 0.005 for jaguars, 1.5E-08 and 0.002 for pumas, and 4.6E-08 and 0.002 for ocelots. For all 14 loci, cumulative P (ID) and P (ID)sib estimates were 3.9E-11 and 5.3E-05 for jaguars, 4.3E-14 and 1.5E-05 for pumas, and 5.5E-15 and 7.1E-06 for ocelots.
In summary, of 1053 scat samples collected across all study sites, 512 (49%) were successfully identified to the species and individual level. In total, we detected 149 individual felids (65 jaguars, 54 pumas and 30 ocelots) in the wild. Jaguars were genetically identified 299 times, pumas 153 times and ocelots 60 times (Table 1). Due to a small sample size for margays (n = 9) and nondetection for jaguarundis, we decided to not include these two species into this manuscript.

[SECTION] characterization of cross-species microsatellites
For the finalized set of microsatellite loci, the number of alleles per locus ranged from 3 to 8 (5.00 AE 1.66, SD) for jaguars, 3-15 (8.00 AE 3.49, SD) for pumas and 3-10 (6.36 AE 1.87, SD) for ocelots. Mean allelic richness was highest for pumas (7.50 AE 3.19, SD), followed by jaguars (5.17 AE 1.56, SD) and ocelots (3.87 AE 0.87, SD). The average expected and observed heterozygosities for all loci were H E = 0.60 AE 0.18 (SD) and H 0 = 0.57 AE 0.20 (SD) for jaguars, H E = 0.65 AE 0.21 (SD) and H 0 = 0.61 AE 0.21 (SD) for pumas, H E = 0.70 AE 0.13 (SD) and H 0 = 0.62 AE 0.18 (SD) for ocelots. Based on mean PIC values, another measure of polymorphism for marker loci, ocelots showed the highest diversity membership coefficient (Q) Fig. 2 Species assignment using Bayesian clustering with STRUCTURE (Pritchard et al. 2000). Bar plot represents the assignment of the Neotropical feline species (jaguar, puma and ocelot) in Belize. Each vertical bar represents one individual. Each genetic cluster (coloured in a different grey shade) represents one species.
(0.66 AE 0.14, SD) followed by pumas (0.62 AE 0.21, SD) and jaguars (0.55 AE 0.17, SD) (Table 2).
No loci deviated significantly from HWE for jaguars. Loci FCA043 (P < 0.000) and F98 (P = 0.011) revealed significant deviations from HWE for pumas after using sequential Bonferroni correction (P ≤ 0.015). For ocelots, loci FCA391 (P = 0.001), FCA275 (P < 0.000) and FCA741 (P = 0.011) deviated significantly from HWE. Linkage disequilibrium was detected after using sequential Bonferroni correction (P ≤ 0.00055) in only one case (FCA096/FCA441 for jaguars).
PCR amplification success across all samples was 61% ranging from 47% to 89% per locus. PCR amplification success for samples with finalized species ID differed significantly among species (H = 17.53, P < 0.000; Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test) with highest mean rates for jaguars (90%), followed by pumas (88%) and ocelots (73%). Pairwise comparisons between species using post hoc Wilcoxon rank-sum tests revealed that PCR amplification success rates for ocelots were significantly lower compared to jaguars (W = 183, P < 0.000, r = À1.14) and pumas (W = 102, P = 0.001, r = À0.88). Genotyping accuracy across all samples was 90%, which also differed significantly among species (H = 29.51, P < 0.000; Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test) with highest mean rates for jaguars (93%) followed by ocelots (86%) and pumas (75%). Post hoc Wilcoxon rank-sum tests revealed significant differences between all species pairs tested. Genotyping error was estimated by calculating mean allelic dropout and false allele rates for all samples collected (ADO, 15% AE 2.8; FA, 2% AE 1.0). Allelic dropout rates for samples with finalized species ID varied significantly among species (H = 9.39, P = 0.009; Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test) with mean rates of 13% for jaguars, 12% for pumas and 17% for ocelots. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests showed that allelic dropout rates were significantly higher for ocelots than for jaguars (W = 42, P = 0.012, r = À0.67) and pumas (W = 39, P = 0.007, r = À0.72; Fig. 3 Relationship between the probability of identity (cumulative) for unrelated individuals (P (ID) ) and siblings (P (ID)sib ) for multiplex 1 (seven loci; used for screening, individual and species identification) in jaguars (n = 65), pumas (n = 54) and ocelots (n = 30). DNA was isolated from faecal samples collected across several study sites in Belize. P (ID)sib < 0.010 was used as criterion for individual identification.

[SECTION] discussion
Selection and performance of cross-species microsatellite loci
Microsatellites represent a powerful type of neutral genetic marker commonly used to answer a variety of population genetic and ecological questions (e.g. Sunnucks 2000; Selkoe & Toonen 2006;Wang 2011;Allendorf et al. 2013). Due to many conservation challenges, species of concern often are studied in a comparative way and cross-species microsatellites have been identified for several different taxa (e.g. Barbara et al. 2007). We successfully cross-amplified 20 published microsatellite loci developed for the domestic cat in three Neotropical feline species. We conducted thorough screening of all loci tested and selected 14 polymorphic markers, which efficiently and reliably identified species and individuals from field-collected, faecal DNA samples of three felid species with highly variable DNA quality and quantity.
Proper selection of genetic markers is crucial because it impacts all subsequent population genetic analyses (e.g. Taberlet & Luikart 1999). To increase the cost efficiency of our study, we arranged the 14 loci in three multiplexes and configured multiplex 1 with 7 highly polymorphic loci, which were used for sample screening, and species and individual identification. Multiplexes 2 and 3 were developed to add additional loci for fine-scale genetic structure or parentage analyses not reported here and were only run for one sample per individual.
The genotyping performance of the microsatellite loci was tested based on several parameters including genetic variation, PCR amplification success, genotyping accuracy and genotyping error rates. Results of the current study suggest that the cross-species microsatellite set optimized here is an efficient and powerful tool for conservation genetic studies of multiple Neotropical felids. The high variability indicates the potential usefulness for examining genetic structure of the target species. Although we conducted this study in tropical Belize and included all faecal samples detected by the scat detector dog (n = 1053), many of which were highly degraded, our analysis showed medium to high mean PCR amplification success rates using nuclear loci (61% AE 12.4, SD) compared with other studies of Neotropical felids with

[SECTION] species and individual identification
Recent studies of Neotropical felids suggested that techniques for individual identification of faecal samples need further improvement in field and laboratory techniques (e.g. Michalski et al. 2011). We addressed this by optimizing a powerful set of cross-species microsatellite loci, which can be used reliably for species and individual identification of co-occurring jaguars, pumas and ocelots based on field-collected faecal samples. In total, we collected 1053 scat samples from the wild and successfully genotyped 49% of the scats to the species level and individual level. We used probability of identity estimates to assess statistical confidence for individual identification with P (ID)sib < 0.010 as the deciding criterion (Mills et al. 2000;Waits et al. 2001). The discriminatory power of the probability of identity estimates for this primer set was high, which indicates a strong resolving power between individuals, even when close relatedness among study animals may be an issue.
To increase the efficiency of this study, we used the same nuclear markers to identify species by examining species-specific alleles and applying Bayesian clustering analysis to verify species assignment. The application of species-specific alleles for species identification of faecal samples collected in the field has been mainly used for wildlife forensics to differentiate between several big cats (e.g. Singh et al. 2004) or to detect hybridization between two wild feline species (bobcat and lynx; Schwartz et al. 2004). Here, we demonstrated the potential of this approach for individual-based monitoring of multiple wild felid species on a local geographic scale; however, before application in other areas, it will be important to verify that these alleles remain species-specific. Besides species identification, cross-species microsatellite loci have a wide application and are especially useful when several closely related species at risk need to be managed and conserved simultaneously. Nonetheless, limitations of this approach (e.g. Barbara et al. 2007) need to be considered.
In conclusion, we strongly encourage the development of rigorous field and laboratory protocols especially for noninvasive genetic studies conducted in tropical environments hostile to DNA samples. The combination of the most informative markers and the assessment of locus-specific success and error rates both within and among three target species helped to optimize a set of polymorphic nuclear primers, which improved our ability to efficiently and accurately identify genotypes (at the species and individual level) from often highly degraded scat samples. Additionally, using a microsatellite marker set that amplifies across species represents an efficient and powerful way to study multiple co-occurring species on both the individual and population levels, and simultaneously to evaluate the conservation status (demographics, genetic diversity and connectivity) of potentially threatened species.

[SECTION] title
An evaluation of hair-snaring devices for small-bodied carnivores in southwest China

[SECTION] abstract
Human population growth is a major threat to the biodiversity of mammals in China. Rapid development of infrastructure, pollution, and poor enforcement of environmental laws in China have altered the landscape and accelerated the extinction rates of mammals. To maintain biodiversity and conserve the mammals of China, it is essential to develop monitoring protocols for species of concern that are efficient, cost-effective, and current. It is now common practice for ecologists to survey mammals of interest using noninvasive sampling methods. These sampling techniques are affordable, require no handling of the target animals, and generally yield large samples. In China, such sampling methods have rarely been used and evaluated. For this study, we recorded the behavior of masked palm civets (Paguma larvata) and Siberian weasels (Mustela sibirica) to determine their relative preference for using different hair-snaring devices and evaluated the effectiveness of each device at collecting hair. Our goal was to determine which genetic sampling method(s) should be used to study masked palm civets and Siberian weasels in the future in Southwest China. In March-June of 2014, we monitored 13 hair-snare stations throughout the Main Valley of Laohegou Nature Reserve, Sichuan Province, China. Genetic analysis revealed that we collected 373 hair samples from civets and 47 hair samples from weasels over 104 and 26 sessions, respectively. Both civets and weasels seemed to prefer lure sticks to ground cubbies; however, the latter were more effective at collecting civet hair. Although glue sheets from lure sticks collected large samples of guard hair (> 10), no device in its current design was consistently effective at collecting weasel hair. We suggest researchers in Southwest China use ground cubbies as described in this study to collect hair from masked palm civets and test other cubby designs (e.g., longer gun brushes or smaller in size) for collecting hair from Siberian weasels.

[SECTION] 590
JOURNAL OF MAMMALOGY polluted the environment, reducing biodiversity throughout the country (Liu et al. 2003;Liu and Diamond 2005). For instance, according to Jiang et al. (2015), 178 of 673 species of mammals (~26%) are currently threatened in China. To maintain mammal biodiversity in China, natural resource managers must develop wildlife conservation programs and policy based on reliable information about the distribution and abundance of species.
Ecological monitoring is an important component of wildlife conservation (Nichols and Williams 2006). Other than giant pandas (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), few mammal species, including widely distributed small-bodied mammalian carnivores, have been monitored in China (Li et al. 2010). Some of the mammal monitoring programs that do exist (e.g., the national giant panda survey), however, use outdated sampling protocols (State Forestry Administration 2006;Garshelis et al. 2008), resulting in the development of conservation programs based on equivocal information. Similar to many developing regions of the world, it is essential to develop standardized sampling protocols for mammals of concern in China that are efficient, cost-effective, and current.
Many researchers use noninvasive genetic methods to sample rare and elusive mammals (Long et al. 2008). Unlike traditional sampling that relies on radiotracking, which is often expensive, time-consuming, and intrusive (because it requires capture and handling), noninvasive genetic sampling methods are affordable, efficient, and do not require handling the target animals (Weaver et al. 2005;Kelly et al. 2012). Moreover, genetic sampling can yield relatively large samples for rare or elusive mammal populations (Kelly et al. 2012).
Researchers often target the fur of mammals when conducting studies that rely on noninvasive genetic sampling (Kendall and McKelvey 2008). Hairs collected from hair-snaring devices provide investigators physical evidence of species presence, which is not generally subject to observer bias. In particular, researchers identify species by examining the morphological structure of hair (Lobert et al. 2001) or using genetic methods (Foran et al. 1997). Hair follicles can provide high quality DNA, especially when samples are large (e.g., > 10 hairs- Kelly et al. 2012;O'Mahony et al. 2015). Investigators commonly use microsatellite genotypes derived from DNA in hair follicles to estimate population abundance and density and to evaluate the growth rates, genetic diversity, gene flow, or social structure of populations (Waits and Paetkau 2005). Hair shafts are also useful to researchers as they contain other biochemical markers such as stable isotopes. Such ecological tracers are commonly used to estimate the proportional contributions of important resources to the diets of mammals (Phillips 2001;Hopkins and Ferguson 2012;Parnell et al. 2013;Phillips et al. 2014).
Hair collection methods are divided into baited and passive methods (Kendall and McKelvey 2008). Baited methods use scent lure and/or bait to attract animals to the hair-snaring devices (e.g., hair corrals, rub stations, lure sticks or posts, and cubbies), whereas passive methods include objects animals rub on instinctually (e.g., rub trees) or accidently (e.g., hairsnares that target travel routes- Kendall and McKelvey 2008).
Previous studies have evaluated the effectiveness of both baited (Weaver et al. 2005;Zielinski et al. 2006;Castro-Arellano et al. 2008;Pauli et al. 2008;Burki et al. 2010;Heurich et al. 2012) and passive methods (Clevenger and Sawaya 2010;Karamanlidis et al. 2010) for collecting hair from free-ranging mammalian carnivores. McDaniel et al. (2000) and Monterroso et al. (2011) compared the attractiveness of different scent lures for hair-snaring, while other studies compared genetic sampling methods to other noninvasive techniques (e.g., remote cameras, detection dogs, snow tracking) to determine the most appropriate method to use in future studies (Harrison 2006;Long et al. 2007;Ruell and Crooks 2007;Sawaya et al. 2011;Johnson et al. 2013).
Although several noninvasive genetic studies have used fecal material to study wildlife in China (Zhang et al. 2008;Zhang et al. 2009;Hu et al. 2010;Yang and Jiang 2011;Chang et al. 2014), no study to our knowledge has evaluated the relative success of different genetic sampling methods in China. For this study, we recorded the behavior of masked palm civets (Paguma larvata) and Siberian weasels (Mustela sibirica) to determine their relative preference for using different hair-snaring devices (lure sticks with barbed wire or glue sheets, and 1-and 2-door triangular ground cubbies) and evaluated the effectiveness of each device at collecting their hair in Laohegou Nature Reserve, Sichuan Province, China (Fig. 1). Although we recognized that remote cameras were effective at detecting a wide diversity of wildlife in our study area and other locations in Southwest China, including civets and weasels (Li et al. 2012), we focused our research efforts on testing potential devices used for genetic sampling of civets and weasels, as these species do not seem to have unique stripe patterns or spots that can be easily identified from photographs (O' Connell et al. 2011). We evaluated lure sticks and ground cubbies because they collected guard hair from civets and weasels in our study area (J. B. Hopkins, pers. obs.; Fig. 1) and from fishers (Martes pennanti; which have a similar body size as civets) in North America (Schwartz et al. 2006), respectively. We were interested in using lure sticks for future genetic sampling because, in addition to collecting hair for our target animals, giant pandas occasionally destroy ground cubbies (Fig. 2). The goal of our study was to determine the genetic sampling method(s) we should use in the future to estimate the occupancy rates, abundances, and diets (via stable isotopes from hair) of masked palm civets and Siberian weasels in Southwest China.

[SECTION] materials and methods
Study area.-Laohegou (Old Creek Valley) Nature Reserve (110 km 2 ; 32°30′N, 104°42′E) is located in the Minshan Mountains of Sichuan Province, China (Fig. 1). From 1975 to 1998, Laohegou was primarily used for harvesting timber by the local government. Following the national logging ban in 1998, Laohegou was converted to protected land under the auspices of the National Forest Protection Program (Li et al. 2012). In 2012, The Nature Conservancy China and the Sichuan Nature Conservation Foundation began the process of establishing Laohegou as the 1st Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/article/97/2/589/2459748 by SCD -UNIVERSITE DE TOURS user on 05 June 2025 land trust reserve in China (Huang et al. 2014). This study was part of a new effort to develop noninvasive genetic sampling methods for monitoring carnivores in the new nature reserve.
The landscape in Laohegou is steep (~40% of the reserve is steeper than 40°) and rugged-the exceptions being the valley bottoms and ridgelines. Elevation in Laohegou ranges from 1,160 m at the bottom of the Main Valley to 3,479 m at the summit of Motianling Mountain. Temperatures range from -4°C to 12°C and annual precipitation is 950-1,300 mm. The forest types along an elevational gradient include evergreen forest (< 1,800 m; mainly secondary forest because of past logging), deciduous forest (1,800-2,400 m; with patches of planted forest), conifer-deciduous mixed forest (2,400-2,800 m), coniferous forest (2,800-3,200 m), and alpine meadow (> 3,200 m). Bamboo is found at all elevations in the forest understory.
Our study area was restricted to the Main Valley in Laohegou (~70 km 2 ); a watershed that receives 15 separate drainages and is surrounded by mountain ridges (Fig. 1). Along the Main Valley outside Laohegou's boundaries, local people are primarily agriculturalists and some are pastoralists. Local people from the nearby Gaocun Township have historically used the Main Valley in Laohegou for harvesting wood for fuel, hunting animals and gathering plants for food, raising bees for honey, and collecting herbs for traditional Chinese medicine.
Laohegou is at the north edge of a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China (Brooks et al. 2006). Using remote cameras, Li et al. (2012) detected 9 species of mammalian carnivores and 7 species of ungulates, including giant pandas, Asiatic black bears (Ursus thibetanus), Asian golden cats (Catopuma temminckii), leopard cats (Prionailurus bengalensis), masked palm civets, yellow-throated martens (Martes flavigula), Siberian weasels, Chinese ferret badgers (Melogale moschata), hog badgers (Arctonyx collaris), wild boar (Sus scrofa), forest musk deer (Moschus berezovskii), tufted deer (Elaphodus cephalophus), Reeve's muntjac (Muntiacus reevesi), takin (Budorcas taxicolor), Chinese serow (Capricornis milneedwardsii), and Chinese goral (Naemorhedus griseus). Although Li et al. (2012) did not identify rodents by species, Wang et al. (2003) identified 21 species to the northeast in Tangjiahe National Nature Reserve.
Hair-snaring devices.-We recorded the behavior of our target species to determine their relative preferences for using 4 types of hair-snaring devices and evaluated the effectiveness of each device at collecting their hair. Hereafter, we refer to devices generally as lure "sticks" or ground "cubbies". We evaluated 1-door and 2-door cubbies and refer to sticks with barbed wire as "barbed-sticks" and those with glue sheets as "sticky-sticks" (Fig. 3). We cut each stick to 130 × 5 × 5 cm and pounded each into the ground (30 cm). For barbed-sticks, we wrapped barbed wire with 6 barbs around the upper half  of the stick (Fig. 3). For sticky-sticks, we evenly spaced and fastened 6 glue-impregnated cardboard sheets designed to trap mice (5 × 2.5 cm; Catchmaster, Atlantic Paste & Glue Co., Brooklyn, New York) to the upper half of the stick using thumbtacks (Fig. 3). We constructed ground cubbies out of plastic (Guangyu Packaging Material Co., Ltd., Zhongshan, China) in a similar fashion as those specified in Schwartz et al. (2006), except 1-door cubbies had 3 gun brushes rather than 6 (Fig. 3). We used 8-cm gun brushes (diameter = 0.8 cm; Aolei Brushmaking Factory, Shanghai, China) for all cubbies, reducing the possibility of a weasel entering the trap and not touching a gun brush. We fastened each cubby to the ground using bamboo stakes.
We baited each device with a chicken wing and scent lure (Carman's Magna-Glan Lure, Russ Carman, New Milford, Pennsylvania). We nailed 1 chicken wing to the top of each stick and applied scent lure to the edge of a sponge (with reinforced top) that acted as a spacer between the stick and the chicken wing (Fig. 3). It is important to note that sponge spacers were used to retain the scent, while reducing the possibility of the lure contaminating hair samples and the top of the wood stick. We also fastened 1 chicken wing to the inside, center of each cubby using a strand of bailing wire and applied scent lure to the tip of a small branch of bamboo jammed into the ground next to each cubby.
Sampling.-In March-June of 2014, we monitored 13 sets of devices (hereafter, stations) at locations where we had previously detected civets and weasels via remote cameras in the Main Valley (Fig. 1). At each station, we installed 3 devices (both stick types and a 2-door cubby) in a triangular array on flat ground along game trails (Fig. 3). Half way through the experiment, we installed a 1-door cubby at 5 stations where animals had visited (Fig. 3). We positioned all devices 1-m apart to ensure that animals would not climb or jump from 1 device to another, guaranteeing passage over the barbs, gun brushes, or glue sheets before feeding on the bait. We used 2 different infrared-triggered remote cameras (one at each station) to detect animals and to examine their behavior: RECONYX PC 900 (RECONYX, Inc., Holmen, Wisconsin), which were set to take 10 pictures after each trigger without delay; and Ltl-6210MC (Ltl Acorn Electronics Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China), which were set to take 3 pictures and 12 s of video after each trigger without delay.
We attempted to visit each station every 4 days to collect hair samples, re-bait sticks and cubbies, and replace memory cards and batteries. We collected hair samples from barbs in the field by removing each hair sample using forceps and sterilizing each barb with a lighter. If we collected hair samples on glue sheets or gun brushes, we first removed each unit, replaced it, and then inserted each sample into a separate coin envelope for transport. In the laboratory, we used forceps to disentangle hairs from gun brushes. We sterilized forceps (before handling each hair sample and after hair was removed from gun brushes) in the lab by the flame of an alcohol lamp to avoid DNA contamination. We stored all envelopes in a sealed glass jar with desiccant until genetic analysis was conducted at Peking University.
Genetic analysis.-We attempted to identify the species of each hair sample using genetic analysis. Our genetics laboratory team was "blind" to the information recorded by remote cameras (i.e., species ID) and to the geographic location of the station from which the hair was collected. Preliminary experiments indicated that we could obtain sufficient DNA from 5 guard hair follicles; therefore, we clipped 5 guard hair roots and extracted DNA from each sample with Trans Direct Animal Tissue PCR Kit (TransGen Biotech Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). If < 5 guard hairs with follicles were present in the sample, we used what follicles were available. We incubated hairs at 55°C in 30 μl AD1 and 5 μl AD2 of lysis buffer for 20 min; inactivated at 95°C for 3 min on a H 2 O 3 -PRO drybath (Coyote Bioscience, Inc., Beijing, China); added 30 μl AD3 buffer; and stored in -20°C. For species identification, we amplified a fragment of 16S rRNA gene (ca. 380 bp in length) using the primers 16s-F: 5′-GAGAAGACCCTATGGAGC-3′ and 16s-R: 5′-ATAGAAACCGACCTGGAT-3′; as determined during this study, this fragment unambiguously assigned all known mammalian species in the study area.
We performed the PCR amplification (with a Thermo Thermal Cycler; Type: 5020) in 20 μl of reaction mixture: 1 μl genomic DNA, 1 μl of each primer (10 μmol/l), 2 μl of dNTPs (2.5 mmol/l), 2 μl of 10× EasyTaq buffer (Mg 2+ plus), 1 μl of EasyTaq polymerase (5 U/μl, TransGen), and 12 μl of ddH 2 O. We denatured the amplification conditions at 94°C for 3 min; conducted 35 cycles of denaturing at 94°C for 30 s; annealed at 55°C for 30s; and conducted extension and final extension at 72°C for 20 s and at 72°C for 10 min, respectively. We checked the PCR products on 1% agarose gel and then sequenced on an ABI PRISM 3730 Genetic Analyzer from both directions with the same primers for PCR amplification. We obtained sequences for identifying species (P. larvata: KP233214.1; M. sibirica: NC_020637.1; Niviventer confucianus: NC_023960.1) with BLAST in GenBank.
Analytical procedures.-We measured the relative preference each species had for the devices using photos and videos recorded by remote cameras. We also measured the relative effectiveness of devices by evaluating the ability of each device at collecting guard hair from each species. We defined a "session" as the time period between our visits to a station. We defined each "detection" as a positive identification of a species from a photo or from DNA derived from hair.
We used 2 statistical methods to evaluate the relative preference of devices for each species. An animal "visited" a certain device when an individual climbed a lure stick or entered a cubby (Fig. 3; Supporting Information S1). As determined by remote cameras, we assessed the relative preference animals have for devices by recording the number of sessions each device was visited first and the total number of recorded visits at each type of device. We used a set of chi-square tests to determine if the number of first visits for each species were different than expected among devices for each configuration and between sticks and cubbies at 4-device stations. We used a Kruskal-Wallis test to determine if average number of visits per session for each species at 4-device stations were different among devices, and Mann-Whitney U-tests to compare the average number of visits between sticks and cubbies, between the 2 types of cubbies, and between the 2 types of sticks.
We used 3 analyses to evaluate the effectiveness of each device at collecting guard hair. We restricted our analyses to guard hair because follicles from guard hair generally contain higher quality DNA than underfur (Paetkau 2003). We defined a "hair sample" as all hairs collected from a single barb, glue sheet, or gun brush during a single session. We assigned each hair sample to 1 of 3 groups according to the number of guard hairs (1-5, 6-10, > 10) collected in each sample. We grouped hairs as such because we found that 5 hair follicles was an optimum sample size for identifying a species via genetic analysis of a hair sample. In addition, because genotyping success for individual identification is typically higher for carnivores when samples consist of 10 hairs or more (Goossens et al. 1998; O' Mahony et al. 2015), and pilot work has shown that hair samples for civets and weasels are either very large (much greater than 10 hairs) or small (≤ 5), we decided to categorize samples by size when collected, aiming to pay particular attention to samples with > 10 guard hairs.
For the first 2 analyses, we compared the average number of hair samples collected at each device and the average number of hair samples with > 10 guard hairs. We constrained these analyses to sessions when devices either collected hair or collected hair with > 10 guard hairs. We used a Kruskal-Wallis test to determine if devices collected similar numbers of hair samples (both total number of samples and samples with > 10 guard hairs) per session. We then used Mann-Whitney U-tests to compare the average number of hair samples collected per session between sticks and cubbies, between the 2 types of cubbies, between the 2 types of sticks, and to conduct pairwise comparisons of devices that collected > 10 guard hairs. For our final analysis, we compared the detection rates of all devices, including cameras. We defined the detection rate of a device as the number of sessions a species was detected by a device by the total number of sessions the species was detected by all devices.
We used R (R Core Team 2015) to conduct all statistical analyses. We used the aforementioned statistical analyses and a qualitative assessment of photos and videos to determine which methods were "best" for future genetic sampling of civets and weasels in Southwest China. Even though we set α = 0.05, we note that rejecting or failing to reject the null based on P values was not the goal of most comparisons. Instead, we were more interested in using these results (e.g., from comparing means) to help inform our decision as to what methods were best to use in our future studies.

[SECTION] results
We conducted our survey from 10 March to 16 June of 2014 (170 sessions, 713 trap-nights; Supporting Information S2). We evaluated 3-device stations over 107 sessions and 4-device stations (which includes a 1-door cubby) over 63 sessions. We visited each station every 4.2 ± 1.8 days. We photographed 4 carnivores (leopard cat, masked palm civet, Siberian weasel, and hog badger), 3 ungulates (Reeve's muntjac, tufted deer, Chinese goral), and several rodent species. We collected 536 hair samples, but lost 15 of the samples collected by the stickysticks during transport from the field (n = 521; Supporting Information S2). We identified 81% of the hair samples (n = 424) to species using genetic analysis and failed to identify 97 samples due to inadequate amounts of DNA (n = 65) or extraction (n = 10) or sequencing (n = 22) failure. Of these 97 samples, 75% (n = 73) are samples with 1-5 guard hairs, 2% (n = 2) with 6-10 guard hairs, and 23% (n = 22) with > 10 guard hairs.
We identified 3 species of mammals using genetic analysis: masked palm civet (88%, n = 373), Siberian weasel (11%, n = 47), and Chinese white-bellied rat (1%, n = 4; N. confucianus). We detected at least 1 civet or weasel during 131 of 170 (77%) sessions using remote cameras or genetic identification and detected both civet and weasel at 7 stations during 36 (21%) sessions. We detected civets during 117 (69%) sessions (10 stations) and weasels during 51 (30%) sessions (7 stations; Table 1). We also detected hog badgers by remote camera during 7 (4%) sessions at 5 stations and leopard cats during 3 (2%) sessions at 3 stations.
Animal preference for devices.-Our remote cameras photographed civets and weasels during 112 and 49 sessions (96% of all sessions for each species), respectively (Table 1). We recorded the number of first visits in 53 (3-device) and 51 (4-device) sessions for civets and in 17 (3-device) and 25 (4-device) sessions for weasels (Table 2). We found that both civets (χ 2 = 27.824, d.f. = 3, P < 0.001) and weasels (χ 2 = 10.04, d.f. = 3, P = 0.018) visited devices first at different frequencies at 4-device stations, but this was not the case for 3-device stations (civets: χ 2 = 2.868, d.f. = 2, P = 0.238; weasels: χ 2 = 0.118, d.f. = 2, P = 0.943; Table 2). We also found that each species first visited sticks and cubbies at different frequencies when present at stations (civets: χ 2 = 18.843, d.f. = 1, P < 0.001; weasels: χ 2 = 4.84, d.f. = 1, P = 0.028). Based on chi-square results as well as photographs and video of both species, it is likely that sticks were visited more often than cubbies on the first occasion (Table 2).
We found that the number of visits by each species during each session were likely different at both device configurations (Table 3). We found that civets visited devices at different frequencies at 3-device (χ 2 = 17.162, d.f. = 2, P < 0.001) and 4-device stations (χ 2 = 11.898, d.f. = 3, P = 0.008); this may also be true for weasels (3-device: χ 2 = 5.017, d.f. = 2, P = 0.081; 4-device: χ 2 = 7.320, d.f. = 3, P = 0.062; Table 3). We found that both civets and weasels visited sticks more frequently than cubbies (civets: U 97,37 = 2375.5, P = 0.002; weasels: U 44,27 = 792.5, P = 0.010). We also learned that civets and weasels visited both 1-and 2-door cubbies (civets: U 20,17 = 217.5, P = 0.090; weasels: U 15,12 = 87.5, P = 0.899) and the 2 kinds of lure sticks at similar frequencies (civets: U 49,48 = 1160, P = 0.907; weasels: U 23,21 = 204, P = 0.361).
Device effectiveness.-All hair samples (n = 521) had at least 1 guard hair. As validated by genetic analysis, we collected 373 hair samples from civets and 47 hair samples from weasels over 104 and 26 sessions, respectively. We did not collect any hair samples during 46 of the 170 (27%) sessions. Two-door cubbies collected 282 hair samples in 106 sessions (X = 2.7, mode = 3) and 1-door cubbies collected 131 hair samples in 56 sessions (X = 2.3, mode = 3; Supporting Information S2). Sticky-sticks and barbed-sticks collected 84 and 24 hair samples in 46 (X = 1.8, mode = 1) and 16 (X = 1.5, mode = 1) sessions, respectively (Supporting Information S2). We found that devices did not collect the same number of hair samples (χ 2 = 14.736, d.f. = 3, P = 0.002; Fig. 4). We learned that ground cubbies collected more hair samples than lure sticks per session (U 162,62 = 3387, P < 0.001), whereas the 2 types of ground cubbies likely collected a similar number of samples per session (U 106,56 = 3223.5, P = 0.343) and sticky-sticks collected more hair samples than barbed-sticks (U 46,16 = 204, P = 0.005).
Of the 521 samples collected, 41% had > 10 guard hairs, 15% had 6-10 guard hairs, and 44% had ≤ 5 guard Table 1.-Number of detections and detection rates for each hair-snaring device that detected masked palm civets (Paguma larvata) and Siberian weasels (Mustela sibirica) at the Laohegou Nature Reserve in the Sichuan Province of China, 2014. We calculated the detection rate of a device as the number of sessions a species was detected by a particular device by the total sessions the species was detected by all devices. We note that civets and weasels were detected during 63 and 30 sessions at 4-device stations (which include 1-door cubbies), respectively; therefore, totals for 1-door cubbies (49 for civets and 3 for weasels) were divided by these values, not the values listed under total detections in the table.   4). Two-door cubbies collected the most hair samples with > 10 guard hairs, whereas barbed-sticks collected the fewest (Table 4). We found that devices did not collect the same number of hair samples with > 10 guard hairs (χ 2 = 10.390, d.f. = 3, P = 0.016; Table 4). We learned that barbed-sticks likely collected less hair samples with > 10 guard hairs than other devices per session (barbed-sticks versus sticky-sticks: U 21,10 = 45, P = 0.004; barbed-sticks versus 1-door cubbies: U 36,10 = 120, P = 0.039; barbed-stick versus 2-door cubbies: U 70,10 = 210, P = 0.016), whereas sticky-sticks may have performed better than 1-door cubbies (U 36,21 = 484.5, P = 0.048) and similarly to 2-door cubbies (U 70,21 = 883, P = 0.120). We found that both cubby devices collected a similar number of large guard hair samples (U 70,36 = 1359, P = 0.445; Table 4).
Not surprisingly, we found that remote cameras were most effective at detecting both civets and weasels (Table 1). We found that both types of ground cubbies were more effective at collecting more guard hair samples from civets, whereas sticky-sticks performed better than other devices at collecting guard hair from weasels; although detection rates were low (Table 1). In contrast, barbed-sticks were ineffective at collecting guard hair from both species, and neither stickysticks nor cubbies were particularly effective at collecting hair from civets and weasels, respectively (Fig. 4; Supporting Information S2).

[SECTION] discussion
We recorded the behavior of masked palm civets and Siberian weasels to determine their relative preference for using 4 different types of hair-snaring devices and evaluated the effectiveness of each device at collecting guard hairs from each species. We found that 1) both civets and weasels may have preferred to use lure sticks over cubbies, 2) both types of cubbies were effective at collecting guard hair from civets, and 3) cubbies, in their current design, need to be modified to collect hair from weasels.
We found that both civets and weasels preferred to climb lure sticks before entering ground cubbies (Table 2). These results may be indicative of their natural behaviors. In China and elsewhere, masked palm civets are semiarboreal, often foraging for fruit in trees (Zhou et al. 2008), whereas Siberian weasels feed on rodents, birds, fruits, and pine nuts (Wu 1999;Smith et al. 2010;Chiang et al. 2012). It is reasonable to speculate that climbing sticks to feed on bait may be less dangerous and more intuitive than entering cubbies for civets and weasels; however, we note that weasels tend to burrow for shelter and to prey on rodents (King et al. 2007b), making smaller cubbies potentially more attractive, especially if they were positioned in fallen logs or under woody debris.
Civets visited sticks more often than cubbies (Table 3). Because we are currently not capable of identifying individual civets using genetic analysis, it is unknown whether a single animal or multiple animals used the sticks when detected on multiple occasions during a single session. Although multiple visits by the same individual during a session would potentially increase the opportunity to obtain an individual identification via genetic analysis, visits by different individuals during a single session could lead to genetic cross-contamination. In particular, if multiple individuals left hair on a single barb, there would be risk of pooling alleles from more than 1 individual. To eliminate the potential of genetic cross-contamination in future studies, researchers could limit DNA extraction to 1 hair per sample; however, this strategy would increase amplification error rates (Pauli et al. 2008). Alternatively, researchers could use baited cubbies, as they generally received 1 visit from a civet each session, or design a single-sample monitoring device used to collect hair from small-bodied carnivores (e.g., Pauli et al. 2008).
Although we found that cubbies are less attractive than sticks to civets and weasels, cubbies are effective at collecting guard hair samples from civets (Table 4; Fig. 4; Supporting Information S2). Based on the examination of videos from  remote cameras, it seems civets do not generally pass through a 2-door cubby from end to end; instead, they typically enter 1 entrance to feed on the bait and exit the same door by backing out (Supporting Information S1). We found that 1-and 2-door cubbies may have collected a similar number of samples with > 10 guard hairs per session (Table 4), suggesting that 1-door cubbies are likely a more efficient and cost-effective device because they have half the number of collection units (i.e., 3 gun brushes versus 6 gun brushes, 6 barbs, or 6 glue sheets).
It is likely that weasels (220-420 mm; 0.5-1.2 kg) leave less hair in cubbies than civets (400-690 mm; 3-7 kg) because of their small body size (Smith et al. 2010). Based on photographs and videos, it is likely that weasels squeezed their bodies between the gun brushes and either passed directly through to the other side of the cubby or turned around in the center of the cubby and exited the same way they entered. Based on video footage, we assume that few hairs are collected from weasels because they do not back out of the trap after eating the bait and there is little contact between their body and the gun brushes. Longer gun brushes or smaller cubbies could remedy this problem by narrowing the space in the device, thereby forcing weasels to back out like civets.
Cubbies detected civets more often than other hair-snaring devices (Table 1). One-and 2-door cubbies collected hair from civets during most of the instances in which civets were known to be present at a station (Table 1). In contrast, sticks rarely detected the presence of civets via DNA when detected by cameras (Table 1). Sticky-sticks collected more hair than barbedsticks, which rarely collected hair samples (Table 4; Fig. 4; Supporting Information S2). Although detection rates were low, we found that sticky-sticks were the most effective device for collecting hair from weasels (Table 1; Supporting Information S2) and glue sheets were effective at collecting large samples of guard hair from both civets and weasels when they collected hair (Table 4). Similar to other studies that use glue sheets to collect hair (Foran et al. 1997;Zielinski et al. 2006;J. B. Hopkins, pers. obs.), our results suggest that glue sheets are effective at collecting hair from small carnivores if they remain fastened to the sampling device. In some instances, we found that glue sheets were damaged, missing from the device, or stuck to animals (from photos). When exposed to moisture and/ or sunlight for long periods, glue sheets can become less sticky. Mowat and Paetkau (2002) found that snow, and especially rain, soften the paper backing on glue sheets, rendering them useless in some instances. As suggested by Kendall and McKelvey (2008), we recommend the use of glue sheets with a plastic backing. We also note that exposure to moisture and/or sunlight can cause DNA degradation in hair follicles, significantly reducing genotyping success rates (Stetz et al. 2014). To reduce exposure to moisture and sunlight, Zielinski et al. (2006) used a ground cubby with glue sheets, whereas Foran et al. (1997) and Mowat and Paetkau (2002) used wooden 1-door tubes mounted on trees (with the opening facing down). If using glue sheets, we suggest that researchers customize ground cubbies (triangle or tube) according to the body size of the target species; such devices could yield excellent results in Southwest China.
All hair-snaring devices used in this study were inexpensive, lightweight, portable, and easy to install under a variety of conditions. Automated (King et al. 2007a) or single-sample devices (Pauli et al. 2008) do not meet the same criteria of low cost and ease of transport. In general, sticks are easier to use because they can be made out of wood. Plastic sheets for cubbies and gun brushes can be bought (see known manufactures in China in "Methods") and transported to study areas in rural China. Two-door cubbies provide more opportunities to collect hair but at a higher cost when compared to 1-door cubbies. We calculated the cost of a 2-door cubby at 60 RMB (~$10 USD), which includes a plastic sheet, 6 wire brushes, 6 nuts and bolts, and scent lure. The cost of sticks was much lower (20 RMB or ~$3 USD). When compared to gun brushes, glue sheets are also effective at collecting large guard hair samples (> 10 hairs; Table 4) but are more challenging to handle when installing and removing them from the device. In addition, removing and cleaning hairs from glue sheets can require a xylene wash (Foran et al. 1997), which can be a tedious and hazardous process.
We recommend the use of both remote cameras and cubbies for future population studies of masked palm civets and Siberian weasels in Southwest China and potentially elsewhere. Remote cameras had the highest detection rates for both civets and weasels. In fact, it was rare when devices collected hair but photographs were not taken for civets and weasels (Table 1). Because remote cameras require minimal labor and provide a variety of information, including confirmation of the species presence at a certain time (Long et al. 2008), we suggest researchers use cameras for biodiversity surveys in China and include them if possible for genetic surveys. Our focus in this study, however, was the use of hair-snares for genetic sampling. Our ultimate goal is to estimate population parameters and diets of the small-bodied carnivores in Southwest China using genetic and stable isotope analyses of hair; this cannot be accomplished using remote cameras alone. Although ground cubbies were very effective at collecting guard hair from civets, they were not effective at collecting hair from weasels. We suggest researchers test the effectiveness of cubbies that are smaller in size (with and without glue sheets) or use longer gun brushes, constraining weasels to a more confined space in the cubbies. Unfortunately, we were limited in our ability to use tree cubbies like Foran et al. (1997) and Mowat and Paetkau (2002) because trees are generally small and not uniformly available in Laohegou. It is possible, however, that trees can be used to accommodate cubbies at other study areas in Southwest China. Using tree cubbies would likely reduce the potential of giant pandas (Fig. 2) or Asiatic black bears damaging devices along game trails. Regardless of the sampling devices that researchers decide to use to collect hair from small-bodied carnivores in Southwest China, we hope this study motivates researchers to use noninvasive methods to sample mammals of concern in China.
