[SECTION] title
A comparative study of the fecal characters of Japanese serow (Capricornis crispus) and sika deer (Cervus nippon)

[SECTION] abstract
The fecal pellets and fecal pellet group characters of two ungulates, the Japanese serow and sika deer, were compared in Tokushima, Japan, where the species occur sympatrically. Species identification based on 82 fecal DNA samples revealed that 28 and 54 fecal pellet groups were from Japanese serow and sika deer, respectively. The mean values of three fecal pellet groups characters, the maximum diameter, the proportion of adherence of fecal pellets (maximum number of adhering pellets/total pellet number), and pellet number, were significantly different between the two species. These values reflect the differences in their defecation behaviors, and piled fecal pellet groups of Japanese serow can be clearly distinguished from those of sika deer. A stepwise discriminant analysis selected only one fecal pellet group character, the proportion of adherence of fecal pellets, and provided the highest correct classification rate (82.1% for Japanese serow and 88.9% for sika deer). The proportion of adherence of fecal pellets is an important parameter for discriminating between Japanese serow and sika deer on field surveys.

[SECTION] (no title)
Quantification of fecal pellet groups is the most widely used index to estimate the population size and density of ungulates (Mayle et al. 1999). However, in habitats where several ungulate species coexist, accurate identification of the species producing the fecal pellets is most important, as misidentification of species often results in overestimation of the density of a target species (Theuerkauf et al. 2008). Many studies have successfully identified species by the deposition features of ungulates, such as the sizes (Russo and Olhausen 1987;Chame 2003;Chapman 2004) and defecation rate (Chapman 2004;Abaturov et al. 2008). However, distinguishing the feces of some ungulate species can be difficult because the size and the amount of feces produced by each individual varies with age, body size, and seasons (Mitchell and McCowan 1984;Rogers 1987;Chame 2003). Therefore, for visually indistinguishable species, the pH of feces and noninvasive fecal DNA have been used for discrimination (Elliott and Longhurst 1984;Kurose et al. 2005;Sugimoto et al. 2006;Kim et al. 2008;Yamashiro et al. 2010).
Two large ungulate species, the Japanese serow (Capricornis crispus) and sika deer (Cervus nippon), inhabit in Japan. In the past, these species have been generally allopatric, but in recent years, their distributions have begun to overlap due to an increase in the sika deer population (Tokida 2008). The population sizes and densities of these two species have been assessed using fecal pellet counts or fecal pellet group counts. Thus, the identification of fecal pellet groups between these two species is extremely important. Takatsuki et al. (1981) revealed that the Japanese serow deposits a larger number of feces than the sika deer from the observation of captive animals. Based on their findings, most field monitoring of the Japanese serow uses the criteria "a fecal pellet group of more than 200 pellets as being from the Japanese serow" (The Agency for Cultural Affairs-Japan 1994).
The Japanese serow was promoted to "special national monument" status in 1955, and population trends and habitat conditions have been monitored since 1985. As usual, in each protected area, two survey programs are conducted (a primary survey program every 6 or 7 years by specialists, and a supplemental survey program annually by local volunteers). The misidentification of Japanese serow and sika deer feces in supplemental survey programs has been pointed out (Tokushima and Kochi Prefectures Board of Education 1996) because of limits to each volunteer's ability to collect precise data. Therefore, we developed an identification method for the two species based on fecal DNA sampling (Yamashiro et al. 2010). We demonstrated that 41.4% of the sika deer's fecal pellet groups were misidentified as those of the Japanese serow by local volunteers (supplemental survey in Tokushima Prefecture in 2008; Yamashiro et al. 2010). Genetic analysis using noninvasive sampling is effective for monitoring the Japanese serow. However, application of the DNA-based species identification method to all fecal samples is unrealistic because genetic analyses are time-consuming and costly. Therefore, we need to develop a more convenient method that is applicable to field surveys. To the best of our knowledge, morphological differences between fecal pellet groups of Japanese serow and sika deer have not yet been studied quantitatively under natural conditions. The features of fecal pellet groups in the wild may be different from those of captive animals. Therefore, we should construct more morphologically precise identification criteria of the Japanese serow's fecal pellets under natural conditions.
In the present study, we identified fecal pellet groups of two species, the Japanese serow and sika deer, using DNA markers and investigated whether the two species can be differentiated based on fecal morphology.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] study site and fecal sampling
The study was conducted on Mt. Yatsurasan and Mt. Maruzasa in Tokushima Prefecture, Shikoku, Japan. In October 2011, we placed three quadrats (100 × 100 m) at altitudes of about 700 m on Mt. Yatsurasan (sites 1-3), and one quadrat at an altitude of approximately 1,400 m on Mt. Maruzasa (site 4). Within the quadrats, we selected all fresh fecal samples without distinguishing between Japanese serow and sika deer and measured the maximum diameter of each fecal pellet group (PG-MD). After photographing the fecal pellet groups, 10 pellets from each pellet group were preserved in a 15-ml tube with 99% ethanol, and all remaining fecal pellets were collected in a nylon bag.

[SECTION] genetic analysis
Fecal DNA was extracted following the method of Zhang et al. (2006). We identified the Japanese serow and sika deer using PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism (PCR-RFLPs) of the mitochondrial cytochrome b (Cyt b) gene developed previously by Yamashiro et al. (2010).

[SECTION] morphological analysis of feces
We counted the pellet number (PN) in each pellet  Seven fecal pellet measurements were made according to criteria set out by Àlvarez (1994); total length (TOL), maximum body diameter of the pellet body measured at the midpoint of TOL (MAB), maximum length from the point of body inflexion with the tip to the middle of the base (BL), maximum diameter measured 2 mm from the most extruding point of the base along the longitudinal axis of the pellet (MAD), MAB/TOL, and MAD/TOL (Fig. 1).
To examine the degree of aggregation of the fecal pellets, we calculated the proportion of adherence of fecal pellets per total number of pellets (PG-AD) using photographs of the feces (Fig. 2). After counting the maximum pellet number adhering to each other within one pellet group, we calculated the ratio of adhering pellets for the entire sample of pellets (maximum number of adhering pellets/total pellet number).

[SECTION] statistical analysis
For the seven fecal pellet measurements (TOL, MAB, BL, MAD, MAB/TOL, MAD/TOL, and BL/TOL) and three fecal pellet group characters (PG-MD, PG-AD, and PN), the difference between the Japanese serow and sika deer was examined by Student's t test (StatView, version 5.0; SAS Institute, Cary, NC). A stepwise discriminant analysis on seven fecal pellet measurements and three fecal pellet group characters were used to determine the best combination of variables that would separate the two species. The program were performed using Excel-Tokei 2010 (Social Survey Research Information Co., Ltd.).

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] species identification of the fecal pellet groups based on pcr-rflps
In total, 88 fecal pellet groups were collected at four sites. We were able to amplify the Cyt b gene in 82 of 88 (93.1%) fecal samples. According to identification method based on PCR-RFLPs, 28 fecal pellet groups were from Japanese serow and 54 were from sika deer.

[SECTION] fecal morphology
Six fecal pellet shapes (A, D, E, G, H, and I) were found in Japanese serow and all 10 fecal pellet shapes (A-J) were found in sika deer (Table 1). More than two fecal pellet shapes were seen within one fecal pellet group of Japanese serow and sika deer.  The means ± SD of the seven fecal pellet measurements and three fecal pellet group characters of the two species are presented in Table 2. Four (MAB, MAD, MAB/TOL, and MAD/TOL) of seven fecal pellet measurements were significantly different between the two species (Table 2; P < 0.005), however, the ranges of these measurements overlapped. Ranges of PG-MD of the Japanese serow's fecal pellet groups and those of the sika deer were from 7.1 to 39.0 cm and from 15.4 to 303 cm, respectively. The mean of PG-MD was significantly different between Japanese serow and sika deer (24.0 ± 7.8 and 70.7 ± 71.0, respectively; Table 2; P < 0.001). The mean ± SD of PG-AD was 80.2 ± 27.2% in Japanese serow (ranging from 21.1% to 100%) and 18.7 ± 15.9% in sika deer (ranging from 2.0% to 79.6%), and these values were significantly different (Table 2; P < 0.001).
A significant difference was found in the mean ± SD of PN between Japanese serow and sika deer (261.7 ± 161.3 and 70.3 ± 36.0, respectively) (Table 2; P < 0.001), although values of PN varied widely between the two species (19-569 pellets and 11-175 pellets for Japanese serow and sika deer, respectively; Table 2). Figure 3 shows the distribution of pellet number within fecal pellet groups of the Japanese serow and sika deer found at four sites. In Japanese serow, 10 of 28 fecal pellet groups (35.7%) contained less than 200 pellets (Fig. 3).
A stepwise discriminant analysis selected only one fecal pellet group character (PG-AD). Percentages of correct classification with PG-AD were 82.1% (23 of 28 fecal pellet groups) for Japanese serow and 88.9% (48 of 54 fecal pellet groups) for sika deer (Table 3).

[SECTION] discussion
Generally, morphological characteristics of fecal pellets such as the size and shape have been used to identify ungulate species (Chame 2003). For red deer (Cervus elaphus) and fallow deer (Dama dama), fecal pellet morphologies can be used to identify species, sex, and age class (Àlvarez 1994). Here, we could not find unique fecal pellet shapes that could be used to discriminate between Japanese serow and sika deer. Moreover, the ranges of all seven fecal pellet measurements overlapped, although the feces of the Japanese serow were significantly narrower than those of the sika deer. Therefore, our results suggest that these species cannot be distinguished solely on the basis of fecal pellet shape and size.
From our results, the mean values of three fecal pellet group characters, PG-MD, PG-AD, and PN, significantly differed between Japanese serow and sika deer. These differences in fecal pellet group characters might be due to their differences in defecation behaviors. The Japanese serow tends to defecate by crouching in the same place, resulting in an aggregated fecal pellet group (piled feces) with a larger pellet number than sika deer (Morishita and Murakami 1979). In contrast, sika deer often defecate while walking, resulting in scattered fecal pellet groups (Morishita and Murakami 1979). Therefore, piled fecal pellet groups of Japanese serow may be distinguished from those of sika deer by three fecal pellet group characters (PG-MD, PG-AD, and PN). However, several ambiguous fecal pellet groups were found in the wild habitat (Fig. 3).
The pellet number (PN) has been considered as the most important index for discriminating between the two species (more than 200 pellets as being from the Japanese serow), from comparative study of pellet numbers between captive Japanese serow and sika deer (200-360 pellets in Japanese serow and 81-95 pellets in sika deer; Takatsuki et al. 1981). In the present study, our results also supported this index because PN of sika deer never exceeded 200. However, PN within one pellet group ranged widely from 19 to 569 and from 11 to 175 in Japanese serow and sika deer, respectively. To our knowledge, little available information exists on fecal pellet numbers of wild Japanese serow, although Morishita and Murakami (1979) reported that the fecal pellet number of Japanese serow in the wild ranged from 39 to 285 in Aomori Prefecture and from 8 to 2,047 in Ishikawa Prefecture. Defecation rates, decomposition periods, and pellet numbers of animals are often estimated from observations of captive individuals. However, these values have been noted to vary widely between wild individuals and captive ones (Rogers 1987) because the amount of feces produced by each individual varies with age, season, quality, and amount of ingested food, as well as its absorption capacity (Chame 2003;Tolleson et al. 2005). These wide variations in pellet number found in wild ungulates may be affected by the differences in the quantity and quality of available foods (Togari and Kunishige 2001;Chame 2003;Tolleson et al. 2005). If Japanese serow monitoring relies solely on the criterion of "more than 200 pellets," approximately 35.7% of fecal pellet groups will be misidentified, which will lead to an underestimation of Japanese serow density.
A stepwise discriminant analysis selected only one fecal pellet group character, PG-AD. From a stepwise discriminant analysis, five of 10 fecal pellet groups of Japanese serow consisting of less than 200 could be correctly identified. In the present study, an overall correct classification rate of 86.6% for Japanese serow and sika deer may be sufficiently high because an example of the classification rates of successfully identified species was 80.8% for red deer and 77.8% for fallow deer feces (Àlvarez 1994). PG-AD is an important parameter for discriminating between Japanese serow and sika deer on field surveys, however, high PG-AD were also found on six of 55 fecal pellet groups of sika deer. If more accurate distinction is required, fecal DNA analysis will help for identification of ambiguous fecal pellets groups.

[SECTION] title
Breaking down scats: degradation of DNA from greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) faecal pellets

[SECTION] abstract
Isolating DNA from scats (faeces) of threatened species is a valuable, non-invasive method for identifying individuals. To establish whether genotyping of greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) individuals from faecal pellets collected in the field can be useful for population monitoring, an understanding of the DNA degradation rates is necessary. To determine the relationship between time and degradation of bilby faecal DNA, and assess whether a two-step elution process during extraction results in better-quality DNA, faecal pellets were collected from captive individuals, maintained under seminatural conditions, then harvested at known periods. DNA was amplified from faecal pellets with a 99% success rate and error rates of less than 5% up to 14 days after deposition. The amplification rate decreases, and the rate of allelic dropout increases with time, but DNA can still be amplified at rates above 60% and error rates below 15% at 90-180 days. We found that a second elution step was unnecessary, with more DNA amplified over a longer period using the first eluate. Viable DNA exists on bilby faecal pellets for a long period after deposition, which is useful for obtaining genetic samples for population monitoring programs and studies on population genetics.

[SECTION] introduction
Utilising scats (faecal pellets) as opposed to sourcing tissue or blood for DNA samples has the benefit of reducing direct impacts to species being studied (Murphy et al. 2000;Piggott and Taylor 2003b;Vynne et al. 2012;Ramón-Laca et al. 2015). This is particularly useful in the case of threatened or rare species, of which many may be vulnerable to disturbance (e.g. Puechmaille and Petit 2007;Baldwin et al. 2010). Isolation of DNA from faeces has been successfully undertaken for several threatened species across a variety of environments, from snow leopards (Panthera uncia) in the alpine regions of Nepal (Karmacharya et al. 2011), to mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei) in the forests of Uganda (Nsubuga et al. 2004), and African elephants (Loxodonta africana africana) in savannah grasslands (Archie et al. 2003). Although it is now a well established method for identifying individuals (Ernest et al. 2000;Adams and Waits 2006;Brinkman et al. 2010a;Rodgers and Jane cka 2013), few studies have incorporated faecal DNA as a component of ongoing monitoring programs compared with direct sampling techniques, mainly due to the limitations associated with obtaining DNA from non-invasive samples (Waits and Paetkau 2005;Schwartz et al. 2007). More recently researchers have developed an increased awareness of the need to understand and evaluate the specific degradation rates of the faecal DNA of the target species to ensure the quality of genotyping approaches (Piggott 2004;Brinkman et al. 2010b;Panasci et al. 2011;DeMay et al. 2013;Woodruff et al. 2015).
Time has been found to have a significant effect on the amplification rates of faecal DNA. Murphy et al. (2007) analysed the effects of time on the degradation of DNA from brown bear (Ursus arctos) faeces and found that genotyping errors increased over time across different environmental conditions. Sample age, particularly 1-3 days since deposition, reduced the ability to amplify DNA. Santini et al. (2007) also found faecal DNA from wolves (Canis lupus) to degrade quickly with a significant difference in the rate of amplification after just three days. Panasci et al. (2011) found an increase in amplification failure and errors with time and recommended that coyote faeces of less than five days since deposition are preferable for DNA extraction. However, they were also able to successfully amplify DNA from some samples after this time. Woodruff et al. (2015) studied faecal DNA degradation from the Sonoran pronghorn (Antilocapra americana sonoriensis) and also found genotyping reliability to decrease over time, with the most significant drop in amplification (decrease of 61%) occurring between 7 and 14 days since deposition. Piggott (2004) studied the impacts of time on faecal DNA of European red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) and brushtailed rock wallabies (Petrogale penicillata) in Australia. For both species, she found that age since deposition resulted in a decline in amplification rates and an increase in genotyping error rates. No amplification was obtained from samples 180 days since deposition and the highest-quality DNA and reliable genotyping was obtained from samples up to seven days from deposition.
DNA has been successfully extracted from faecal pellets of many threatened marsupial species in Australia (e.g. Alacs et al. 2003;Piggott et al. 2006;Walker et al. 2009;Ruibal et al. 2009;Smith et al. 2009;Wedrowicz et al. 2013). One of these species, the greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) is a burrowing marsupial that was once widespread across most of mainland Australia (Marlow 1958;Southgate 1990;Friend 1990;Gordon et al. 1990;Johnson and Southgate 1990;Abbott 2001Abbott , 2008;;Bradley et al. 2015) but now is found in only 20% of its former range (Southgate 1990). A better understanding of bilby density, abundance and population distribution is critical in determining appropriate strategies for the conservation and management of this species, with this being noted as a key research priority and knowledge gap for the bilby particularly in Western Australia (Bradley et al. 2015;Cramer et al. 2016).
The bilby is a cryptic, trap-shy and wide-ranging species (McGregor and Moseby 2014), which makes the implementation of traditional and direct fauna monitoring techniques, including capture-mark-recapture methods through trapping, very difficult for this species due to the intensity, time and high level of resources that would be required (Southgate et al. 1995;Lollback et al. 2015). Non-invasive methods to monitor fauna species that use evidence of the target species, such as tracks, burrows, dens, pellets and scats, are becoming increasingly preferred methods, particularly for species that are highly dispersed or elusive (Piggott and Taylor 2003a), including the bilby (Southgate et al. 2005;Southgate and Moseby 2008;Burrows et al. 2012;Lollback et al. 2015). Bilby faecal pellets are easily identified in the field as they have a distinct physical appearance and can often be observed amongst other bilby signs, particularly at diggings (Southgate et al. 2005). They are also easy to collect and store, involving reduced resources and effort than would otherwise be required for trapping, and can provide an alternative source of information for monitoring (Southgate 2005;Lollback et al. 2015).
Previous success of DNA extraction from greater bilby faecal pellets provides a reliable and efficient non-invasive method for identifying bilby individuals (Smith et al. 2009), and may therefore be useful in gaining an understanding of population size and density.
The degradation of DNA from bilby faecal pellets, however, has not yet been explored. The need to understand faecal DNA degradation rates when using this as a source for identifying individuals in a species monitoring program was raised by Piggott (2004), particularly with species such as the bilby, where populations are often remote and individuals are at low densities, making it difficult to source fresh samples regularly.
Studies on faecal samples from both herbivorous and carnivorous species have shown that the age of the faecal sample contributes significantly to the ability to extract and amplify DNA, with fresh samples resulting in more reliable amplification with fewer genotyping errors than found with older samples (Lucchini et al. 2002;Piggott 2004;Santini et al. 2007;Panasci et al. 2011). Therefore, it is useful to know, particularly for monitoring or for obtaining DNA for other genetic studies, up to what age samples still yield DNA and what the quality of DNA is at a particular age.
DNA extracted from faecal matter includes DNA from mixed sources and/or low levels of target DNA (Taberlet et al. 1996;Morin et al. 2001). A common problem is the ability to obtain enough high-quality DNA for reliable genotyping, as opposed to tissue or blood samples that have significantly more target DNA and fewer inhibitors (Piggott and Taylor 2003a). A technique that is sometimes used to maximise the quantity of DNA available for PCR is performing a second elution phase at the end of the DNA extraction process, which allows for the elution of any retained DNA in the silica membrane of a spin column without diluting the first eluate (QIAGEN 2006). Despite having reduced DNA quantities remaining within the second eluate, it is considered that the amount of potential inhibitors remaining for a second elution is also reduced, therefore allowing for cleaner and better-quality DNA. With inhibition being a potential cause of genotyping failure (Ramón-Laca et al. 2015) using such a technique may improve the amplification rate for DNA extracted from bilby scats and may reduce the genotyping errors observed.
In order to establish whether DNA from faecal pellets can be used for reliable monitoring of bilbies, an understanding of the degradation of the DNA is required. The aims of this study were to examine the relationship between DNA degradation from bilby faecal pellets over time, and to determine whether the twostep elution protocol improves the amplification rate of DNA extracted from bilby faecal pellets. We expected that the rate of amplification of DNA would decline over time and the rate of genotyping errors, both false alleles and allelic dropouts, would increase over time as the DNA degrades. We also predicted that DNA amplified using a second eluate would increase the rate of amplification and decrease the rate of genotyping errors by providing higher-quality DNA through a reduction in potential inhibitors.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] faecal pellet collection and experimental design
Faecal pellets were collected from three captive male bilbies housed individually at Kanyana Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre in Lesmurdie, Western Australia. Over a 20-day period in January and February 2015, 63 samples were collected within 24 h of deposition. Captive individuals were used in this study in order to obtain an accurate deposition time, and to eliminate the possibility of additional environmental factors and varying diet amongst individuals to influence the rate of DNA degradation, all of which would be impossible to control for if faecal pellets were collected from a wild population.
Each pellet was placed on dry, prewashed sand in a 5 cm Â 5 cm square labelled ceramic dish and transported to the Department of Parks and Wildlife, Wildlife Research Centre at Woodvale, Western Australia. Samples were placed in a position allocated at random in an enclosure measuring 90 cm (W) Â 90 cm (L) Â 45 cm (H), constructed from 3-mm wire. The enclosure was covered by a sheet of 0.5-cm clear Perspex and secured onto a wooden pallet which was 15 cm off the ground. The enclosure was placed in the field on a concrete slab in a semishaded area with surrounding trees. The enclosure was used to prevent animals (e.g. foxes, crows) disturbing the pellets. The enclosure was kept on the pallet off the ground to prevent flooding of the dishes in case of rain. The Perspex prevented rain directly falling on the experiment whilst allowing normal air flow and sunlight. It allowed us to control potential rainfall impacting the scats and prematurely terminating the experiment and kept the effects of rainfall constant across the experimental period.
On each sampling day at Kanyana, three faecal pellets from each of the three individuals were collected and all samples were assigned to a single treatment period. Collection of faecal samples continued until a total of 21 pellets per individual were collected. The seven treatments covered the time periods in days (1, 7, 14, 21, 30, 90 and 180) of the duration between initial pellet collection from Kanyana and the harvesting of the pellets from Woodvale and immediate DNA extraction. The experiment was performed primarily over the summer months in order to best simulate the northern Western Australian conditions experienced within bilby habitat. The temperature conditions recorded in the Perth metropolitan area over the treatment period ranged from 0.8 C to 40.0 C with a relative humidity from 21% up to 99% (Bureau of Meteorology 2015).

[SECTION] dna extraction
Extractions were undertaken using the QIAGEN QIAamp Fast DNA Stool MiniKit with modifications that included a wash of the faecal pellets (Piggott and Taylor 2003a), the use of Poly-A carrier RNA and an extended incubation period for DNA elution (Morin et al. 2001). The wash of epithelial cells from each pellet was performed with 1.5 mL to 5 mL of SLP buffer (see Deuter et al. 1995 for SLP buffer) followed by a 10-min incubation at 70 C (Piggott and Taylor 2003a). Carrier RNA was included in the process (Roeder et al. 2004) after the second incubation step to assist in the retention of the small quantities of target DNA within the membrane of the spin column, therefore enhancing the recovery of the DNA (Shaw et al. 2009;QIAGEN 2014). A two-step elution process was undertaken at the end of the extraction protocol. Elutions were performed using 50 mL of buffer ATE left to incubate at room temperature for 20 min and then spun in the centrifuge for 2 min in order to elute the DNA from the spin column. DNA was then pipetted into a labelled 1.5-mL microcentrifuge tube and the spin column placed back into the same collection tube for the second elution step. A second 50 mL of buffer ATE was then added to the spin column and left to incubate for a further 20 min before eluting the DNA, which was then pipetted into another labelled 1.5-mL microcentrifuge tube. DNA samples were stored in a À20 C freezer until PCR.

[SECTION] pcr amplification and fragment analysis
PCR amplification was undertaken using three bilby-specific polymorphic microsatellite markers (Moritz et al. 1997;Smith et al. 2009) (refer to Table 1) amplified in a single multiplex. Three PCR replicates using the Qiagen Multiplex PCR Plus Kit were used for each scat sample. PCRs were carried out using the same Eppendorf Thermal Cycler for every PCR. For each PCR replicate, 2 mL of DNA was used in a 12.5-mL reaction with PCR cycling and annealing conditions as per the protocol recommended by the manufacturer for the multiplex kit. A modified extension period of 30 s per cycle was used (Smith and Hughes 2008), rather than the manufacturer's recommendation of 90 s.
Plates containing PCR products were stored in a À20 C freezer until being prepared for fragment analysis. PCR product was analysed on an ABI3730XL Sequencer and sized using Genescan LIZ 500 size standard (Applied Biosystems).
Scoring of alleles was undertaken using GeneMapper Software 5.0. Results were reviewed manually in order to ensure correct scoring of alleles and to confirm genotyping errors, both the presence of false alleles and allelic dropouts. The Day 1 treatment period samples were used as references to establish genotyping errors, as these produced identical results across all faecal pellets and PCR replicates for each individual. Allelic dropouts were recorded as per the definition and protocol employed by Broquet and Petit (2004), where one allele from an individual that exhibited heterozygosity at a locus in the reference genotype was not observed in the replicate sample (either extraction or PCR) for that individual. An allele was considered a false allele where DNA amplification was successful but an allele was observed that was inconsistent with the reference genotypes (Bonin et al. 2004;Broquet and Petit 2004;Waits and Paetkau 2005).

[SECTION] statistical analysis
Repeated-measures mixed-model ANOVA was used to compare the effects of elution and time on the amplification, false allele and allelic dropout rates. The first repeated-measures factor, elution, consisted of two levels, Elution 1 and 2. The second repeated-measures factor was time, and consisted of seven periods when scats were harvested: 1, 7, 14, 21, 30, 90 and 180 days. Individual animals were included in the model as a random, blocking factor, though we neither report the statistics of this factor nor the interaction of this factor with elution or CTA CAA GTC TGA TAA TTC CAG GC Moritz et al. (1997) time. The Greenhouse-Geisser Epsilon (GG-P) was used because it is a more conservative adjustment of the F ratio. All proportions were arcsine-transformed (Zar 1999) into degrees before analyses.

[SECTION] results
DNA amplification was successful across all three loci (B22, B41 and B55), providing consistent results for all three individuals for the first two treatment periods (Days 1 and 7) across Elution 1 (Appendix 1). Although these genotypes were obtained from faecal DNA rather than tissue or blood, the fact that genotypes were 100% consistent across all extraction and PCR replicates for these first two treatments indicates that these results could be reliably used as genotyping references for which subsequent results could be adequately compared to assess amplification success and determine genotyping errors. Time had a significant effect on the amplification rates of bilby faecal DNA (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P < 0.001). As time progressed for both Elutions 1 and 2, the ability to amplify DNA from bilby scats decreased, although at no point did it achieve consistent non-amplification over the 180 days of this experiment (Fig. 1). There was also a significant difference in the rate of amplification between the two elution steps (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P < 0.001). A higher proportion of samples were successfully genotyped from Elution 1 than from Elution 2 (Fig. 1). The interaction between time and elution was also significant (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P = 0.002). The amplification rate of DNA from the second eluate decreased with time at a higher rate from the 14-day treatment period than the DNA from the first eluate (Fig. 1a). There were no significant main effects or interaction of time and elution on the proportion of false alleles recorded within individual genotypes (Table 2).
Time had a significant effect on the rate of allelic dropout (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P = 0.015), with the proportion of allelic dropouts increasing over time (Fig. 1). There was a significant effect of elution on allelic dropout (Table 2: P = 0.006; GG-P = 0.006). There were more allelic dropouts observed from DNA in the second eluate than using DNA from a single elution step (Fig. 1). There was no significant interaction of time and elution on allelic dropout (Table 2).

[SECTION] discussion
This study set out to determine how age since deposition affects the amplification of DNA from bilby scats. Our study showed that amplification rate decreases and allelic dropout rate increases in DNA extracted from bilby scats as time since deposition increases. We also found that a two-step elution process, contrary to our initial hypothesis, does not increase amplification rates or decrease error rates in DNA extracted from bilby scats.
Despite the decrease in amplification rate over time, even at 90 and 180 days since deposition, we were able to successfully amplify DNA from faecal pellets and clearly identify the three individuals used in this study, with the rate only dropping as low as 63% for Elution 1 (at 90 days) and 21% for Elution 2 (at 180 days) (Fig. 1a). Our results show that there is potential to identify bilby individuals that were in a particular area up to the six-month time frame. For extracting DNA from bilby scats, from both a time and cost-effectiveness perspective, the optimal timeframe for scat collection would be within two weeks from deposition, with ~99% amplification success for one elution step being achieved and low rates (<5%) of genotyping error (Fig. 1).  As with other faecal DNA and microsatellite studies (Lucchini et al. 2002;Piggott 2004;Miller et al. 2010), allelic dropout was the most common genotyping error associated with this experiment. This is consistent with previous findings by Morin et al. (2001) whereby allelic dropouts are more prevalent when the original quantity of template DNA is low, which appears to be the case in relation to our amplification rate results: as amplification rates decrease, due to the reduction in DNA quantity and quality over time, the rate of allelic dropout increases.
The low rate of false alleles observed in this study is likely to be a result of the low presence of false alleles across the experiment generally, with non-amplification being more likely than the production of false alleles. Where false alleles were observed these were generally sporadic (Morin et al. 2001), only present in single samples and not often reproduced across scat samples from the same individual or PCRs.
The premise that a two-step elution process would produce higher-quality DNA due to fewer inhibitors in the second elution phase was not upheld in this study. The ability to amplify DNA from Elution 2 samples showed that DNA was still in the spin column after the first elution, particularly for the first two time treatments, however Elution 1 samples provided greater than 60% amplification throughout the experimental period (Fig. 1a) and exhibited a lower allelic dropout rate than the second eluate (Fig. 1b). The amplification rates of the second round of eluted DNA decreased at a much quicker rate from the 14-day treatment period compared with the first eluate (Fig. 1a). It is also reasonable to expect that this may be the case because a reduction in available epithelial cells from which to obtain DNA from the samples over time could also mean that there will inevitably be less DNA for the second elution phase, too low to result in successful DNA amplification and subsequent genotyping. The consequence of using Elution 2 to determine genotypes is that the rate of amplification decreased significantly quicker than that for Elution 1 over the same period, therefore should pellets be collected that are more than a week old the likelihood of non-amplification and the risk of genotyping errors being observed will increase. Based on these results it is not considered worthwhile performing a twostep elution method as part of the DNA extraction protocol for bilby scats and it would be more cost-effective and efficient to complete more PCR replicates using just one elution. Additional methods that may also improve the success and efficiency of DNA extraction and PCR processes, that were not tested as part of this experiment, include combining eluates to increase the amount of total DNA in the final sample and utilising quantitative PCR to better understand the quantity of DNA before further fragment analyses.
Several factors such as rainfall and the diet of individuals are likely to impact DNA preservation on faecal pellets or may result in different inhibition in the amplification of bilby DNA. Rainfall has been identified as being a prominent factor in the decay rates of scat DNA (Piggott 2004;Brinkman et al. 2010b). In our study we controlled for the effects of rainfall by using a clear Perspex roof over our experimental treatments. This ensured that the effects of rainfall events were constant across the time treatments and prevented a catastrophic rain event prematurely terminating the experiment but allowed natural sunlight and UV penetration. In the field, the rate of DNA decay may well increase after rainfall events and result in more rapid overall decay, with spikes in decay rate rather than the more evenly decreasing relationship observed in this study. Therefore, the occurrence of rain should be considered before sampling bilby scats in the field for DNA extraction.
The diet of the captive bilbies used in this study consisted of mealworms, seed, dog biscuits, fruit and vegetables. The diet of wild bilbies includes lepidopteran larvae, termites, ants, grasshoppers, spiders and beetles, seed, bulbs (Cyperus bulbosus) and fungi (Burbidge et al. 1988;Gibson 2001;Southgate and Carthew 2006). Differences in diet may lead to differences in decay rates of faecal DNA, particularly if the diet affects the moisture content within the pellets. DNA from faecal pellets containing more moisture may decay at a higher rate, similar to that due to increased moisture caused by rainfall (Piggott 2004;Brinkman et al. 2010b). Since the captive animals used in this study were all fed the same diet, this variation was controlled for in our design. Overall, however, since water conservation is a priority for bilbies, and as such very little water is lost through excretion of faeces and urine (Gibson and Hume 2000a, 2000b, 2004;Gibson et al. 2002), the inherent dryness of bilby faecal pellets likely contributes to the long viability of the faecal DNA.
The environment in which bilby faecal pellets are deposited may also influence the ability to obtain viable DNA from them. Bilby faecal pellets can be found either in the open but more often than not around foraging sites as well as buried within the spoil of diggings or burrows. The faecal pellets collected from the captive individuals in this experiment were found in both situations, either on top of the sand in the enclosure or buried within it whilst the individual had been foraging. It is possible that the act of burying the scats could have an effect on the number of epithelial cells retained on the scats to be able to be washed off for DNA extraction. In contrast, faecal pellets from wild populations that are located in the open are exposed to wind and direct UV radiation, which buried pellets are not, and the DNA may therefore degrade more rapidly as a result of this.
In addition to the factors mentioned above, for wild bilby populations, seasonal changes both in diet, as a result of resource availability (Gibson 2001), and the external environmental conditions (Piggott 2004) such as humidity, rainfall, temperature, UV radiation and ash content if collected from recently burnt habitat, may also influence the ability to extract bilby DNA and successfully genotype individuals. The order in which the selected faecal pellet was deposited may also influence the amount of DNA on the pellet (Walker et al. 2009), highlighting the need for multiple or repeat extractions where an initial extraction may not have been successful.
Incorporating genetics as a component of an overall conservation and management strategy for bilbies not only allows for the identification of individuals and the potential for monitoring populations, it may also assist in gaining a better understanding of the movement of individuals across the landscape and survivorship over time (if an individual is identified through faecal DNA at different locations or on multiple monitoring trips). It could also be used in further population genetics studies (Southgate and Adams 1994;Moritz et al. 1997), including assessment of population fragmentation across the Pilbara and Kimberley regions of Western Australia and across Australia as a whole.
This study found that, under seminatural conditions, viable DNA exists on bilby faecal pellets for a long period and can be amplified with a 99% success rate and low error rates up to 14 days after deposition. The amplification rate decreases, and allelic dropout rates increase, gradually with time, but DNA can still be successfully amplified at rates above 80% and error rates below 11% at 30 days, and amplification rates above 60% and error rates below 15% at 90-180 days. We found that a second elution step was unnecessary. DNA was more successfully amplified using the first eluate with fewer allelic dropouts and a decreased rate of decline in amplification rates. This means that DNA can be successfully amplified from bilby faecal pellets for a long period after deposition, which can be useful for obtaining genetic samples for population monitoring programs and studies on population genetics. FILE: Aquatic Conservation - 2016 - Boothroyd - Environmental DNA  eDNA  detection and habitat occupancy of threatened spotted.grobid.tei.xml

[SECTION] title
Environmental DNA (eDNA) detection and habitat occupancy of threatened spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus)

[SECTION] abstract
1. Determining the occurrence and site occupancy of rare and endangered species can be challenging, particularly without causing harm or stress to the species of concern.2. Environmental DNA (eDNA) detection was used to assess habitat occupancy by spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus), which is federally listed as Threatened in Canada, with known occurrences limited to a small number of locations in southern Ontario.3. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays were developed to detect spotted gar eDNA, which was detected in all but one previously recorded location. The eDNA method was shown to be more effective than traditional netting for detecting spotted gar habitat use.4. The use of qPCR allowed for quantification of substantial variation in detection strength (copy number) among replicate eDNA samples, with implications for establishing sampling designs for detection and surveillance.5. The use of eDNA for detection and monitoring of aquatic species of conservation concern shows great potential as a non-invasive method for assessing species occurrences and habitat occupancy, as well as for informing targeted sampling by conventional capture methods.

[SECTION] introduction
Global biodiversity is experiencing accelerating losses from human impacts on environments and ecosystems (Butchart et al., 2010). While many conservation efforts have focused on terrestrial systems, higher trajectories of species loss in freshwater ecosystems indicate urgent conservation needs (Abell, 2002;Strayer and Dudgeon, 2010).
Freshwater fishes alone comprise one quarter of living vertebrate species, and recent assessments suggest that more than 30% are threatened (Singh, 2002). The rapid decline of North American freshwater fish diversity has continued despite increased knowledge and implementation of environmental and species protection laws (Jelks et al., 2008;Williams et al., 2011). Knowledge of a species' distribution and abundance is vital to understanding their ecology, and critical for conserving populations (Thompson, 2004).
Canada's Species at Risk Act (SARA) legislates the protection of critical habitat, which is habitat required for persistence of listed threatened or endangered species (S.C. 2002, c.29;Rosenfeld and Hatfield, 2006). As critical habitat can vary substantially among different life stages, defining and mapping it can be challenging (Rosenfeld and Hatfield, 2006). The information required to define critical habitat can be costly and time consuming to obtain, particularly in complex aquatic ecosystems (Ficetola et al., 2008;Takahara et al., 2012).
The use of environmental DNA (eDNA) is an emerging method for detecting the presence of low-abundance aquatic species that has applications for identifying occurrences of rare or endangered species, as well as invasive species during early colonization stages (Ficetola et al., 2008;Takahara et al., 2012;Thomsen et al., 2012;Biggs et al., 2015). Although eDNA has largely been used for invasive species surveillance (Ficetola et al., 2008;Jerde et al., 2011;Dejean et al., 2012), the method's sensitivity also makes it valuable for detecting rare species where they are present at low densities and difficult to find (Thompson, 2004;Thomsen et al., 2012;Janosik and Johnston, 2015;Laramie et al., 2015;Sigsgaard et al., 2015). Habitat sampling using eDNA has distinct advantages over traditional sampling methods such as netting that rely on invasive and/or selective capture, as DNA from sloughed tissues is collected from water samples without having to capture or directly encounter the species of interest (Darling and Mahon, 2011;Jerde et al., 2011;Sigsgaard et al., 2015). Thus, noninvasive species detections using eDNA have the additional benefit of avoiding any potential stress or mortality caused by sampling (Putman, 1995;Olson et al., 2012;Thomsen et al., 2012). As well as providing clear benefits for documenting occurrences of species of conservation concern, eDNA detections can also focus conservation efforts at appropriate sites and enable population monitoring with less cost and effort than relying solely on traditional sampling methods (Ficetola et al., 2008;Dejean et al., 2011, Sigsgaard et al., 2015).
The spotted gar (Lepisosteus oculatus) is a North American freshwater fish with a distribution that is largely limited to the Mississippi River basin and the Gulf of Mexico, but also includes disjunct populations in the Great Lakes basin (Figure 1; Page and Burr, 1991). The spotted gar is designated as Threatened within Canada, with only three confirmed populations: Long Point Bay, Pelee National Park, and Rondeau Bay in Lake Erie (COSEWIC, 2005). There are also recent records from the Bay of Quinte and Hamilton Harbour in Lake Ontario, and historic records from Lake St Clair (COSEWIC, 2005).
Major threats to the species in Canada include pollution and habitat loss, as adult spotted gar prefer shallow, clear, vegetated habitat within lakes and rivers (Glass et al., 2012;Gray et al., 2012). As the spotted gar is listed under Canada's federal Species at Risk Act (SARA), a recovery strategy must be developed and implemented for the species, including identification and protection of critical habitat (Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). Current data on the species' distribution, abundance, and habitat use is vital for developing the recovery strategy.
In this study, quantitative eDNA methods were used to document the occurrence of DNA from spotted gar in historically identified habitats across its Canadian range and infer habitat use or occupancy to help inform conservation efforts for this threatened species. The objectives of this study were to: (1) test the effectiveness of the eDNA detection method for species-specific detection of spotted gar; (2) assess the presence of spotted gar in historical and contemporary sites in south-western Ontario; and (3) assess detection power and repeatability of eDNA for potential application to other aquatic species of conservation concern.

[SECTION] methods

[SECTION] field sampling
Locations with known and historically documented occurrences of spotted gar in Canada (Table 1, Figure 1) were sampled for eDNA testing. Long Point Bay, Hillman Marsh, Point Pelee, and Rondeau Bay in Lake Erie; the Thames River, a tributary to Lake St Clair; and, Hamilton Harbour in Lake Ontario (Figure 1) were all targeted for sampling based on historical and recent records (Table 1, COSEWIC, 2005;Bouvier and Mandrak, 2010;Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010;Staton et al., 2012).
To compare detection sensitivity of eDNA versus conventional sampling, nearshore habitats within Long Point Bay were also sampled using 1.2 m fine-mesh (6.35 mm bar mesh) fyke nets. A total of 47 fyke net sets, averaging 24 h, were set at multiple sites in Long Point Bay between 28 May and 7 June 2012, during the known spawning season for spotted gar (Tyler and Granger, 1984;Snedden et al., 1999;Glass et al., 2012). Netting sites were chosen based on identified critical habitat and areas considered to potentially support spotted gar (Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010;Staton et al., 2012). Nets were placed in shallow areas adjacent to shore to target spawning-related movements and left for 24 h (range 18.5-38 h owing to weather conditions). All nets and sampling gear were bleached and rinsed after retrieval to prevent DNA cross-contamination. The netting was conducted under a Species at Risk scientific permit issued by Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO), and was done in accordance with guidelines set by the DFO's Canada Centre for Inland Waters Animal Care Committee (Protocol Number: AUP # 1017). Water samples for eDNA testing were collected at each recent and historically known location for spotted gar (Table 1, Figure 1), sampling 10 sites within each general location and taking five replicate 1 L water samples per site. For the Thames River, three 1 L water samples were collected from each of 16 sites. Owing to logistical delays, water sampling was carried out from 19-25 June 2012 instead of coinciding with the netting effort. All sampling followed protocols established by Mahon et al. (2010), which include multiple safeguards and quality checks to reduce contamination and minimize the possibility of false positive results (Mahon et al., 2010). Post-collection samples were stored in 60 L coolers with ice packs to prevent DNA degradation. Negative controls (one 1 L sample of clean water per cooler) were also brought into the field to test for contamination from handling among environmental samples. As described above, all sampling gear was bleached and rinsed between locations to prevent DNA cross-contamination. Three 1 L water samples were collected from the Otonabee River (Peterborough, Ontario) to act as field controls, since there are no known or historical records of spotted gar within the Otonabee River. These precautions are necessary because of the high sensitivity of polymer chain reaction (PCR), which can make it prone to contamination during field sampling or laboratory processing (Darling and Mahon, 2011).

[SECTION] filtering
Water samples were filtered within 3-18 h of collection. Water was filtered using a filter funnel attached to a vacuum source, with two types of fine-pore filters: 1.0 μm pore size Whatman TM 47 mm GF/B filters and 1.2 μm pore Whatman TM 47 mm GF/C filters. Previous work under controlled conditions showed that DNA yields from these two filter types were not significantly different (C. Wilson, unpubl. data). All filters were stored at -80°C until extracted to prevent DNA degradation (Anchordoquy and Molina, 2007).

[SECTION] extractions
DNA was extracted from the water filters using MoBio Power Water extraction kits. The manufacturer's extraction protocol was followed with the following modifications: (1) extractions were made in 15 mL tubes rather than the bead tubes provided; (2) samples were agitated using an orbital shaker for 30 min rather than 5 min; (3) after the shaking stage for GF/C filters, an additional 500 μL of PW1 was added and the samples were vortexed; and (4) final elution was done with low TE (10 mmol L -1 Tris pH 8, 0.1 mmol L -1 EDTA) instead of the PW6 solution provided. Extracted samples were stored at -20°C to prevent DNA degradation. Genomic DNA was also extracted from 12 reference samples of spotted gar (fin clips preserved in 80% ethanol) from several Lake Erie locations (Point Pelee, Long Point, Rondeau Bay) and Missouri, USA using an alkali extraction protocol (Dissing et al., 1996).
Successful extraction of DNA for both reference and environmental samples was confirmed by gel electrophoresis, visualizing 2 μL of DNA from each extraction with SYBR Green stain in a 1.5% agarose gel alongside a 100 bp mass ladder (Bioshop Canada). qPCR Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was used to test the detection efficacy of spotted gar eDNA, using species-specific primers and probe designed to amplify and detect a 61 bp segment of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I (COI) gene based on L. oculatus sequences in BOLD (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007). The COI gene is well-suited for eDNA detection of species of interest, based on species-diagnostic differences between most species and the rapidly growing global database of DNA barcodes based on COI sequences (Hebert et al., 2003;Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007). The barcoding region of COI has the additional benefit of being flanked by two highly conserved 'universal' primer sites for PCR, which simplifies obtaining DNA barcodes from novel species of interest (Hebert et al., 2003).
The TaqMan-labelled qPCR probe was designed to have three mismatches from longnose gar (L. osseus), the only other gar species with a Canadian distribution (Page and Burr, 1991). All qPCR reactions were run with TaqMan® chemistry with a total reaction volume of 20 μL consisting of 5 μL undiluted DNA, 10 μL of TaqMan® Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), 0.4 μL each for the qPCR primers and probe [S.GarTaqManF (5′-CTGACTTCTCCCACCCTCATTT-3′), 0.2 μL S.GarTaqManR (5′-CGGCCCCTGCTTCAAT C-3′), 0.2 μL SpottedGarProbe (6FAM-TTCTCCT TTTAGCCTCATC-MGBNFQ)], and 3.8 μL ddH 2 O. Reactions were carried out in a StepOnePlus thermocycler (Life Technologies), using an initial denaturation at 95°C for 2 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C denaturation for 1 s and 60°C annealing for 20 s. Two replicate qPCR reactions were run for each sample, and two series of qPCR standards (10-fold dilution series of spotted gar COI PCR product from 10 6 to 10 0 copies per reaction) and two negative controls were run on all sample plates. The resulting standard curves were used to quantify starting copy number estimates of template DNA in the environmental samples. qPCR was also used to test a subset of environmental samples for inhibition using an Internal Positive Control (IPC; Life Technologies). For this subset of IPC controls, 20 μL qPCR reactions were run with TaqMan® chemistry, consisting of 5 μL undiluted DNA, 10 μL of TaqMan® Fast Advanced Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), 0.4 μL each of S.GarTaqManF, S. GarTaqManR, and SpottedGarProbe, 1.2 μL ddH 2 O, 2.2 μL of 10× Exo IPC Mix, and 0.4 μL 50× Exo IPC DNA.

[SECTION] establishing a detection threshold
Determination of whether or not a result is a 'positive' detection requires careful interpretation and appropriate quality checks and controls. Darling and Mahon (2011) suggested defining a priori criteria and thresholds to distinguish clearly between positive and negative detections, minimize observer bias, and work toward consistent scoring and interpretation. For qPCR, the assay's sensitivity depends on many factors including sampling and DNA extraction procedures, target rarity in samples, presence of inhibitors, and amplification conditions (Foy and Parkes, 2001). Method sensitivity is associated with the detectable lower limit of the method, or the limit of detection (LOD), which can be defined to give insight into the lowest detection limit for a qPCR assay (Burns and Valdivia, 2008). Generally, the LOD is conveyed as the amount of analyte the analytical method detects successfully at a minimum 95% of the time (Ros-García et al., 2012). In the present study the 1 DNA copy/5 μL had a high failure rate (45%), resulting in the 10 DNA copies/5 μL being set as the LOD and threshold for detection. Confident detections were defined as samples that consistently amplified at or above the 10-copy detection threshold. If the samples showed qPCR detection while the negative field and laboratory control samples did not, it was inferred that spotted gar DNA was present at the sampling site.

[SECTION] sequencing
A subset of samples with positive detections, including at least one positive from each site with positive detections, were amplified using conventional PCR primers developed for a 260 bp segment of spotted gar COI (Bronnenhuber and Wilson, 2013), bidirectionally sequenced using BigDye 3.1 sequencing chemistry (Applied Biosystems), and visualized on an AB3730 capillary sequencer (Applied Biosystems) to ensure that the amplified DNA was from spotted gar. In cases where multiple positive detections occurred at a site, a representative subsample was sequenced. All sequences were proofread using Sequencher 5.1 (Gene Codes, Inc.) and identified using the BLAST tool on Genbank (www.ncbi. nlm.nih.gov) to look for homologous sequences. Sequences were also visualized using MEGA version 5 (Tamura et al., 2011) alongside samples from spotted gar and longnose gar obtained from Genbank and BOLD (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007) to confirm species identity of DNA from the environmental samples.

[SECTION] mean copy number
The mean copy number of target DNA within the environmental samples was calculated by taking the arithmetic mean of the qPCR replicates from all filters for each site. Any sites that had negative control samples amplified above the detection threshold (10 copies/5 μL) were assumed to be a result of error or contamination ('false positive' data; Darling and Mahon, 2011) and were therefore excluded from the mean calculation data.

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] netting data
The 47 net sets over 6 sampling days (28-30 May, 5-7 June) in Long Point Bay captured a total of 7737 fish from 31 species (means and standard errors of 164.6 + 22.5 and 9.9 + 0.5 respectively; data not shown), including three longnose gar. Despite the extensive netting effort, only three spotted gar were captured, all of which were caught at Long Point Bay Site 2 (Figure 2).

[SECTION] edna detections
Spotted gar DNA was successfully amplified from sites within five of the six sampling locations Long Point Bay, (E) Thames River, and (F) Hamilton Harbour with detections categorized by samples yielding starting DNA copy numbers greater than 100 copies/5 μL in at least one sample (green), starting copy numbers greater than 10 copies/5 μL and less than 100 copies/5 μL in at least one sample (yellow), and no detection or starting copy numbers less than 10 copies/5 μL in all samples (red). The square symbol in Long Point Bay indicates the location where live spotted gar were captured.
(Figure 2), with positive detections at 30-90% of sampled sites. Detections were not uniform: DNA concentrations shown in Figure 2 represent maximum rather than mean values of DNA copy number detected from filters or qPCR replicates at each site. Sampling locations with positive detections had 1-8 sites below the cutoff detection threshold (≥10 copies/5 μL), 3-8 sites with eDNA detections between 10 and 100 copies/5 μL, and < 5 sites with eDNA detections greater than 100 copies/5 μL (Figure 2). No positive detections for spotted gar DNA were obtained from the Hamilton Harbour locations based on the predefined minimum detection threshold (Figure 2). Data from field samples associated with detections in negative cooler and filtering controls (14% of the negative controls) were excluded from the results. The field controls from the Otonabee River (outside the species range) did not yield positive detections, and the subset of samples tested using the exogenous Internal Positive Control showed no evidence of PCR inhibition.
The qPCR surveillance yielded reproducible results at control DNA concentrations down to 10 copies/5 μL and environmental samples at concentrations below 100 copies/5 μL (Figure 2). Several locations yielded at least one sample with an estimated DNA concentration between 10 and 100 copies/5 μL (Figure 2), despite lower mean concentrations (Figure 3). Although qPCR results from a number of locations yielded putative detections of spotted gar DNA at concentrations below 10 target copies/5 μL (Figure 3), these were not considered to be positive detections as they fell below the predefined detection threshold.
All positive eDNA results that were sequenced matched reference spotted gar sequences obtained from GenBank, as well as the Canadian reference sequences in BOLD (Ratnasingham and Hebert, 2007). The amplified region had nine speciesdiagnostic mismatches between the reference sequences for spotted and longnose gar. The environmental sequences showed 96-100% homology with spotted gar, compared with a maximum homology of 95% with longnose gar.

[SECTION] mean copy number
Replicate samples within sites exhibited substantial variation in DNA yield, despite water samples being taken in close proximity to each other (≤50 m) within a site (Figure 3). In general, sites with a higher mean number of copies of spotted gar eDNA had greater within-site variability (Figure 3). Both within and among sampling sites, a small fraction of the replicate samples consistently had high copy number detections (Figure 2) with the remaining replicates having low copy number detections (Figure 3).

[SECTION] discussion
This study demonstrated that eDNA is an effective tool for documenting occurrences and habitat occupancy of spotted gar, and showed eDNA detection success similar to other freshwater studies with locations known to be inhabited by the species having high detection success (Goldberg et al., 2011;Thomsen et al., 2012;Biggs et al., 2015;Janosik and Johnston, 2015). This study differed somewhat from most other eDNA studies on species at risk by its scale, documenting positive detections over most of the species' Canadian range.
Spotted gar DNA was successfully detected at all sampled Lake Erie locations (Hillman Marsh, Point Pelee, Long Point Bay, Rondeau Bay), as well as the Thames River. There have been recent collections of spotted gar at these locations, excluding the Thames River (Table 1; Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010;Glass et al., 2012). In addition, the rates and levels of eDNA detection were generally consistent with what is known about spotted gar abundance in the sampled locations, with the exception of sites in the Thames River and Hamilton Harbour (discussed below). Three locations (Hillman Marsh, Point Pelee, Rondeau Bay) had detections at a majority of the sites sampled. Rondeau Bay and Point Pelee also have the largest population estimates for spotted gar in Ontario, the population status of these populations were assessed as 'good' and 'fair', respectively (Table 1; Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). Other studies similarly found that detection rates were higher in areas with higher density estimates for target organisms (Pilliod et al., 2013;Laramie et al., 2015). While collection data for spotted gar are limited at Hillman Marsh, the habitat is suitable for spotted gar (Snedden et al., 1999;Ostrand et al., 2004;Glass et al., 2012), and spotted gar have been captured in the area (Table 1, N. Mandrak, unpublished data 2012). Long Point Bay had DNA detections at three of 10 sampled sites; by contrast, netting efforts for spotted gar within the bay met with minimal success, resulting in the population status being categorized as 'poor' (Table 1, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). In 2010, 129 fyke net sets targeting the species caught only six individuals, and only 17 adults had been captured before then (Glass and Mandrak, 2014). The limited number of site detections in Long Point Bay may therefore reflect a low density of spotted gar in the area; other studies have demonstrated increased probability of detection with increasing density or biomass of the target species (Pilliod et al., 2013;Takahara et al., 2013;Moyer et al., 2014).
The detection of spotted gar DNA at eight of the 16 sites sampled within the Thames River was unexpected, as spotted gar are considered to be extirpated within the Lake St. Clair catchment (Table 1; COSEWIC, 2005; Department of Fisheries and Oceans, DFO, 2010). Although there is one historical record for spotted gar from the Thames River area of Lake St Clair, none have been recorded for over half a century (COSEWIC, 2005). Follow-up netting in 2013 (40 24 h fyke net sets, 365 m of trammel net, and 1530 s of boat electrofishing) in the vicinity of the positive eDNA detections failed to detect spotted gar, although 27 species including more than 400 longnose gar were captured (Marson et al., 2014). Similar species detections using eDNA have been reported from other studies sampling for rare and long-unobserved fish species: Janosik and Johnston (2015) reported detection of eDNA from the slackwater darter (Etheostoma boschungi) at a site with no record since 1970, and Sigsgaard et al. (2015) detected European weather loach (Misgurnis fossilis) eDNA at a site where the species had not been observed for 20 years. These support the use of eDNA as a highly sensitive detection method for aquatic organisms, allowing detection of rare species in areas that went many years without record.
Although recent sampling yielded many longnose gar and no spotted gar from the Thames River (Marson et al., 2014), the possibility that the qPCR tests could have amplified eDNA from longnose gar despite primer and probe mismatches was excluded by sequence confirmation of positive eDNA results as belonging to L. oculatus (98-100% homology to spotted gar reference sequences). As previous studies have demonstrated that hybridization among gars can occur, it is possible that the eDNA detections were from hybrid fish with spotted gar maternal ancestry (Herrington et al., 2008).
Despite records of spotted gar in Hamilton Harbour (COSEWIC, 2005), eDNA sampling failed to detect its presence. The lack of detection may have resulted from spotted gar leaving the area after spawning, as the harbour was the last location sampled and sampling occurred almost a month after the peak spawning time for spotted gar (Tyler and Granger, 1984). General observations of spotted gar have documented spawning along the shore (where current eDNA sampling occurred) in the spring, followed by post-spawning movement into the broader lake habitat (Snedden et al., 1999;Glass et al., 2012). This underscores the importance of a strong spatio-temporal sampling design (Darling and Mahon, 2011): repeated sampling throughout the year would also provide insight into seasonal variation in habitat occupancy, which would provide important information when establishing critical habitat for protected species. The apparent lack of detection of spotted gar DNA in Hamilton Harbour may also have been due to the detection threshold used (10 copies/5 μL), potentially excluding valid low-quantity detections. This is a recognized shortcoming of measures to prevent false positives, which can create a bias towards the error of false negative detections (Darling and Mahon, 2011). Despite this possibility, having an a priori cutoff threshold is a necessary precaution to safeguard against false positives from potential contamination, and enable robust confidence in positive detections (Darling and Mahon, 2011).
The successful detection of spotted gar DNA at five of the six sampled locations highlights that eDNA can be used as a tool to detect rare species in both lentic and lotic environments. To date, many eDNA studies have focused on small lentic pond environments (Ficetola et al., 2008;Dejean et al., 2012;Takahara et al., 2013). eDNA detectability in lotic environments is probably influenced by additional factors such as flow (Deiner and Altermatt, 2014;Laramie et al., 2015;Strickler et al., 2015). Although eDNA studies within lotic systems have reported successful detection of rare species (Goldberg et al., 2011;Thomsen et al., 2012;Jane et al., 2015;Laramie et al., 2015), studies focusing on lentic environments have often reported more consistent success rates (Ficetola et al., 2008;Thomsen et al., 2012). Detection of spotted gar where they are considered extirpated, and thus presumably present at low density, suggests that the eDNA method may be used as a highly sensitive method of rare species detection, even within lotic environments.
A criticism and perceived limitation of using eDNA as a monitoring tool for rare and invasive species is that eDNA detections identify the presence of the target species' DNA rather than individuals themselves (ECALS, Environmental DNA Calibration Study, 2013). Posited alternative sources of DNA include carcasses, effluent from live food markets and pet shops, sewer runoff, bird droppings, or contaminated sampling gear (Darling and Mahon, 2011;ECALS, Environmental DNA Calibration Study, 2013, Merkes et al., 2014). As the spotted gar is a rare and protected species in Canada, however, it is unlikely that the positive DNA detections in this study resulted from any of these sources. As it is illegal to trade native fish species in Canada, spotted gar is protected under SARA, and the gar pet trade largely consists of the similar-looking but genetically divergent Florida gar (Lepisosteus platyrhincus). Spotted gar is a rare top-level predator; although limited bird predation may occur on juvenile gar (Page and Burr, 1991), it is unlikely that DNA was transported via bird droppings, particularly over large distances or into novel locations. Thus, positive eDNA detections should be reliable indicators of the occurrence of spotted gar in or near sampled areas, and similar arguments would hold for other endangered taxa.
For eDNA to be accepted as a valid monitoring technique, it must meet a number of criteria including accuracy, precision, and repeatability (Invasive Species Advisory Committee, ISAC, 2012). The substantial variation observed among replicate samples within detection sites has been reported in other studies as well (Ficetola et al., 2008(Ficetola et al., , 2015;;Foote et al., 2012;Klymus et al., 2015). Variability among replicate samples could be contributed to by non-homogeneous mixing, heterogeneity of fish distribution in the water column, or inefficiencies in DNA extraction and testing (Goldberg et al., 2011;Mahon et al., 2013;Eichmiller et al., 2014). The number of positive detections among replicate samples provides an estimate of detection probability, which is valuable for designing efficient sampling protocols.
Detection probability is likely to vary based on species characteristics, local density, and sampling location; therefore, ideal replicate numbers will probably be study-specific (Darling and Mahon 2011;Takahara et al., 2012;Moyer et al., 2014). For example, Schmidt et al. (2013) found that the detection probability for Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis increased with the number of replicate water samples taken, with a plateau at five for robust detection. For community 'metabarcoding' (multispecies detection from eDNA samples via next-generation sequencing) Ficetola et al. (2015) suggested that the number of replicates should vary with detection probability, with a minimum of eight needed for species with low detection probabilities (<0.5) to limit false absences. As pointed out by Pilliod et al. (2013) and Jane et al. (2015), detection probability is also expected to vary with source biomass.
The variation in detection strengths within and among sites also indicates potential limitations in spatial resolution for mapping habitat use with eDNA. In systems where both target (source species) movements and sampling medium (water) are literally fluid, detection levels should not be overinterpreted. Because eDNA and fish both move, inferences from this study should probably be made at the larger location scale (local bay/harbour/river) rather than individual sites sampled within general locations. In standing water environments such as small ponds (Dejean et al., 2011;Takahara et al., 2012Takahara et al., , 2013;;Eichmiller et al., 2014;Moyer et al., 2014) and simple stream systems (Goldberg et al., 2011), site detections may sufficiently represent sampled habitats. Patchy distribution of eDNA detections has also been reported for common carp (Cyprinus carpio), with significantly higher eDNA detection rates in high-use areas (Eichmiller et al., 2014). In larger water bodies, however, eDNA detection probabilities are influenced by a number of factors, including the distance from the source, site conditions, and number of fish present in the area (Darling and Mahon, 2011;Takahara et al., 2012). Care should therefore be taken in interpreting the spatial scale and resolution of results from larger flowing systems or water bodies, as detections at sampling points may reflect distant or upstream rather than local contributions (Deiner and Altermatt, 2014), and will also be influenced by flow rate and proximity or distance from biological sources (Pilliod et al., 2013;Jane et al., 2015;Klymus et al., 2015). Accordingly, more research is needed to strengthen the application of eDNA for identifying critical habitats sensu Rosenfeld and Hatfield (2006) for species of conservation concern.
The detection of spotted gar at the majority of their previously documented locations across their Canadian range (COSEWIC, 2005) has demonstrated the efficacy and sensitivity of eDNA surveillance for aquatic endangered species. Although this study supports the use of eDNA as a tool for monitoring and detecting aquatic endangered species to focus conservation efforts, eDNA surveillance should be used to augment and focus conventional sampling methods rather than replace them. The high variability within replicate samples and potential rejection of low-copy data demonstrate the limitations of current eDNA methodology, and it is unlikely to replace capture methods to provide information on population size or demographic structure. As this new methodology matures, collaborations between the scientific community and management agencies should work towards establishing rigorous protocols and thresholds to maximize the information benefits from eDNA studies. With thoughtful sampling design and validation testing, eDNA applications have excellent potential for documenting species occurrences and facilitating habitat protection for threatened and endangered species.

FILE: Estimating Abundance and Survival in the Endangered Point Arena Mountain Beaver UsingNoninvasive Gen.grobid.tei.xml
