1-Sampling of faeces 2-Estimation of non  To assess the adequacy of the method for DNA amplification of specific prey in faeces, controlled feeding experiments were conducted with each prey and with the three prey together.
The percentage of fed prey that were ingested was checked by visual observation of the number of remaining prey individuals 24 h after feeding. When Mysidae specimens were supplied as a single prey type (day 1), 97% AE 5 of them were ingested. In four cases of six, all the prey supplied were ingested by the seahorses. In seahorses fed Palaemonetes alone (day 5), the average percentage of prey ingestion was 92% AE 9; three of six seahorses consumed 100% of the prey. For Artemia (day 7), 93% AE 13 of prey were ingested; five of six seahorses consumed all the prey. Of the mixed diet (day 3), all the Mysidae and Palaemonetes, but only 76% AE 31 of Artemia were ingested.
Faecal samples were collected in all the feeding trials. Most faeces (71%) were found the day after feeding (days 2, 4, 6 and 8) (list of faecal sampling in Data S2); in other cases, faeces from a single feed were released over 2 days (e.g. days 3, 5, 7 and 9), and the results for faecal samples that corresponded to the same feeding event were compiled for clarity (Table 2).
Observation of the faeces under a binocular lens showed different degrees of prey digestion. For example, in the fae-ces composed of Palaemonetes, undigested parts of the carapace were observed (Fig. 2).
For each gene, the prey bank library comprised the two Mysidae taxa, Leptomysis spp. (Genbank accession number of COI: KC763187, of 28S: KC763185, of 18S: KC763182) and Siriella spp. (28S: KC763186 and 18S: KC763181), the sequence of P. varians (COI: KC763188, and 18S: KC763180) and the sequence of Artemia spp. (28S: KC763184 and 18S: KC763183). Genbank sequences were chosen to complete the three missing sequences when PCR failed to amplify the gene. (More details about these sequences are given in the legends to the Data S3.)
Alignment of 28S sequences revealed greater evolutionary distances between species than in 18S or COI alignments (see Data S3). Moreover, the mutation rate differed by gene, COI alignment showing a homogeneous mutation rate (mainly restricted to the third position of the codon) and the ribosomal genes (18SrDNA and 28SrDNA) showing a heterogeneous mutation rate due to the alternation between hypervariable regions surrounded by more or less conserved regions (illustrated in Data S4).
The suitability of COI, 18SrDNA and 28SrDNA genes for detecting prey-specific DNA short sequences was compared by assessing the presence of specific regions for the design of group-specific primers. High divergence between sequences in both COI and 28S alignments made it difficult to detect regions that were conserved in both Mysidae taxa but were specific to that group and not to the other prey (P. varians and Artemia spp.). In contrast, 18S alignment offered possibilities for designing group-specific primers because of the availability of numerous regions displaying the required taxonomic specificity for Mysidae. Moreover, the larger size of the 18SrDNA gene (1800 bp) than the region commonly available for 28SrDNA (900 bp) and COI (600 bp) facilitated the finding of specific regions. Thus, 18SrDNA was chosen as the target gene.
A total of 30 specific primer sets were designed (see Data S5), making it possible to test 44 primers (17 targeted P1, 12 targeted P2 and 15 targeted P3). Electrophoresis of PCR products led to the exclusion of some primers, principally because of PCR failure or migration of the corresponding PCR products into multiband profiles. In the retained primer set, we systematically selected one that amplified the shorter amplicon (Table 1), as the probability of detecting target DNA on a degraded DNA matrix (due to the digestive process) is enhanced by minimizing the amplicon size (Zaidi et al. 1999;Deagle et al. 2006;Sint et al. 2011).
The quality of DNA extraction was reasonable, and the PCR results were robust. Three quarters of the A 260 /A 230   2. For 31 faecal samples and three prey-specific primer sets, 54 amplifications succeeded, showing strong repeatability of PCR replicates (4/4), except for four PCRs for which the repeatability varied between 1/4 and 3/4. The DNA of at least one prey species was detected in all faecal samples except one (97% PCR success rate), which was the sample containing the lowest DNA concentration (6 ng ll À1 for specimen M N81 at day 3; see Data S2).
DNA of the prey species that had been fed was detected consistently in faeces 24 h after feeding. Surprisingly, Art-emia DNA was also detected 24 h after feeding with Palaemonetes and on day 2 in the faeces of one seahorse (F N89) fed wild Mysidae. Palaemonetes DNA was not detected in faeces 48 h after feeding, and use of another Palaemonetes-specific primer set confirmed this result (data not shown). In contrast, Mysidae DNA was detected in faeces 72 h after feeding in 50% of cases.
To confirm the specificity of the primer pairs, 18 randomly chosen PCR products (6 per specific primer set) were sequenced by GATC Biotech (Cologne, Germany). The BLAST on Genbank allowed identification of the sequences obtained with the Mysidae-and Artemia-specific primer set with high confidence (E-value, <E-10). Furthermore, the BLAST results showed that both Mysidae taxa were amplified (see more details in Data S6). For the amplicons obtained with the Palaemonetes-specific primer set, the corresponding sequences showed identical Max scores for numerous Genbank sequences belonging to Decapoda.
The molecular protocol for analysing the diet of H. guttulatus developed in this study includes (i) the design of preyspecific primers targeting 18SrDNA, (ii) verification of effective prey DNA extraction from the predator faecal matrix with successful PCR amplification, and (iii) validation in adequate feeding trials with the three targeted preys.
The choice of the target gene is critical in developing molecular methods for diet analysis, which should be guided by the required taxonomic level for prey identification. In this study, we developed specific discriminative primers for the three prey, with the added constraint that primers for Mysidae amplify both Leptomysis and Siriella.
COI genes generally have a higher mutation rate than nuclear genes (Brown et al. 1979;L opez et al. 1997;Ballard 2000;Mueller 2006), decreasing the percentage sequence similarity between species. In our case, sequences in COI revealed high divergence, which made it difficult to find specific regions common to the two Mysidae taxa but discriminatory for the other two prey and for the predator. Furthermore, the mutation rate among the COI in our target species was found to be homogeneous, with mutations mainly found every third codon (i.e. favouring synonymous mutations). This made it difficult to design a  species-specific primer with this gene (Harper et al. 2005, Harper et al. 2006;Admassu et al. 2006) and hampered the search of specific regions for both Mysidae taxa (see Data S4). Ribosomal genes are not protein-coding genes, and the mutation rate is heterogeneous, with alternation of hypervariable regions and more or less conserved regions, depending on the taxa (see Crease & Colbourne 1998for crustaceans, and Wuyts et al. 2001, 2002 for other Eukaryota). The mutation rate is structured by loop regions and functional regions, which can be viewed in the secondary structure of the ribosomal subunit (e.g. for 18S see Wuyts et al. 2001). In our case, the 28SrDNA gene showed high divergence between sequences, and specific regions for both Mysidae species were rare. However, Conserved regions were more frequent in 18SrRNA, allowing for the design of group-specific primers.
Ribosomal genes are generally more suitable than COI for detecting micro-organisms in the digestive system (e.g. 16SrRNA for bacterial flora, Matsuki et al. 2002;Baker et al. 2003) and are often preferred for designing groupspecific primers for prey detection in diet analysis (e.g. Dodd 2004;Vences et al. 2005). The reason commonly advanced is that ribosomal genes have a lower mutation rate than COI (e.g. discussed by Corse et al. 2013), enhancing the likelihood of specific regions (King et al. 2008). As we argue in this paper, this is due mainly to mutation rate dynamics, which are heterogeneous in ribosomal genes and homogeneous in protein-coding genes. In ribosomal genes, the mutation rate depends on the region, with higher rates in less conserved regions. In 18SrDNA, species-specific primers can be designed in regions with high mutation rates (Ward & Adams 1998), and familyspecific (Corse et al. 2010) or 'universal' primers (Miquelis et al. 2000) can be designed in regions with lower mutation rates.
Group-specific primers (e.g. for Mysidae and Decapoda) are more suitable for establishing predominant groups in trophic ecological studies of species with a wide range of prey, such as wild seahorses, than highly accurate prey determination (e.g. genus or species level). In this study, the three group-specific primer sets targeted different taxonomic levels. Mysidae primers targeted an 18SrDNA region for both taxa, Leptomysis and Siriella, which are commonly present in the habitat of seahorses and are potentially part of their diet. For Palaemonetes, we targeted a highly conserved region for Decapoda, so the primers will be suitable for detecting not only Palaemonetes in feeding trials (as no other Decapoda were used) but also the presence of Decapoda in the diet of wild individuals. For Artemia, which are not prey for seahorses in nature, the primers used were specific to that genus, as Artemia will have to be detected only in feeding trials in captivity.
Our study illustrates the trade-off that must be made in the choice of target locus and the desired taxonomic information in analysis of prey in faecal DNA. In general, we have established that in dietary studies in which highly accurate prey determination (e.g. species taxonomy) and sequencing of amplicons are required, COI is the most suitable gene (Ratnasingham & Herbert 2007;Meusnier et al. 2008). In a study that requires a higher taxonomic level (like the present study), group-specific primers can be used, and 18SrDNA is recommended.
The DNA extraction kit used in this study satisfied the quality level required for DNA-based analysis of H. guttulatus faeces. Although the mean values of A 260 /A 280 were within the range indicated by the manufacturer to prevent PCR trouble-shooting, the low A 260 /A 230 mean value would suggest that contaminants (e.g. salts or organic compounds such as peptides) were co-purified. Because of the digestion process, a low prey DNA concentration coupled with PCR inhibitors in faeces can increase the risk for false-negative results (failure of amplification when target DNA is present in the sample), which may bias diet interpretation (Deagle et al. 2005;King et al. 2008). However, the PCR success rate and the results of the reproducibility tests suggest that co-purified contaminants had a limited impact on PCR efficiency and that a purification step (e.g. with QIAGEN spin columns that eliminate co-extracted products), which might reduce the DNA concentration, is unnecessary. In only one case did faecal extraction fail to amplify at least one prey (M N81 on day 3), probably due to a low DNA concentration.
Systematic detection in faeces of the prey ingested the previous day, together with the PCR success rate, validate the accuracy of the protocol. If false-negative result bias had been important, inconsistency between the feeding trials and molecular detection or a weak PCR success rate would have been expected (Deagle et al. 2005). Our results show that the protocol allows the detection in faeces of ingested prey and the detection of prey in successive faeces varying by type of prey. For example, Mysidae were detectable in faeces up to 3 days after feeding in 50% of cases, while Palaemonetes was not detected after 2 days. Feeding trials with known prey or with selected representatives of potential prey groups allow comparisons of preyspecific gut passage or retention time and can indicate potential biases in the analysis of faeces from wild specimens (Beukers-Stewart & Jones 2004). Numerous studies of animals in captivity show that the sensitivity of molecular approaches offers an opportunity to monitor the gut passage of prey (Tollit et al. 2003;Deagle et al. 2005;Sheppard et al. 2005;Greenstone et al. 2007;Hosseini et al. 2008;Dunshea 2009;Oehm et al. 2011). As the feeding trials in our study were conducted with equivalent daily feeding ratios (dry weight) of prey, and the daily meals were fully consumed in most cases, the results reflect preyspecific differences in gut passage time. Such heterogeneous passage time may be a source of misinterpretation in prey analysis, as the frequency of detection of prey may be influenced by its retention time in the gut. For example, the consumption of a prey with a long gut retention time may be overestimated in relation to other prey with shorter passage times. Assessing differences in the passage time of different types of prey and understanding the causes should help to prevent such misinterpretation for studying wild specimens.
Gut passage time in fish is influenced by several environmental parameters, such as temperature (Bromley 1994;Bochdansky & Deibel 2001), meal size (Windell 1967;Bagge 1977;Dos Santos & Jobling 1995;Andersen 1998) and the intrinsic characteristics of the prey, such as size (e.g. Adams & Breck 1990), energy density (e.g. Windell & Norris 1969;Grove et al. 1978;Dos Santos & Jobling 1988) and digestibility (e.g. Berens & Murie 2008).
In seahorses, the temperate species H. guttulatus has a longer gut passage time than the tropical species Hippocampus kuda. In 6-month-old juvenile H. kuda fed a mixture of Artemia nauplii and Mysids, Tanu et al. (2012) observed complete clearance by gut dissection after 24-h starvation. In our study, the gut of adult H. guttulatus was not completely empty after 24 h, and ingested prey were still detectable in faeces 2-3 days later. This difference may be due not only to the species but also to the culture temperature (18 °C for H. guttulatus and 27 °C for H. kuda), which inversely correlates with gut passage time (Bromley 1994).
Prey size is often negatively correlated with gut passage rate (e.g. Mills et al. 1984;He & Wurtsbaugh 1993), although this finding should not be generalized; for example, Andersen (1999) did not observed an effect of size on gut passage time in Merlangius merlangus and reported that the energy density and biochemical composition of prey had a greater effect. With regard to the influence of prey digestibility, it was shown in yellow rockfish Sebastes chrysomelas fed on Percomorpha spp. that the crustacean exoskeleton remains longer in the fish gut than prey containing fewer indigestible hard parts (such as fish) (Hopkins & Larson 1990). In that study, it was hypothesized that enzymatic attack on the prey in the gut would be delayed due to the chitinous exoskeleton of the crustacean. The reported gut passage time of crustaceans by fish is especially heterogeneous (Tyler 1970;MacDonald et al. 1982;Dos Santos & Jobling 1995;Andersen 1999;Berens 2005), probably due to wide variation in the exoskeleton structure of different crustacean species (Bobelmann et al. 2007). In vendace (Coregonus albula) and whitefish (Coregonus lavaretus) larvae, Sutela & Huusko (2000) observed that hardbodied zooplankton (e.g. Bosmina and Daphnia spp.) was evenly distributed in the fish gut, whereas soft-bodied prey (e.g. Synchaeta and Polyarthra spp.) were concentrated in the first quarter of the gut. These studies illustrate the possible relationship between gut passage and digestibility of prey, by morphological analysis of the remaining hard parts. Although the sensitivity of the molecular methods may be different, it is likely that the presence of prey DNA in consecutive faeces also correlates with prey digestibility.
In this study, the larger prey Palaemonetes was detected for a shorter time in faeces than smaller prey, such as Mysidae. In addition, the presence of remains of Palaemonetes in faeces (Fig. 2) suggests that the exoskeleton of this prey type is poorly digestible. Mechanical structures to break down the chitinaceous exoskeletons of crustaceans are lacking in seahorses, which suck and swallow the entire prey through a simple intestinal tract with no stomach (Bergert & Wainwright 1997;Lin et al. 2007;Tanu et al. 2012). The absence of a specialized structure in the gut to permit retention of a food bolus might explain the negative correlation between prey size and prey passage time in Hippocampus. Moreover, for equal daily meals, larger prey present a smaller surface for enzymatic digestion. Unfortunately, there are no published data on digestive enzymatic activity in seahorses or other Syngnathids. A recent study of bacteria associated with the intestinal tract of H. kuda mentions characterization of bacterial extracellular enzymes, which may play a role in digestion (Tanu et al. 2012). Strong endogenous chitinase activity has been detected in fish such as rainbow trout (Lindsay et al. 1984) and cobia larvae (Fines & Holt 2010), in which there are no mechanical structures to break down the chitinous exoskeletons of crustacean prey. Further study is needed of the biochemistry and digestibility of prey and of the digestive enzymatic equipment (chitinases, proteases, lipases and carbohydrases) in H. guttulatus.
Owing to differential gut passage times, the faecal DNA matrix on any given day might reflect a number of feeding events over several days, emphasizing the need to define an adequate time frame for molecular analysis. In the present study, the temporal frame of molecular analysis in faeces ranged from 24 h (prey were always detected the day after their ingestion) to 72 h (Mysidae were detected up to 3 days after their ingestion). These results indicate that molecular analysis of faeces collected from wild seahorses reflects at least the past 72 h of feeding activity. In some seahorses that fed exclusively on Mysidae, Artemia DNA was detected in faeces released 24 h later (day 2; Table 2). As the Mysidae fed in this study were captured in the wild, they would not have Artemia in their gut. Therefore, it is feasible that Artemia DNA detected in faeces of the seahorses fed Mysidae represented residuals of Artemia fed 48 h previously, implying that prey can remain for 48 h in the gut and that 24 h of fasting is insufficient to ensure gut emptiness. Palaemonetes are also cultivated by a continuous supply of Artemia, and detection of Artemia in faeces of seahorses collected 24 h after feeding with Palemonetes (day 6) would also be due to secondary predation rather than the remains of primary consumption of Artemia (day 3).
Secondary predation occurs when a primary predator that has consumed the target prey is consumed by a second predator (or scavenger), in which the remains of the target prey are found (modified from Harwood et al. 2001). Numerous studies have shown the reliability of PCR-based methods for detecting such indirect predation using faecal DNA analysis. For example, DNA of aphids ingested by spiders was detected in the digestive tract of carabids (Sheppard et al. 2005). In contrast, et al. (2008) found potential sources of error in analyses of the diet of arthropods due to the detection of prey DNA after secondary cannibalistic and intraguild predation. Both of these studies were conducted by molecular analysis of gut contents, and, to the best of our knowledge, there are no published results on secondary predation detection in faeces of vertebrates. Secondary predation must be systematically considered to avoid false interpretation of trophic web chains (King et al. 2008). Detection of secondary predation by DNA-based methods depends on the time between ingestion of a given prey by a second prey and ingestion of the second prey by the predator. In carabids fed on spiders, Sheppard et al. (2005) detected secondary predation 20 h after ingestion of their last food, when spiders were ingested immediately after aphid consumption. The time decreased significantly (a few hours) when spiders were ingested by carabids 4 h after aphid consumption. Such studies highlight the influence of the time between the two predation events on the detection of secondary predation. In our case, the time between the ingestion of Artemia by Palaemonetes and the ingestion of Palaemonetes by Artemia was not long enough to prevent secondary predation, indicating the need for longer prey starvation in future feeding trials. Feeding trials limited to a few prey-predator interactions should be reliable for assessing the time frame of prey-predator ingestion. In more complex systems such as seahorses in nature, however, where they have a wide prey spectrum, capturing and analysing samples of the potential prey in the habitat of the predator should be the alternative to assessing secondary predation.
The agreement between the results for ingested prey and DNA analysis of faeces shows that the molecular protocol developed in this study ensures correct identification of prey fed to H. guttulatus, with no false-negative results. The method is useful for monitoring the gut passage time of prey and shows that the gut passage time of crustaceans in Hippocampus is species-dependent, probably due to differences in their digestibility and the enzymatic activity in the stomach-less gut of seahorses. Furthermore, the method is sensitive for detecting secondary predation among experimental prey. Both differential gut passage time and secondary predation should be considered to avoid misinterpretation of food regimes in wild specimens.
Hence, the technique could be used in further studies of feeding in captivity and could be adapted for studies in the wild. For example, as H. guttulatus forage mainly on crustaceans, the use of order (e.g. Decapoda)-or family (e.g. Mysidae)-specific primers within the Crustacea subphylum should be sufficiently informative for studying the feeding behaviour of this species. Coupling this strategy with nextgeneration sequencing, including a method to inhibit amplification of predator DNA (e.g. use of a selective blocking primer, Vestheim & Jarman 2008), should significantly increase the resolution of diet analysis. Nevertheless, in both cases, it will be essential to build a bank of prey from the seahorse habitat to apply the molecular approach to wild specimens. Furthermore, knowledge of the biochemical composition of the prey and their digestibility by predators would provide a better understanding of predator-prey interactions.

[SECTION] title
Improved Molecular Assay for Sex Identification of the Endangered Crested Ibis (Nipponia nippon) Based on the CHD1 Gene and a Sex-linked Microsatellite Locus

[SECTION] abstract
Sex identification of monomorphic birds, especially endangered avian species, is essential for ecological study and biodiversity conservation. In this study, two popular primer sets of 2550F/2718R and P2/P8, which were designed to amplify different fragments of chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding protein 1 (CHD1) genes mapped on both Z and W chromosomes in birds, were used to identify for the first time the sex of individuals of the endangered species crested ibis (Nipponia nippon) in a large number of samples. An improved primer set of 2467F/2530R was re-designed to be specific to crested ibis following their conserved sequences derived from the 2550F/2718R primers. PCR products of the new primers were conveniently visualized with two bands of 552 base pairs (bp) and 358 bp for females, but a single band of 552 bp for males in routine 1.8% agarose gel. Similarly, the P2/P8 primer set amplified two fragments of 398 bp and 381 bp from females but one fragment of 398 bp from males; however, a high resolution involving 10% polyacrylamide gel had to be employed to resolve the 17 bp insertions/deletions (in/dels) present between the two amplicons in females. In addition, a microsatellite locus NnNF05 was validated to be sex-linked and shown to be effective in the sexing of crested ibis, supporting its utility in non-invasive sampling. This study provides a rapid, convenient, and reliable molecular assay for improving sex identification in the monomorphic and monogamous crested ibis, and thus facilitates the selection of breeding pairs in captive programs and reintroduction initiatives.

[SECTION] introduction
It is necessary to correctly identify sex for wildlife conservation as well as evolutionary and ecological studies (Miyaki et al., 1998;Birkhead et al., 2001;Dubiec et al., 2006). In avian species, females have heterogametic sex chromosomes Z and W, whereas male birds are homogametic ZZ (Ellegren, 2001). The sex chromosome-linked chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding protein (CHD1) gene is one of the universal targets for molecular sexing in birds (e.g., Ellegren, 1996;Griffiths et al., 1996). Two homologous CHD1 genes are mapped on each W or Z chromosome. They share relatively conserved exons while carrying highly polymorphic introns, often in different nucleotide lengths between the two genes. These structural differences allow the clear differentiation of PCR amplicons from homologous fragments of the CHD1-W and CHD1-Z genes; however, the level of homology between different fragments of the two genes varies among bird species (e.g., Kahn et al., 1998). Primer sets such as 2550F/2718R (Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999), P2/P8 (Griffiths et al., 1998) and 1237L/1272H (Kahn et al., 1998) were subsequently designed to target different introns of the two genes, of which the latter two sets were found to flank the same intron (Jensen et al., 2003). Sex identification with a microsatellite locus, which requires a only minimal amount of template DNA, which can often be recovered from shed feathers, fecal samples, or historical specimens, is appropriate for non-invasive sampling, as has been reported in several bird species, such as whooping crane (Jones and Glenn, 1999) and falcon (Nesje and Røed, 2000).
The crested ibis (Nipponia nippon) is monogamous, and since 2000 has been listed as "Endangered" in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (BirdLife International, 2012). With the continuous conservation efforts made since the rediscovery of a remnant wild population in China in 1981, the population of crested ibis has increased both in the wild and in captivity (Zhang and Ding, 2008;Ding, 2004Ding, , 2010)). However, as a phenotypically monomorphic bird spe-cies, mistakes were sometimes made during the selection of breeding pairs for captive and reintroduction program. A sufficient and convenient method is needed to correctly identify the gender of individuals of this species at different ages. In the present study, the primer sets of 2550F/2718R and P2/ P8 were tested and then improved for sex identification of crested ibis. In addition, a sex-linked microsatellite locus NnNF05 was validated for non-invasive sampling.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] sampling and genomic dna extraction
Blood samples from 33 crested ibis individuals whose sexes were known from management records (20 males and 13 females) were collected from the Shaanxi Crested Ibis Captive Breeding Center, Yangxian County, Shaanxi Province, China in 2010. The blood samples were collected from wing vein and mixed with an equal volume of anticoagulant buffer (0.1 M Tris-Cl, 0.1 M EDTA and 1% SDS, pH 8.0). All the samples were stored at -80°C. Total genomic DNA was extracted following a conventional phenol/chloroform protocol (Sambrook and Russell, 2001). After qualification and quantification using a NenoDrop-1000 spectrophotometer (NanoDrop Technologies Inc., Wilmington, USA), the DNAs were diluted with TE buffer to around 100 ng/μl and stored at -20°C.

[SECTION] amplification of chd1 gene fragments using previously reported primers
Six individuals with relatively large quantity of genomic DNAs (three females and three males) were selected to test the effectiveness of PCR amplifications using the two primer sets of 2550F/ 2718R and P2/P8 with detailed sequences as reported in Fridolfsson and Ellegren (1999) and Griffiths et al. (1998), respectively. The amplification was performed in 20 μl volume containing around 50 ng DNA, 0.75 units of Taq DNA polymerase (Tiangen Biotech Co., Ltd., China), 2 μl of 10× Taq buffer, 2 μl of dNTPs (2.5 mM) and 0.3 μl each of the forward and reverse primers (10 pmol/μl). To optimize the PCR conditions, a gradient PCR program involving temperatures ranging from 50°C to 62°C was employed using a T Gradient thermal cycler (Biometra, Göttingen, Germany). The final thermal cycling was performed using a GeneAmp PCR system 9700 thermal cycler (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) started with 5 min at 94°C, and followed by 30 cycles of 40 s at 94°C, 30 s at 55°C (2550F/2718R) or 52°C (P2/P8) and 30 s at 72°C, and finished by a final extension of 7 min at 72°C. The PCR products in 3.5 μl each were resolved by 1.8% agarose gel electrophoresis containing Gold View TM Nucleic Acid Stain (SBS Genetech Co., Ltd, China) to confirm their quality and quantity. Three microliters of denatured PCR products of P2/P8 were further loaded in 10% nondenaturing polyacrylamide gel (Acr:Bis = 29:1) for 12-14 h electrophoresis in 1× TBE buffer at 4°C and 160 V, and the gel was silver stained for visualization.

[SECTION] direct sequencing and cloning of the pcr products and redesigning of primers for chd1 genes
Two strong bands around 450 bp and 650 bp each of the PCR products from one female while a single strong band around 650 bp from a male amplified with the 2550F/2718R primers (Fig. 1) were purified and then directly sequenced by the BigDye ® Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems) involving the two PCR primers.
Based on the conserved regions inside the 2550F/2718Rderived sequences (their designations were determined based on the 5′-primer sequence nucleotide of a full length murine (Mus musculus) CHD1 mRNA sequence; Delmas et al., 1993;Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999), a pair of crested ibis specific primers (2467F: 5′-CGT CAG TTT CCC TTT CAG-3′ and 2530R: 5′-CCA GTG CTT GTT TCC TCA-3′; primer designations were scored according to a complete chicken Gallus gallus CHD1 mRNA sequence with a GenBank accession number of AB465210; Okada et al., 2009) was re-designed and then applied to all individuals following the same PCR conditions but with an annealing temperature at 52°C.
The PCR product of a male bird amplified using P2/P8 primers was purified and then directly sequenced using the two PCR primers, following the same procedure as described for the 2550F/ 2718R primers. The two PCR products from a female were ligated into a pMD 18-T vector (TaKaRa, China) and transformed into DH5α-competent cells. The clones were cultured overnight on LB/ Ampicillin/IPTG/X-gal plates for blue/white selection and the positive clones were further confirmed by PCR amplification with universal primers of M13-47 and M13-48. A total of 10 positive clones were sequenced using the two M13 primers.
The raw sequencing data was manually edited using Chromas version 2.23 (http://www.technelysium.om.au/chromas,html) and aligned with MEGA5 software (Tamura et al., 2011).

[SECTION] sex-linked microsatellite locus
All 19 polymorphic microsatellite loci without chromosome assignments of crested ibis (Ji et al., 2004;He et al., 2006) were included in this study to screen for possible sex-linked marker(s) following similar PCR conditions. The denatured PCR products were loaded into a non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel, as described for P2/P8 PCR products. Microsatellite locus showing different conformations of males from females was chosen for genotyping using a fluorescent-labeled forward primer at its 5′-end and an ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems) for all the samples.

[SECTION] results
Molecular sexing involving the two previously reported primer sets for all 33 crested ibis was found to be in complete agreement with their management records, confirming the utility of these primers. However, the 2550F/2718R set showed some non-specific PCR amplifications apart from the two expected bands of approximately 450 bp and 650 bp with relatively high intensities (Fig. 1). The newly designed primers of 2467F/2530R significantly improved the PCR specificity for crested ibis. The reduced PCR products by 105 bp enhanced the relative size contract between the two PCR amplicons with easy and clear resolution in routine 1.8% agarose gel (Fig. 2; left). All females had two PCR products of 552 bp and 358 bp (the two sequences were submitted to GenBank with accession numbers of KC545379 and KC545380) while males shared a single The PCR amplification with P2/P8 primers was found to be specific and non-polymorphic for either sex across all samples (Fig. 2; right); however, the two amplicons of 398 bp and 381 bp each (the cloned sequences were submitted to GenBank with accession numbers of KC545381 and KC545382) from females had to be resolved using a 10% polyacrylamide gel (Fig. 3) for their limited 17 bp in/dels. The males only shared the 398 bp PCR amplicon.
Alignment of the four new crested ibis sequences generated with 2550F/2718R and P2/P8 primer sets against both complete mRNA sequence (AB465210) and spliced genomic DNA sequence of chicken CHD1-Z gene (between 6,228,619-6,273,882 in NW_003764319.1; Bellott et al., 2010) as well as the homologous partial CHD1-W gene (since the 8th exon in NW_003766117; International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004) using the Splign program (Kapustin et al., 2008) identified highly homologous regions in the chicken CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes. We confirmed that these two primer sets target two different introns, the former spanning the 16th and 17th exons (Fig. 4A) while the latter crossing the 22nd and 23rd exons (Fig. 4B). Further BLAST query of the 552 bp and 358 bp-long sequences against the GenBank nucleotide collections identified their high homology with the partial CHD1-Z (AY464013, 96%) and CHD1-W (AY464014, 98%) genes of black-faced spoonbill (Platalea minor; Cheng et al., 2006). The BLAST results also demonstrated that the complete long fragment (398 bp) from the P2/P8 primers was similar (90% identify) to the homologous portion of Indian vulture (Gyps indicus) CHD1-Z gene (HQ236387; Ghorpade et al., 2012) while the short fragment (381 bp) was close (94% identity) to the homologous portion of Magellanic penguin (Spheniscus magellanicus) CHD1-W gene (GU451239; Zhang et al., 2012). Taken together, these suggest the wellconserved nature of the homologous CHD1-Z and CHD1-W gene fragments across avian species.
Only one microsatellite locus, NnNF05, showed different conformations between males and females in polyacrylamide gel documentation. Based on the sequence of a cloned NnNF05 fragment (AJ699416; Ji et al., 2004), a new pair of PCR primers (NnNF05Fa: 5′-TGA AGG CAG GTG GAG AAG T-3′ and NnNF05Ra: 5′-TAT GCA GCT GAG GAG GAG A-3′) was re-designed to amplify a relatively small fragment around 170 bp that was genotyped using the Genetic Analyzer. The genotyping data illustrated that all the females had two alleles in 172 bp and 169 bp, while all males only shared the 172 bp allele.

[SECTION] discussion
Accurate sexing provides critical information for population structure monitoring which involves sex ratio data, as well as for the selection of mating pairs in any effective conservation program. Steroid sexing and karyotyping are either unreliable or time-consuming (Malagó Jr et al., 2002;von Engelhardt and Groothuis, 2005) while laparoscopy could be harmful and even lethal to some birds. For these same reasons, these methods are unsuitable for sex determination in crested ibis. Several previous studies on the molecular sex identification of crested ibis (Itoh et al., 2001;Li et al., 2001;Park et al., 2011;Kasuga et al., 2012) were all based on PCR amplifications involving different primer combinations targeting the same single fragment of W-linked EE0.6 sequence that was cloned from Oriental white stork (Itoh et al., 1997) and chicken (Ogawa et al., 1997). However, a correct identification of this EE0.6 fragment from crested ibis required a duplex PCR involving species specific primers (Park et al., 2011;Kasuga et al., 2012) as well as an internal control, e.g., the conserved exon of common W and Z chromosome-linked spindlin gene (Itoh et al., 2001) or the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene (Park et al., 2011), to exclude possible false negatives due to technical failure (Itoh et al., 2001).
The P2/P8 has been a commonly used primer set for sex identification in avian species (e.g., Griffiths, et al., 1998;Jensen et al., 2003;Cerit and Avanus, 2007); however, length differences between the CHD1-Z and CHD1-W introns were found to be varied among species and it may be necessary to use a polyacrylamide gel if such differences are to be limited (e.g., Miyaki et al., 1998;Dawson et al., 2001;Jensen et al., 2003). The length polymorphisms of CHD1-Z introns and thus resultant heterozygous CHD1-Z alleles, as found in male upland sandpiper (Bartramia longicauda), can certainly complicate the interpretation of PCR amplifications (Casey et al., 2009). When these primers were first applied to crested ibis (Kim et al., 2012), two PCR products each of CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes around 400 bp and 380 bp, respectively, were generated and proved to be very difficult to separate, even in 3% agarose gel. The products were further sequenced for the development of a duplex PCR involving two forward (pci1 and pci2) and one reverse (pci3) primers targeting two shorter fragments of 233 bp for CHD1-Z (AB620020.1) and 129 bp for CHD1-W (AB620021.1) genes, which were nearly identical to the two longer homologous P2/P8 sequences obtained in this study. The nonpolymorphic nature of either CHD1-Z or CHD1-W fragment among large number of samples nevertheless validated the utility of the P2/P8 primers in the sexing of crested ibis.
Kikuchi and Ishii (2002) adopted the P1/ P2 primers (Griffiths et al., 1996) for PCR amplification and cloning of two very short sequences from crested ibis, 64 bp each of the CHD1-W (AB049443.1) and of CHD1-Z (AB049444.1) genes, which were completely identical to our partial P2/P8 sequences located within the 23rd exon carrying three SNPs. Two of these SNPs were subsequently selected for the development of PCR-RFLPs for sex identification. However, digestion with HaeIII and MboII enzymes of PCR products from males were incomplete, making the discrimination of such digestions between males and females difficult, necessitating the use of a 6% or 8% polyacrylamide gel to resolve such small digested products. Alignment of the P1 primer sequence against to our P2/P8 sequences identified one or two nucleotide mismatches to the crested ibis CHD1-Z or CHD1-W gene, confirming the presence of non-specific amplifications of such short fragments by the P1/P2 primers (Kikuchi and Ishii, 2002).
As shown in our data, the size difference of the 16th intron was much larger than that of the 22nd intron between CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes in most bird species. Therefore, a pair of crested ibis specific primers, the 2467F/2530R flanking the 16th intron, was re-designed in this study based on the conserved DNA sequences of partial CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes first generated using the 2550F/2718R primers that were originally designed following the cDNA sequencing of chicken CHD1-W and CHD1-Z genes (Ellegren and Fridolfsson, 1997;Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999). When the oligonucleotides of the four primers were aligned to available homologous genomic DNA sequences in CHD1-W and CHD1-Z genes of different bird species (Fig. 5), the original 2550F/2718R primers showed a few mismatches across species or between these two genes in the same species, and were thus expected to lead to nonspecific amplifications, as was observed in the case of crested ibis, or even to allele drop out or null alleles (Robertson and Gemmell, 2006;Kasuga et al., 2012). The 2467F/2530R also had similar levels of mismatches across these species; thus, the concept of developing 'universal primers' for sexing different bird species must be approached cautiously (Griffiths et al., 1998;Fridolfsson and Ellegren, 1999;Dawson et al., 2001;Jensen et al., 2003;Casey et al., 2009).
In conclusion, the P2/P8 primers flanking the 22nd intron were further validated for their utility in sex identification in crested ibis, but the limited size difference of two PCR products in females complicated their discrimination. The redesigned 2467F/2530R primers targeting its 16th intron of both CHD1-Z and CHD1-W genes of crested ibis only involved a single PCR reaction with a single amplicon in males or two amplicons in females with a size difference in 194 bp within the 16th intron, which can be easily virtualized in routine agarose gel. The detection of the sex-linked microsatellite locus of NnNF05 offered an option for molecular sexing through fluorescence genotyping, which is thought to be appropriate when dealing with non-invasive samples and can also be integrated into multiplex PCRs with other microsatellite loci for population genetic studies (Jones and Glenn, 1999;Dubiec and Zagalska-Neubauer, 2006). All three sets of primers (2467F/2530R, P2/P8 and NnNF05) generated smaller PCR products from the W than from the Z alleles, ensuring the detection of W alleles following a probable preferential amplification. Therefore these primers may offer advantages in avoiding the potential problem of mistyping females as males. It is expected that the improved molecular assay for sex identification validated and developed in this study will facilitate further studies on the behavior and population ecology as well as breeding management of crested ibis.

[SECTION] title
Development and application of a molecular sexing protocol in the climate change-sensitive American pika

[SECTION] abstract
Non-invasive sampling paired with molecular sexing provides a valuable tool for the study of elusive mammals, yet species-specific assays are required to ensure accurate identifications. The American pika (Ochotona princeps) is one example, having emerged as a focal mammalian species for studies of metapopulation dynamics and extinction risk in the face of climate change. Despite extensive study, knowledge of sex-specific patterns has been limited to small sample sizes given the need for live-trapping and field-based sexing. Here we describe a molecular sexing protocol designed to reliably determine sex from non-invasively collected hair. Our polymerase chain reaction-based method co-amplifies a male-specific sex-determining gene Y fragment and a species-specific autosomal microsatellite, the accuracy of which was validated on 15 internally-sexed individuals. Subsequent application to 157 hair samples demonstrated high rates of amplification success (96.0 %) and unambiguous sex determination (94.7 %), revealing a strong male-bias in the sample and one instance of inaccurate, field-based sex identification.

[SECTION] (no title)
Traditional methods for sampling mammals include livetrapping, tagging, and morphological sexing prior to release (Wielgus and Bunnell 1994). Although effective for many species, this method is not ideal for elusive mammals that are secretive by nature, typically resulting in low sample sizes (Banks et al. 2003;Piggott and Taylor 2003). Furthermore, some species lack external genitalia resulting in difficult live-sexing (Williams et al. 2004). Due to such barriers facing the study of elusive mammals, an alternative strategy is to combine non-invasive sampling and genetic approaches. This method facilitates increased sample sizes (Banks et al. 2003) and associated inferences of population history (Morin et al. 1993) and sex-specific patterns (Zgurski and Hik 2012), while minimizing impact on the sampled individual (Taberlet and Luikart 1999).
American pika (Ochotona princeps) are small, elusive mammals of conservation concern due to the threat of contemporary climate change (Smith et al. 2004). Applying non-invasive sampling and genetic approaches to the study of pikas is of great importance, as they are difficult to live trap, have poorly distinguished genitalia (Duke 1951), and are easily stressed (MacArthur and Wang 1974;Smith 1974). Previous work tested a polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis of the sex-linked zinc finger gene (ZFX/ZFY) modified from Fontanesi et al. (2008), which had limited amplification success due to the large fragment size (*430 bp) and the degraded nature of the DNA that is characteristic of using hair as a starting material (Henry and Russello 2011).
Here, we developed a molecular sexing protocol designed to reliably identify sex in American pika using non-invasively collected hair samples.
Our method uses a multiplex PCR to co-amplify fragments of the sex-determining gene Y (SRY; *117 bp, malespecific) and a higher molecular weight (179-203 bp), species-specific autosomal microsatellite [Ocp10; Peacock et al., unpublished (Genbank Acc. No. GQ461705)], using a multi-tube approach (Taberlet et al. 1996). Molecular sexing using the SRY fragment has been previously employed in mammals (Palsbøll and Vader 1992;Vanpe ´et al. 2013); however, to our knowledge this method has not been applied to American pika. Our assay was designed based on the following parameters: (1) a small fragment size for SRY to enable amplification from degraded DNA; (2) a larger autosomal, species-specific fragment to act as a positive PCR control; and (3) sufficient size differential to enable agarose gel electrophoretic detection of multiple bands.
DNA extraction protocols for liver (n = 7) and hair (n = 177) samples followed Henry and Russello (2011) (see below for sample details). PCRs were carried out on an ABI Veriti thermal cycler in 12.5 lL reactions containing: 5-10 ng DNA, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 50 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.8 lM of each SRY primer (Table 1), 0.8 lM of each microsatellite primer (Table 1), 200 lM dNTPs, 10 lg bovine serum albumin, and 1U AmpliTaq Gold DNA polymerase (ABI). Cycling parameters were: 95 °C for 10 min, 40 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 48 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s, and a final extension at 72 °C for 7 min. PCR products were run on a 1.5 % agarose gel containing 2.5 % SYBR Safe (Invitrogen). Samples with the Ocp10 and SRY fragments present were males, and samples with only the Ocp10 were females (Fig. 1).
This protocol was validated using samples from individuals of known sex and multiple starting materials (eight hair, seven liver), all of which were accurately diagnosed using our method. The protocol was subsequently applied to 157 pika hair samples collected from a population in Oregon, USA that were previously identified as unique individuals of unknown sex through microsatellite genotyping (Robson 2013). The assay was repeated twice for each sample; in cases of incongruence, a third replicate was performed and a majority rule was applied. Overall, 150 (96.0 %) of the samples were successfully amplified, 142 (94.7 %) of which showed no inconsistency in sex determination between trials. Of the eight (5.3 %) samples that showed an inconsistency, four experienced allelic dropout of the SRY fragment between trials while the other four exhibited an incorrect size for the SRY lower molecular weight band. It should be noted that previously successful microsatellite genotyping of these samples might have reduced the occurrence of false alleles. The resulting sex ratio was male-skewed (60 % male: 40 % female); however, the degree to which this pattern is biologically meaningful or prone to ascertainment bias associated with the sampling method requires further study. This method was also applied to 12 hair samples collected from livetrapped individuals during an independent study of American pikas in British Columbia in order to confirm field-based sex identification. Of the 12 samples molecularly sexed, 11 were correctly identified in the field (data not shown). The lone discrepancy involved a juvenile, demonstrating the utility of the molecular test for  In summary, our method provided high rates amplification success and reliable sex identification in the American pika from non-invasively collected hair samples. When paired with genotypic data, this molecular sexing approach will enable future studies of population and demographic history in this temperature-sensitive mammal of conservation significance.

FILE: Habitat fragmentation and its implications for Endangered chimpanzee Pan troglodytes conservation. .grobid.tei (1).xml

[SECTION] title
Habitat fragmentation and its implications for Endangered chimpanzee Pan troglodytes conservation

[SECTION] abstract
Taraba State, Nigeria, is an important conservation site for the Endangered Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee Pan troglodytes ellioti. Gashaka Gumti National Park, Nigeria's largest national park and home to potentially the largest contiguous population of the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee, spans a significant portion of the eastern sector of Taraba and the adjoining Adamawa State. South of the Park, Ngel Nyaki Forest Reserve comprises two forest fragments and holds a small population of chimpanzees. We investigated the existence of patterns in population structure and dispersal within this region, using microsatellite loci extracted from non-invasive sources of DNA. Our results indicate that dispersal and thus gene flow between the groups of chimpanzees at the Park and Reserve is limited, at least more so than it is within the Park, and we identified a biased sex ratio at the Reserve, forewarning of potential conservation concerns in relation to demographic and genetic stochasticity. We discuss conservation actions that may be applicable to sustaining the population within Ngel Nyaki Forest Reserve.

[SECTION] (no title)
T he forest fragments of southern Taraba State, Nigeria, have been recognized as an important conservation site for the Endangered Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee Pan troglodytes ellioti (Morgan et al., ). Chimpanzees are threatened primarily by deforestation and illegal poaching for the bushmeat trade (Kormos et al., ; Morgan et al., ). Within Taraba State both Gashaka Gumti National Park (, km  ) and Ngel Nyaki Forest Reserve (c.  km  ; Fig. ) have relatively high levels of protection for the region. Both are patrolled by rangers and have research stations within or on the periphery of their forest. Researchers and assistants conduct work throughout the forests, providing a practical deterrent to poachers, at least in certain areas. Gashaka Gumti is Nigeria's largest national park; in contrast Ngel Nyaki comprises two small forest fragments. The chimpanzee population in Gashaka Gumti is estimated to be c. , individuals (Morgan et al., ). In Ngel Nyaki nest count surveys have estimated the population to be c.  individuals (Beck & Chapman, ) but observations indicate there may be as many as  (Dutton, ). Little is known about the ranging behaviour of the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee and whether it varies from that of other subspecies, but population genetic theory dictates that stochastic factors having a negative impact on persistence become increasingly important in determining the viability of diminishing and isolated populations (Frankham et al., ). Gashaka Gumti and Ngel Nyaki are bisected by one of the few paved roads in the region (Fig. ). The villages of Yelwa and Maisamari are located along the section of the road between the Park and the Reserve and are surrounded by agricultural land. We investigated the population structure and patterns in dispersal and gene flow between the Park and the Reserve, using microsatellites extracted from non-invasive sources of DNA.
During January-April  a total of  faecal samples were collected in Gashaka Gumti and Ngel Nyaki, of which  yielded amplifiable DNA. From these  samples we identified  unique genotypes, using a multiple tubes procedure (Navidi et al., ). The number of amplifications required to confirm a genotype was determined by a probability formula; heterozygotes were amplified at a minimum twice per allele (with at least one visible heterozygote), and homozygotes three times, with the exception of one locus. As a result of higher rates of allelic dropout and false alleles at this locus, heterozygotes were amplified a minimum of three times, and homozygotes four times (Morin et al., ). The majority of the samples were typed for - loci, three samples were typed for six loci, one for five loci, and another for four loci.
We found no evidence of departures from Hardy-Weinburg equilibrium, or of linkage disequilibrium. We tested for isolation by distance using a mantel test and found a correlation between genetic dissimilarity and geographical distance (r = ., P = .) when all the samples were included in the analysis. There was no correlation (r = ., P = .) when the analysis was restricted to samples collected only in Gashaka Gumti. We investigated potential patterns in population structure using an AMOVA (analysis of molecular variance), which indicated that the samples we collected in Gashaka Gumti may be from two groups of chimpanzees, one located in the eastern sector of the Park and one in the central and south-west (F ST = ., P = .). The samples from Ngel Nyaki appeared to be from a third distinct group (F ST = ., P = . and F ST = ., P = ., respectively). We used an assignment test to examine dispersal and gene flow among these groups. Assignment tests generate log likelihood values based on allele frequencies for samples belonging to any pre-designated populations. When individuals are misassigned this may indicate dispersal among the pair of populations being tested, or that allele frequencies are not sufficiently different for the test to be able to discern the true population of origin, potentially as a result of gene flow among the populations. When the samples were grouped according to the results of the AMOVA, seven of the  (%) samples collected in Gashaka Gumti were misassigned to either the eastern or central/south-west group (Fig. Our results indicate that the group of samples from Ngel Nyaki represents a genetically distinct population from the group or groups residing in Gashaka Gumti. This may be attributable to the distance between the two regions, or it may be because the lack of forest, land use, and relatively higher human population density act as a barrier to dispersal. Excluding Gashaka Gumti, the nearest chimpanzee population, to the best of our knowledge, is located  km south. Whether it is possible for chimpanzees to traverse this distance is unknown. There are unsurveyed regions in the vicinity of Ngel Nyaki that could potentially harbour viable chimpanzee populations (Morgan et al., ). The results of the AMOVA suggest there may be at least two genetically distinct groups of chimpanzees within Gashaka Gumti. Chimpanzees are known to form male philopatric communities (Wilson & Wrangham, ), and both of these groups would contain multiple males, which could be driving the genetic differentiation. The assignment test, however, misassigned a significant proportion of the individuals in these groups, suggesting frequent dispersal resulting in gene flow. There were comparatively lower frequencies of misassignments in comparisons between Ngel Nyaki and the groups within Gashaka Gumti, suggesting that individuals do not disperse as frequently between these locations, and gene flow is less common than within the Park. As the log likelihood values are based on allele frequencies, the outcome of the test is dependent on sample size. The sample sizes are modest, and therefore the results should be interpreted with caution.
If the population at Ngel Nyaki is isolated from the National Park, conservation measures need to be considered if it is to be sustained into the future. Investigating whether any other populations exist to the south, east or west, and whether there is any evidence of connectivity between these should be a priority. A complete demographic profile of the population at Ngel Nyaki is critical for making the most informed decisions. We identified eight individuals, of which one was male. If this accurately reflects the sex ratio, the population is already at immediate risk of extinction, from the loss of one sex. However, observations indicate that the population may be larger; if so, knowing the sex ratio will help determine several factors, including the probability of persistence and the rate at which genetic diversity may be lost. The mean expected heterozygosity was ., similar to that reported from a sample of  chimpanzees in Côte d'Ivoire (., Boesch et al., ). The biased sex ratio could result in a rapid reduction in genetic diversity (Frankham et al., ), and therefore we recommend continual monitoring of the population at Ngel Nyaki. Given that a female's inter-birth interval is c.  years (Wallis, ), surveying the genetic diversity in the population should be undertaken every - years to record new births.
Theory suggests that in a population of this size the negative effects of inbreeding depression are a serious concern, and strategies to combat this should be formulated (Frankham, ). Mitigating the accumulation of deleterious alleles requires the introduction of genetic diversity (Frankham, ). If it is apparent that there is no connectivity between Ngel Nyaki and any other region, Gashaka Gumti holds the closest population from which this is possible. A wildlife corridor between the two regions could potentially encourage natural gene flow, although mitigating deforestation in the region is already problematic and the distance between the two regions is not trivial. We consider this endeavour to be worthwhile, however, as it would also benefit other species. Translocation of chimpanzees is another potential solution but this has had mixed results and is complicated by the territorial nature of male chimpanzees (Goossens et al., , ). If there is only one male at Ngel Nyaki and this male dies then attempting male translocation should be considered, but as long as surveys and observations indicate that there are males present this is not a viable solution. Considering that the level of genetic diversity is not dissimilar to that of a larger population, the risk of introducing pathogens, and the number of females present at Ngel Nyaki, translocation of a female to introduce genetic diversity does not seem warranted at this stage. We recommend monitoring of the population at regular intervals, and discussion regarding the feasibility of constructing a wildlife corridor. The Reserve has been designated a Centre for Technical Forest Science, and the presence of a well-established research station makes it a suitable location to observe and study this rare and elusive subspecies.
