[SECTION] title
Estimating Sex-Specific Abundance in Fawning Areas of a High-Density Columbian Black-Tailed Deer Population Using Fecal DNA

[SECTION] abstract
The recent development of fecal-genetic capture-mark-recapture (CMR) methods has increased the feasibility of estimating abundance of forest-dwelling ungulates that are difficult to survey using visual methods. Unless genetic markers differentiating sex are incorporated into such studies, however, genetic CMR approaches risk missing sex-specific differences in population trends. We developed a singlereaction genetic assay for sex and individual identification, including 10 microsatellites and an SRY marker, and applied it in the context of a post-fawning CMR study of Columbian black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus) in forested habitat of coastal California during 2011 and 2012. We measured sexspecific abundance and sex ratios in high-quality summer habitats encompassing 4 distinct fawning areas. We detected a significant interaction between sex and year, indicating different trends in the abundance of males and females. We also detected a significant decline in abundance of females between years (P ¼ 0.045), which agreed with independent telemetry-based estimates, and significant differences in female abundance among fawning areas (P ¼ 0.020) but no significant differences in the abundance of males for either variable (F 1-3,20 < 0.710, P > 0.410). When sex was not considered in the analysis, we found no significant differences in abundance between the 2 years, suggesting that differing trends between the 2 sexes obscured the femalespecific patterns. We estimated average local (i.e., on the high-quality summer ranges) density ( D) for females at 41.0 (AE 5.9) deer/km 2 in 2011 and 29.1 (AE 6.8) deer/km 2 in 2012, and local density of males at 15.7 (AE 3.0) deer/km 2 across the 2 study years. Accordingly, sex ratios differed between years (95% CI ¼ 3.0-4.2 F:M ratio in 2011, 2.0-2.3 F:M ratio in 2012). Incorporating sex and individual markers into a single assay provided a cost-effective means of applying CMR estimation based on fecal DNA to a high-density ungulate population in a forested ecosystem and emphasized the importance of explicitly modeling sex in abundance estimation.

[SECTION] (no title)
the relative importance of top-down versus bottom-up factors affecting population growth rates, which requires information on population abundance (and habitat quality), is fundamental to effective management of ungulate populations (Morellet et al. 2007, Pierce et al. 2012b, Monteith et al. 2014).
Management of ungulate populations also requires an understanding of their demographic composition at any given point in time and potential differences in population trends between sexes (McCullough 1999). Female abundance and trends are particularly important determinants of overall population growth (Gaillard et al. 2000). Because male and female ungulates exhibit different life histories, home range sizes, habitat use patterns, and cause-specific mortality rates, including differential harvest rates from hunting, sex-specific relative abundance estimates are especially valuable (Connolly 1981, Geist 1981, Ebert et al. 2012).
Most traditional approaches to monitoring abundance and composition of ungulate populations involve use of distance sampling through aerial counts or other means, indices (e.g., sign counts, relative abundance counts) or, more recently, capture-mark-recapture (CMR) approaches (Mowat andStrobeck 2000, Acevedo et al. 2008). Each methodology has significant downsides that limit its value or feasibility. Aerial transect counts are expensive, can be hazardous, and unless corrected for sightability using marked individuals (e.g., Wittmer et al. 2005) typically result in imprecise estimates of abundance (Caughley 1974, Bartmann et al. 1986). Aerial surveys also are less feasible in forested habitats where trees obscure sight. Indirect approaches (e.g., pellet deposition counts) yield less accurate correlates of abundance (Fuller 1991) that are less amenable to comparisons among study sites (Morellet et al. 2007). Estimating accurate sex ratios from count surveys also is difficult because of biases associated with differential behavior and microhabitat use of males and females (McCullough 1994) or an inability to differentiate young, antlerless males from females (Wittmer et al. 2005). The CMR methods on the other hand provide statistically robust abundance estimates but involve costly, often invasive capture procedures and require large sample sizes to achieve a useful degree of precision (Pierce et al. 2012a).
The advent of molecular genetic techniques sensitive enough to obtain individual-specific genotypes from lowquantity DNA sources such as fecal pellets and hair has recently opened up promising avenues for adopting CMR approaches to noninvasive sampling schemes (Lukacs and Burnham 2005, Harris et al. 2010, Brinkman et al. 2011). Unique genotypes obtained from DNA in noninvasively collected fecal pellets or hair samples can be used to identify individuals upon initial capture (i.e., identification via DNA) and recapture, enabling the pellet or hair samples to take the place of physically marked individuals. Fecal DNA also can be used to accurately differentiate sexes (e.g., Brinkman andHundertmark 2009, Ebert et al. 2012) and assess sex ratios (e.g., before vs. after harvest; Pierce et al. 2012a). Lastly, the genotypic data generated in such approaches can be used for additional purposes, such as to evaluate genetic diversity or familial relationships (Waits and Paetkau 2005, Yoshizaki 2007, Colson et al. 2013).
Here, we describe a sex-specific CMR study of a Columbian black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus columbianus) population in northern California. The genetic diversity of these deer is among the highest of the species, suggesting correspondingly high density (Latch et al. 2014). Previous studies demonstrated the utility of CMR methods for sexagnostic abundance estimation in low-density deer populations (e.g., Brinkman et al. 2011). The application of CMR approaches to a high-density population affords the advantage of facilitating larger samples sizes and, therefore, the greater feasibility to obtain sex-specific estimates of abundance. On the other hand, larger samples sizes also entail greater expense, necessitating efficiencies to reduce per-sample costs. Therefore, we developed a single DNA-based assay composed of 11 markers to simultaneously estimate sex and individual, which we applied in a CMR framework to estimate the relative abundances of male and female deer among 4 separate fawning areas over 2 years. Specific objectives were to 1) estimate deer abundance from fecal samples collected from 4 summer-range fawning areas within a 150-km 2 area using discrete CMR models, 2) estimate sex ratios using direct (sex-specific pellet counts) and indirect (sex-specific abundance estimates) approaches, and 3) compare these metrics over time and space to explore the potential for this approach to detect spatiotemporal heterogeneity. Lastly, we evaluated these results in the context of demographic parameters estimated during a concurrent 4-year telemetry study based on 136 fawns and 57 females older than 1 year of age from the same population (Marescot et al. 2015).

[SECTION] study area
We conducted our study in the Mendocino National Forest in northern California, USA (Fig. 1). The topography is mountainous with elevations ranging from approximately 400 m to 2,000 m. Climate is considered Mediterranean with generally mild winter temperatures. Average annual precipitation was 132 cm, the majority of which occurred between December and March. Below 1,000 m, winter precipitation was predominantly in the form of rain. During summers, there is little precipitation and humidity is low, which are ideal conditions for DNA preservation on fecal pellets. A detailed description of the vegetation communities can be found in Allen et al. (2014). Black-tailed deer are the only ungulate species traditionally occurring in the study area. Although a recent study reported mule-deer introgression in some northern California Columbian blacktailed deer populations (Latch et al. 2014), we found no evidence of substantial mule deer ancestry in this population based either on morphological characteristics or on sequencing of mitochondrial D-loop DNA (J. L. Brazeal, University of California, unpublished data). Specifically, comparison of sequences (450 bp) from 49 deer captured in the study area (Marescot et al. 2015) all matched or clustered with previously published Columbian black-tailed deer haplotypes and none with continental mule deer haplotypes (Latch et al. 2009;J. L. Brazeal, unpublished data).

[SECTION] methods
The area over which we collected deer pellets extended approximately 150 km 2 and encompassed 4 areas of high quality deer summer habitat. Female deer concentrated in these high quality habitats to give birth and so we refer to them as fawning areas (Cold Spring, Plaskett Meadow, Coyote Rock, and Cherry Hill/Tar Flat; Fig. 1). In each of the 4 distinct fawning areas, we defined a 20-km 2 (5 Â 4 km) sample plot covering a range of elevations including summer habitat used by both sexes. Within each sample plot, we established 4-6 (2011) or 6 (2012) 1.2-km long, 2-m wide belt transects (14,400 m 2 total area), each of which began at a random point in the plot and followed deer trails (when present) that were closest to a random compass bearing, similarly to a previous study of Sitka black-tailed deer (O. h. sitkensis) by Brinkman et al. (2011). We ensured that no portion of any transect was <1.5 km from any other transect; this minimum distance was greater than the average diameter of an adult female home range (McCorquodale 1999, Forrester 2014), ensuring that each transect was an independent sample unit.
For practical reasons associated with a companion study (Marescot et al. 2015), the seasonal timing of our sampling occurred after the birth of fawns each year, such that our abundance and sex ratio estimates included fawns. We sampled transects twice during 2011 (22 Aug-23 Sep) and 4 times during 2012 (16 Jul-19 Sep), with each sampling event separated by 7-10 days in both years. Because of a forest fire, 2 transects in 2012 had to be relocated after the first sampling period and were thus sampled only 3 times. On the first sampling occasion, we collected fresh pellets with a mucous sheen and attempted to clear all pellets from within the 2-m transect, as well as 1 m beyond the boundary on either side. During subsequent surveys, we collected pellets from all groups, presumably deposited since the previous sampling occasion, and cleared remaining pellets from 1-2 m beyond either side. For each pellet group, we recorded the date, time, global positioning system (GPS) waypoint, and habitat description. We collected 4-6 pellets from each pellet group in a tube containing 95-100% ethanol and transferred them to the Mammalian Ecology and Conservation Unit of the University of California Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory for processing.

[SECTION] dna analysis
We developed an assay for fecal genotyping that included 10 microsatellites and 1 sex-typing marker (a highly conserved portion of the SRY gene on the Y chromosome for sex determination; Table 1). We selected these markers from 24 previously published loci (22 microsatellites, 2 sex markers) originally developed for a variety of ruminants on the basis of their performance on both tissue and fecal DNA (Olegario 2013). To characterize parameters (e.g., polymorphism, sexspecificity) of the 11 selected markers in the present population, we used DNA extracted from ear-punch tissue samples collected from 32 individuals (25 adult females, 7 male fawns) during captures for a concurrent study (Marescot et al. 2015). We extracted DNA from deer tissue using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) as per manufacturers protocols. We extracted DNA from the surfaces of fecal pellets in batches of 11 samples with 1 blank as a negative control to assess possible contamination following a protocol modified from Brinkman et al. (2010). We first dried 2 to 4 pellets at 21 8C for 45 minutes to remove residual ethanol. Next, we washed the outside of the pellets in sterile 20-ml scintillation vials with 1 ml to 1.5 ml buffer ATL (Qiagen) for 1 hour. We then used the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit according to manufacturer protocols for blood to extract DNA from the resulting suspension of epithelial cells. We amplified microsatellite markers and the sex marker using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with a Qiagen multiplex PCR kit (Qiagen). The PCR mixtures contained 1 ml genomic DNA extract, 0.5 ml RNase-free water, 5.0 ml Qiagen Multiplex Mastermix, 1.0 ml Q-solution, and 2.5 ml primer mixture (Table 1). We amplified DNA using a thermal profile consisting of a 15-minute denaturing step at 95 8C followed by 33 cycles combining a 30-second denaturation step at 94 8C, a 1.5-minute annealing step at 58 8C, and a 1-minute extension step at 72 8C followed by a final extension step for 10 minutes at 72 8C. We genotyped samples using an ABI 3730 (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, NY) and internal size standards (500-LIZ; Applied Biosystems). We manually scored alleles using electropherograms visualized in Program STRand (version 2.4.89), which provisionally bins DNA fragments into discrete size categories (i.e., alleles) relative to the internal size standards (Toonen and Hughes 2001).
Using the 32 high-quality (tissue) DNA samples, we estimated the average number of alleles per locus (N A ), observed heterozygosity (H O ), expected heterozygosity (H E ), and polymorphic informative content (PIC) using Microsatellite Toolkit (Park 2001). We assessed departures from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) and linkage disequilibrium (LD) using Arlequin Version 3.5 (Excoffier and Lischer 2010). We corrected for multiple comparisons using the sequential Bonferroni correction (Rice 1989). We calculated the probability of identity (P ID ) and, more conservatively, probability of identity for siblings (P ID Sibs) for our loci and the entire multilocus assay (Paetkau andStrobeck 1994, Waits et al. 2001). We also used the average locus-specific P ID and P ID Sibs estimates to calculate probabilities of agreement at 9 loci, 8 loci, 7 loci, etc. Specifically, we used the following probability calculations:
where 10 was the total number of loci, n was the number of matching loci between 2 genotypes, and p was the average locus-specific P ID or P ID Sibs estimate.
The DNA extracted from fecal pellets is typically low quantity and fragmented, necessitating replicate PCRs to reduce rates of allelic dropout in composite genotypes (Bonin et al. 2004). We randomly selected a subset of DNA samples to estimate allelic dropout and false allele rates. We conducted 4 independent PCRs and electrophoresis runs, and genotyped each sample blindly. We excluded from the analysis samples that did not successfully amplify !9 loci in any of the runs. For each of the 47 remaining samples, we produced a composite genotype based on all 4 replicates, and estimated allelic dropout and false alleles based on comparison of individual replicates to composite genotypes (Bonin et al. 2004, Pompanon et al. 2005). Specifically, we identified each of the 470 locus-samples (i.e., 47 samples Â 10 loci) as a heterozygote or homozygote. We then estimated the allelic dropout rate as the proportion of replicate genotypes corresponding to heterozygous locussamples that were homozygous in state. Tentative false alleles were identified when more than 2 alleles were present among the 4 replicates or as an allele unique to a single replicate when the other 3 replicates were homozygous for a different allele. Although we did not find any, we would have confirmed tentative false alleles through additional replications. These estimates represented average per-replicate error rates across all loci. For all other samples in this study, we used a minimum of 2 replicates to form a composite genotype for each sample (see below). Therefore, we squared the per-replicate error frequencies to obtain the minimum expected composite-genotype error frequencies.
Based on the allelic dropout rates estimated in the previous step, we devised a protocol to optimize replication effort. We initially genotyped all samples twice using independent PCRs and based further replication on their quality. Specifically, we considered those samples yielding highquality genotypes (i.e., successful amplification at !7 loci and all loci represented in at least 1 replicate) to be complete based on the 2 replicates. We replicated moderate to lowquality genotypes (first 2 replicates amplifying 4-6 loci with some peak heights higher than standards) up to 5 additional times (for a total of 3-7 replicates) and excluded genotypes with !1 locus missing from composite genotypes from further analyses. We combined replicates into composite genotypes (i.e., 1 per fecal sample) for downstream analyses by assigning any allele that occurred in at least 1 replicate to the composite genotype in Program Gimlet (Valie `re 2002). Any genotyping error remaining after replication and integration into the final composite genotype would result in the possibility that 2 samples from the same individual could have non-identical genotypes (Creel et al. 2003). Conversely, 2 distinct individuals could share the same genotype by chance, with probabilities depending on the polymorphism of our loci (i.e, shadow effect; Mills et al. 2000). Each of these problems would cause biases in downstream abundance estimation. Therefore, we accounted for these potential sources of error by selecting thresholds to minimize or eliminate them (McKelvey and Schwartz 2004). We used the match probabilities described above (eq 1) to select an upper limit of genotype match agreement expected between 2 distinct individuals and used genotyping error frequencies to estimate the lower limit of match agreement expected from 2 genotypes from the same individual. We chose a threshold number of mismatches to distinguish same versus different individuals that would minimize both types of error: incorrectly assigning different (i.e., imperfect) genotypes from the same individual to multiple individuals or failing to distinguish distinct individuals. We then used a pairwise genotype-matching analysis performed in the AlleleMatch package in R to assign composite genotypes to unique individuals based on this estimated maximum threshold number of mismatching loci (Galpern et al. 2012, R Core Team 2012).

[SECTION] population abundance estimates
Because fawn mortality was non-negligible during the sampling periods (Marescot et al. 2015), ours was not in fact a closed population during the survey. Nevertheless, for purposes of analysis, we tested models that assumed a closed population within sample years because such models have fewer parameters and we expected that our sampling periods were sufficiently brief to minimize confounding effects of deaths. We estimated abundance ( N ) for each transect in each year using the Huggins closed capture models in Program MARK (Huggins 1989, White andBurnham 1999), and evaluated whether violations of the populationclosure assumption were statistically detectable. Specifically, we compared the closed-population model to the openpopulation Jolly-Seber model in CloseTest version 3 (Stanley andBurnham 1999, Stanley andRichards 2005). We applied a sequential Bonferroni correction to guard against inflated type I errors associated with multiple comparisons (Rice 1989). Because we sampled transects 4 times in 2012 and only twice in 2011, we had both more reason to expect violations of closure and sufficient statistical power to test the assumptions of closure in 2012. Therefore, we performed tests (for each transect) in 2012, reasoning that if it was not a statistical problem in this year, it likely was not in 2011 either. Along with population closure, we assumed that capture and recapture probability were equivalent because our noninvasive sampling technique was unlikely to affect pellet deposition by deer. Because we sampled only pellets with a mucous sheen (i.e., recently deposited pellets) on the first capture occasion, we assumed that our initial captures were within approximately the same post-deposition timeframe as our recaptures. Thus, to minimize the use of unnecessary parameters, our model included constant capture probability (p) equal to recapture probability (c) for the entire study area. For each year, we combined all encounter histories into a single input file and treated transects as unique groups to estimate p and transect-specific N . We considered multiple captures of the same individual within a sampling occasion a single capture event. We never sampled the same individual on multiple transects in a single sampling occasion. For each transect, we estimated both sexagnostic and sex-specific N . We excluded 2 transects that were affected by the forest fire in 2012 from the Huggins models because they were sampled only 3 times.
Calculation of density estimates from abundance estimates adds another level of uncertainty, in particular uncertainty associated with assumptions about the effective area sampled. Nevertheless, for comparative purposes it can be useful to calculate such estimates with the explicit understanding that they are meaningful only within the context of similarly calculated estimates. Therefore, to convert our abundance estimates to local density estimates ( D), we divided N by the estimated effective area represented by the transect (A ˆ; Parmenter et al. 2003), which we calculated similarly to Brinkman et al. (2011). First, we determined the maximum distance between any 2 samples for each resampled individual. Second, we estimated the median among these individual maximum distances-the median maximum recapture distance (MMRD). Third, we created a buffer beyond the original 2-m wide by 1.2-km long transects equal to the MMRD and used the resulting buffered area as our estimate of A ˆ. To assess abundance differences by sex, year, and fawning area, we compared 2 quantities as dependent variables reflecting abundance: the raw estimates of numbers of individuals sampled (i.e., minimum numbers) and the CMR estimates of abundance ( N ). We treated transects as the sample units and compiled data and estimates for each sex, year, and fawning area separately. To assess interactions, we applied a fully factorial, 2-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for each dependent variable with sex (F, M), year (2011,2012), and fawning area (Cold Spring, Plaskett Meadow, Coyote Rock, and Cherry Hill/Tar Flat) as the independent variables (Zar 1984). Because sampling occasions differed between years, we also conducted a parallel set of analyses based solely on the first 2 transect checks in 2012 to achieve a balanced design. We found no qualitative differences between these analyses and those based on the full data set and therefore present only the latter results. We estimated sex ratios based both on numbers of individuals genotyped and CMR estimates of abundance. To obtain confidence intervals on sex ratio estimates, we expressed them as proportions of samples that were female, estimated 95% confidence limits for these proportions based on the relationship between the F and binomial distributions (Zar 1984), and then back-transformed confidence limits to ratios [i.e., 1/(1 À p)].

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] dna analysis
We estimated the genetic diversity statistics corresponding to the 10 microsatellite markers based on the 32 high-quality deer tissue samples (Table 2). We found no significant linkage disequilibrium, but 2 loci deviated significantly from Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium, CERVID1 and SBTD05, possibly indicating null alleles. As expected, all 7 males were positive for the SRY (Y-chromosome) marker and were hemizygous for the X-linked CELB9 marker, and all 25 females were negative for the SRY locus and were heterozygous or homozygous for the CELB9 locus, consistent with expected inheritance patterns for these sex-linked markers. We calculated the P ID and P ID Sibs conservatively using only the 7 (of 10) microsatellite loci remaining after excluding the X-linked locus and the 2 loci potentially containing null alleles (Table 2). These estimates indicated a negligible probability (<10 À7 ) that 2 randomly selected deer would share identical genotypes and a 1 in 500 chance that 2 siblings would share the same genotype at these 7 loci. The high polymorphism of the 3 additional microsatellite loci (i.e., with X-linkage or possible null alleles) along with the sex-marker increased the resolving power of this assay well beyond these estimates. Based on the conservative P ID and P ID Sibs estimates, this suite of loci should result in essentially all randomly paired individuals (and 98% of siblings) sharing no more than 7 of their 10 loci (Fig. 2). We collected 1,540 pellet samples during our 2-year sampling period. Of these, 1,016 (66%) pellet samples yielded genotypes with !7 microsatellite loci, and 760 (49%) yielded genotypes with all 10 microsatellite loci (Fig. 3). Based on a subsample of 47 samples successfully genotyped 4 times and which yielded !9 amplified loci in 1 or more of the genotypes, we observed allelic dropouts in 1.8% of locusreplicates and no false alleles. This per-replicate error rate corresponded to an estimated allelic dropout rate of 0.03% in genotypes composed from 2 replicates and implied a probability >99.6% that 2 10-locus genotypes of the same individual would agree at !9 loci. Therefore, we chose as our threshold 2 locus mismatches, at or below which genotypes were considered to derive from the same individual and above which genotypes were considered to derive from distinct individuals. We also confirmed that all mismatches could be explained solely by allelic dropout. Empirically, plotting all pairwise differences of numbers of mismatches among all 10locus composite genotypes used in this study revealed a clear bimodal distribution with all comparisons differing either by >3 or <3 loci, but almost never by exactly 3 loci (Fig. 4). Thus, the suite of loci in the assay appeared sufficient to ensure unambiguous assignment of distinct genotypes to the same or different individuals with high confidence.

[SECTION] population abundance indexes and estimates
Of the 760 pellet samples that yielded full genotypes, we identified 404 unique individuals, 9 of which were represented in both years (Fig. 3). The overall sex ratio in numbers of individuals sampled was 2.72 F:M (95% CI ¼ 2.15-3.47), which differed between 2011 (3.68, 95% CI ¼ 2.94-4.74) and 2012 (2.27, 95% CI ¼ 2.05-2.53). Capture probability (p) estimates were similar for females and males but generally higher in 2011 (p F ¼ 0.35, 95% CI ¼ 0.25-0.46; p M ¼ 0.32, 95% CI ¼ 0.17-0.54) than in 2012 (p F ¼ 0.22, 95% CI ¼ 0.18-0.26; p M ¼ 0.19, 95% CI ¼ 0.14-0.27). For most transects in 2012, our Stanley and Burnham Closure Test revealed no significant violations of model assumptions among all transects (P ! 0.25). However, Plaskett Meadows showed significant violation of closure (P ¼ 0.002) due to apparent additions during Table 2. Descriptive statistics of 10 microsatellite loci, including number of alleles (N A ), size range in base-pairs (bp), expected heterozygosity (H E ), observed heterozygosity (H O ), polymorphic information content (PIC), inbreeding coefficient (F IS ), and probabilities of identity of siblings (P ID Sibs) and of randomly selected individuals (P ID ) using 32 black-tailed deer tissue samples from Mendocino National Forest, California in 2011 and 2012. encounter 2 and losses during encounter 3. To test if our model was robust to this violation, we performed and compared CMR analyses based only on the first 2 encounter histories to those based only on the last 2 encounter histories in 2012 (i.e., 2 shorter, independent measurements of the same transect). A paired t-test among the 6 Plaskett Meadow transects indicated no significant difference in the estimates (t 5 ¼ 0.70, P ¼ 0.41) and the 2 estimates were highly correlated among transects (r ¼ 0.98). Thus, estimates of N were apparently robust to the violations of the closure assumption.

[SECTION] locus
Analysis of Huggins model estimates of abundance indicated a significant interaction between sex and year (F 1-3,60 ¼ 3.99, P ¼ 0.05), suggesting that sex ratios differed in the 2 years (Figs. 5 and6). We found no significant 3-way interaction or interactions between year and fawning area or between sex and fawning area (F 1-3,50 <1.09, P > 0.36). Sex ratios derived from abundance estimates mirrored the pattern described above for ratios of numbers of individual females Figure 2. Expected frequency (probability) distribution for genotypematching at 0 to 10 loci in comparisons of any 2 randomly selected blacktailed deer individuals or siblings, illustrating that 99% of randomly chosen individuals share no more than half (5) of their loci and that 98% of siblings share no more than 7 of 10 loci, 2011-2012, Mendocino National Forest, California.
Figure 3. Breakdown of genotyping success in black-tailed deer pellet groups collected in (A) 2011 and (B) 2012. Light gray represents the total pellet groups from which we attempted to extract DNA, gray represents the number of pellet groups that yielded reliable genotypes (>7 loci), dark gray represents pellet groups that yielded full 10-locus genotypes, and black represents the number of unique individuals assigned to all 10-locus genotypes, Mendocino National Forest, California.  and males sampled in the 2 years, with a 3.4 (95% CI ¼ 2.96-4.16) F:M ratio in 2011 and 2.13 (95% CI ¼ 1.97-2.32) F:M ratio in 2012. The follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately on sexes indicated significant differences between years (F 1,30 ¼ 4.37, P ¼ 0.045) and among fawning areas (F 3,30 ¼ 3.83, P ¼ 0.020) for females but no significant differences among the estimates of abundance of males (F 1- 3,20 <0.71, P > 0.41; Table 3). We estimated an MMRD of 126 m based on all individuals sampled more than once in the study (n ¼ 196 individuals), giving us an estimated effective area A ˆ¼ 0.35 km 2 per transect. We used this estimate to convert abundance estimates to per-transect density indices, which we could then average across fawning areas. In 2011, D ranged from 7.80 (AE SE ¼ 2.60) M/km 2 to 18.20 (AE 6.88) M/km 2 and from 24.58 (AE 3.48) F/km 2 to 52.45 (AE 10.75) F/km 2 . In 2012, D ranged from 11.40 (AE 3.26) M/km 2 to 26.38 (AE 12.22) M/km 2 and from 14.36 (AE 3.40) F/km 2 to 41.58 (AE 9.83) F/km 2 across fawning areas.
The average abundance (and density) estimates in the 4 fawning areas were highly correlated with the numbers of individuals sampled, both for females (r ¼ 0.98) and males (r > 0.99). Similarly, the numbers of females were highly correlated with numbers of males across fawning areas, both in terms of numbers of individuals sampled (r ¼ 0.91) and abundance estimates (r ¼ 0.88). Thus, changes in sex ratios detected between the 2 years appear to have affected all fawning areas similarly.
For comparison to our sex-specific estimates of abundance, we also estimated abundance of deer irrespective of sex (i.e., pooling capture histories of F and M) to assess how this would affect statistical resolution. In general, the estimates for each fawning area in the 2 years were similar to those obtained by summing the separate female and male estimates. The ANOVA detected similar differences among fawning areas (F 3,31 ¼ 3.42, P ¼ 0.029) as detected for females above. However, we detected no difference between years (F 1,31 ¼ 0.57, P ¼ 0.46), suggesting that the different trends in females and males obscured the difference in female abundance discovered in the sex-specific analysis.

[SECTION] discussion
We successfully used fecal DNA analyzed in a single assay to estimate site-specific abundance within a high-density deer population with sufficient precision to detect differences in space, time, and sexes. Explicit incorporation of sex in our study proved especially important, enabling us to observe  sex-specific differences in abundance and, consequently, to detect trends in the female segment of the population that would otherwise have been missed. In particular, we detected a decline in females between years that was not evident in our analysis that ignored sex (or of males alone). The declining trend in female abundance observed in the present study was supported by results from a contemporaneous study that used population-specific estimates of fecundity, fawn survival, and adult female survival to estimate population growth based on a Leslie matrix. Resulting estimates of population growth (l) averaged 0.82 (SD ¼ 0.13) over the 4-year period data were collected (i.e., May 2009 to Aug 2013; Marescot et al. 2015). Differences in fawn survival detected in the telemetry study varied tremendously within fawning areas from 1 season or year to the next (e.g., ranging 0.10 to 0.99), precluding direct comparisons with our fawning area-specific abundance estimates. Nevertheless, fawning area also was found to be a significant factor underlying differences in fawn survival probabilities (Forrester 2014, Marescot et al. 2015), in qualitative agreement with the heterogeneity in spatial abundance observed in the present noninvasive CMR study. An important finding of the genetic CMR data beyond that obtained from the telemetry study of adult females and fawns was the lack of detectable spatial and temporal variation in population densities and trends of adult males. Black-tailed deer in the Mendocino National Forest, similarly to other deer populations across much of the United States, were subjected to male-only harvest, such that hunting was potentially the most important mortality source specific to adult males. Moreover, males of polygamous ungulate species tend to have lower survival than females in general (Gaillard et al. 2000). Thus, it is not surprising that we found lower density estimates for males than females. The lower overall density of males and, therefore, smaller sample size, however, also reduced our statistical power to detect spatial differences in males and females. Thus, although the significant interaction between sex and year provided strong support for the observed differences in temporal trends between the sexes, it is unclear whether males and females differed in their spatial distribution over the sampling area.
Population parameters derived from CMR models using noninvasive DNA samples are especially useful in management applications because they are readily comparable across years. These estimates can also be estimated at multiple spatial scales such as seasonal ranges or landscape scales (Brinkman et al. 2011). However, density estimates must be interpreted in the context of the particular study design and not extrapolated beyond the appropriate spatial scale or season. Our study was designed to estimate local abundance in high-quality habitats that were used only during summer following seasonal migrations of deer to higher elevations (Allen et al. 2014) and specifically after fawning, when abundance would be at its annual peak. Because our transect placement was random within preselected fawning areas, our estimates were applicable only to these approximately 20km 2 areas. Extrapolation of our estimates to larger spatial scales, such as over the entire Mendocino National Forest, would likely constitute a significant overestimate if the larger region included patches that were relatively devoid of deer during summer. Additionally, given the average number of fawns birthed per female (1.9), as well as annual mortality of fawns (0.76, most of which occurred from mid-Jun to mid-Sep) and adult females (0.29; Marescot et al. 2015), our postfawning abundance estimates could have been as much as 3 times higher than pre-fawning abundance estimates. Importantly, however, the lack of interaction observed in the present study between temporal trend and spatial heterogeneity indicates that sampling of the same summer ranges across multiple years can provide robust trend data for long-term monitoring.
The assay developed for this study presents a technological advance that can be applied broadly to similar CMR studies of deer and other ruminants. Previous research aimed at developing fecal-DNA CMR approaches for ungulates has provided useful guidelines for field sampling and standards for data accuracy and resolution (e.g., Harris et al. 2010, Brinkman et al. 2011, Goode 2011). Our study built upon and added to these advances in 2 important ways: introduction of a high-efficiency fecal DNA assay and its incorporation of a sex marker, which enabled us to explicitly model each sex independently.
By incorporating 10 microsatellites and a sex marker (i.e., 11 markers) in a single reaction, our assay enabled us to simultaneously minimize error and cost, representing a significant improvement over previous assays. Although we used fewer reactions per sample than previous studies, our proportional success was similar to that observed in previous genetic CMR studies for which samples were genotyped up to 7 times or more (Brinkman et al. 2011, Goode 2011, Ebert et al. 2012). In contrast to previous studies, which either did not incorporate sex markers (or sex) in analyses (Brinkman et al. 2011) or conducted additional assays specifically to determine sex (Goode 2011, Ebert et al. 2012), our incorporation of a sex marker in the same assay used to determine individual genotypes further reduced the number of reactions required. Overall, our error rates were low (e.g., 1.8% allelic dropout vs. approx. 5% in other studies) and polymorphism high (e.g., P ID ¼ 10 À7 vs. up to 0.0003) relative to other studies (e.g., Brinkman et al. 2011, Ebert et al. 2012), although the high polymorphism of our panel was likely due in part to the relatively high genetic diversity in our population (Latch et al. 2014).

[SECTION] management implications
Our particular noninvasive genetic CMR approach allowed us to efficiently quantify 2 important population parameters, sex-specific abundance and sex ratio, in a high-density population of Columbian black-tailed deer inhabiting a forested landscape. These methods proved capable of capturing short-term trends within relatively small, highquality habitat areas that are known to be critical for fawn recruitment (Forrester 2014). We also detected an independently verified (Marescot et al. 2015) short-term decline in the female population that methods agnostic to sex would not have detected. Application of these methods in the future can provide information on sex-specific trends that can be compared to predictions of density-dependent models (Eberhardt 2002) and applied in conjunction with vital rate estimates to assess the relative importance of top-down and bottom-up factors affecting population dynamics (Pierce et al. 2012b). Such information can facilitate decisions about how best to manage populations with respect to harvest rates, predator populations, and habitat. Because the assay used in our study of Columbian black-tailed deer incorporated markers derived from a broad taxonomic range of ungulates including Cervidae and Bovidae, our assay should be broadly applicable to many managed and unmanaged ungulate species.

FILE: Molecular Ecology Resources - 2013 - Wedrowicz - Reliable genotyping of the koala  Phascolarctos cinereus  using DNA.grobid.tei.xml

[SECTION] title
Reliable genotyping of the koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) using DNA isolated from a single faecal pellet

[SECTION] abstract
The koala, an Australian icon, has been added to the threatened species list. Rationale for the listing includes proposed declines in population size, threats to populations (e.g. disease) and loss and fragmentation of habitat. There is now an urgent need to obtain accurate data to assess the status of koala populations in Australia, to ensure the long-term viability of this species. Advances in genetic techniques have enabled DNA analysis to study and inform the management of wild populations; however, sampling of individual koalas is difficult in tall, often remote, eucalypt forest. The collection of faecal pellets (scats) from the forest floor presents an opportunistic sampling strategy, where DNA can be collected without capturing or even sighting an individual. Obtaining DNA via noninvasive sampling can be used to rapidly sample a large proportion of a population; however, DNA from noninvasively collected samples is often degraded. Factors influencing DNA quality and quantity include environmental exposure, diet and methods of sample collection, storage and DNA isolation. Reduced DNA quality and quantity can introduce genotyping errors and provide inaccurate DNA profiles, reducing confidence in the ability of such data to inform management/conservation strategies. Here, we present a protocol that produces a reliable individual koala genotype from a single faecal pellet and highlight the importance of optimizing DNA isolation and analysis for the species of interest. This method could readily be adapted for genetic studies of mammals other than koalas, particularly those whose diet contains high proportions of volatile materials that are likely to induce DNA damage.

[SECTION] introduction
The koala (Phascolarctos cinereus), an endemic Australian icon, is widely distributed along eastern Australia from northern Queensland to South Australia, where it inhabits Eucalyptus forests and bushland (Martin & Handasyde 1999). The combined populations of Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory have recently been listed as Vulnerable under the Environmental Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (effective of 12 May 2012). Threats to populations include disease (Chlamydia and koala retrovirus), dog attacks, cars, bushfires, drought and the loss and fragmentation of suitable koala habitat (EaCRC 2011).
There is now an urgent need for reliable data to assess genetic diversity, predict population trends and forecast the long-term viability of all Australian koala populations. Collecting census data or genetic samples can be difficult, especially when species abundance is low and terrain conditions are challenging. To date, genetic studies of koala populations have relied primarily on collection of blood or tissue samples (Worthington-Wilmer et al. 1993;Houlden et al. 1996b;Lee et al. 2011). Obtaining such samples by animal capture is labour intensive, costly, stressful for the individual animals and raises questions of research ethics for both the scientific community and general public (Swart 2004). Noninvasive genetic sampling, where DNA is recovered from discarded sources such as shed hair, faecal pellets and feathers (Waits & Paetkau 2005), is an attractive alternative to tissue sampling. These techniques provide an opportunity to obtain genetic material from free-ranging animals in their natural environment, without having to catch, handle or even observe them (Taberlet et al. 1999). Noninvasive sampling is especially valuable when studying species that are rare, elusive or difficult to find and capture (Piggott & Taylor 2003b), such as koalas, who inhabit trees that may be over 30 m tall.
Opportunistic collection of faeces has been shown to be a reliable method of obtaining DNA from animals in the wild (Constable et al. 1995;Gerloff et al. 1995;Luikart et al. 2008). By recovering DNA from the epithelial cells that have been exfoliated onto the surface of a faecal pellet, wild animals can be sampled unobtrusively and without the sampling biases inherent in other opportunistic approaches. Faecal samples have been used as a source of DNA for assessing the population structure, breeding behaviour, habitat use and home range of a variety of mammals including the brown bear (Ursus arctos) (Kohn et al. 1995), dugong (Dugong dugon) (Tikel et al. 1996), seals (Halichoerus grypus and Phoca vitulina) (Reed et al. 1997), baboons (Papio anubis) (Constable et al. 1995) and wombats (Vombatus ursinus) (Banks et al. 2002). DNA isolated from faecal samples, however, may be associated with increased rates of amplification failure and genotyping error, in particular allelic dropout and false alleles (Bonin et al. 2004;Pompanon et al. 2005). Genotyping reliability may also be affected by scat storage (Frantzen et al. 1998;Piggott & Taylor 2003a;Soto-Calderon et al. 2009), sampling (Lampa et al. 2008;Stenglein et al. 2010) and isolation methods (Wehausen et al. 2004).
Koala scats are easily distinguishable from those of other species by their characteristic shape, colour and strong eucalypt odour. Scats have been used to estimate koala distribution, abundance and tree use (Jurskis & Potter 1997;Sullivan et al. 2002Sullivan et al. , 2004)), but their use in population genetic studies has not been reported to date. Isolation and amplification of DNA from koala scats may be hindered by the presence of volatile organic compounds and phenolics deriving from the koala's sole diet of Eucalyptus leaves. Eucalypt molecules such as a-pinene, 1,8-cineole and terpinene-4-ol are excreted in koala faeces (Eberhard et al. 1975) and are known to damage cell membranes (Carson et al. 2006), while phenolics could accelerate DNA degradation (Khan & Hadi 1998) and/or inhibit the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) process (Kreader 1996), thereby reducing amplification success.
Here, we present a method that can be used to unequivocally identify an individual koala from a single faecal pellet. This study addressed methods for sampling and storage of koala scats to maximize DNA yield and genotyping reliability, and the application of genetic markers (microsatellite and gender) to provide a DNA profile that will confidently identify an individual koala.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] scat collection and storage
Fresh (<24 h) koala scats were collected from captive koalas at the Phillip Island Nature Park, Victoria, Australia (n = 40). To determine the effect of sample age and weather, scats (n = 16) were placed outside in a position where some were exposed to all weather conditions, including rain and wind, while others remained in a sheltered position that provided sun exposure, but protection from rain. DNA was isolated from two scats in each group at 1, 2, 3 and 4 weeks.
To consider the effect of storage conditions, fresh scats were placed into individual paper bags immediately upon collection (n = 12) or sprayed with 70% ethanol, allowed to air-dry and then placed into individual paper bags (n = 12). Bagged samples were stored, undisturbed, at room temperature, and DNA was isolated from three scats in each group at 1, 2, 4 and 6 weeks after collection.

[SECTION] dna yield and genotyping optimization
Koala scats (n = 270) were collected from wild koalas in temporary care at the Southern Ash Wildlife Shelter, Rawson, Victoria, and captive koalas at Maru Koala and Animal Park, Grantville, Victoria. Scat collection was undertaken within 24 h after pens had been cleaned to ensure consistency in the age of the scats sampled. Scats were collected on wooden toothpicks and stored uncovered for between 6 and 54 h, at ambient temperature in the laboratory until DNA isolation. A subset of fresh scats (n = 36) was stored for 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 weeks (six scats for each time period) before DNA isolation. Each scat was weighed and measured (length and width) prior to DNA isolation.

[SECTION] isolation of koala dna
Intestinal epithelial cells on the surface of the scat were isolated by placing individual koala scats in 7 mL vials with 2 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) which were rolled on a gyratory mixer for 8 min. All of the wash was transferred to a 2 mL microcentrifuge tube avoiding the transfer of visible debris. Cells within the surface wash were pelleted by centrifuging at 2500 g for 5 min. The majority of the supernatant was discarded leaving behind approximately 175 lL of the wash and the pellet. The remaining wash (~175 lL) was thoroughly vortexed (~30-60 s) to resuspend the pellet. DNA was then isolated from collected cells using the QIAamp â DNA stool mini kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer's protocol for the isolation of DNA from stool for human DNA analysis, with modification of the cell lysis steps: 1400 lL of Buffer ASL was added to the wash followed by incubation for 1 h at 35 °C with periodic vortexing (~15 s) each 15-20 min. DNA was eluted in 100 lL (2 9 50 lL) using 5-min incubation periods. The amount of total DNA (koala and foreign) obtained was determined fluorometrically; isolates were stored at À20 °C.
To confirm the presence of koala DNA, a 890 bp region of the mitochondrial control region was amplified using primers KmtL2 and KmtH2 (Fowler et al. 2000). Amplification reactions consisted of 5 lL of GoTaq â Green Master Mix (Promega), 1 lg of BSA, 0.25 lM each of KmtL2 and KmtH2 and 1 lL of DNA template in a total volume of 10 lL. PCR was carried out using an initial denaturation of 3 min at 95 °C, followed by 35 cycles of 94 °C for 1 min, 50 °C for 1 min and 72 °C for 1 min followed by a final 5 min extension at 72 °C.
To assess DNA quality, isolates from the scat collection and storage trial were amplified using nine koala microsatellite markers: K10.1, Pcv2, Pcv6.3, Pcv24.2, Pcv30, Pcv31 (Cristescu et al. 2009), Phc2, Phc4 and Phc13 (Houlden et al. 1996a), where markers were amplified six times per isolate. DNA isolates for the DNA yield and genotyping optimization trial were amplified using 12 koala microsatellite markers, which included all of the markers listed above plus the addition of K2.1, Pcv6.1 and Pcv25.2 (Cristescu et al. 2009), where each marker was amplified eight times for each isolate. Scats stored for 1-10 weeks were genotyped for the 12 koala microsatellite loci using the number of replicates predicted by GEMINI, according to isolate concentration. Resulting DNA profiles were compared to those obtained from fresh scats. Genotyping was carried out on the Applied Biosystems 3730 DNA analyser and GENEMAPPER 3.7 software (Applied Biosystems) by Australian Genome Research Facility, Melbourne, Australia.

[SECTION] amplification success and genotyping errors
The error rates estimation calculator in GIMLET v 1.3.3 (Vali ere 2002) was used to calculate the rates of amplification and genotyping error using allelic frequencies determined in GENALEX 6.5 (Peakall & Smouse 2012). GIM-LET defines amplification success as the number of successfully amplifying loci divided by the total number of loci for which amplification was attempted. Consensus genotypes were generated using the threshold rule, where an allele must appear at least twice to be accepted. Using the error rates calculated, the PCR repetition batch module of GEMINI v 1.3.0 (Vali ere et al. 2002) was employed to estimate the minimum number of replicates required to obtain reliable genotypes. Replicate simulations were run (n = 250), using hypothetical populations consisting of 20 individuals, taking 50 samples (with replication) on one sampling occasion. Regression analysis and statistical comparisons between amplification and error rates obtained were carried out using t-tests, ANOVA or the general linear model using Minitab â 15 Statistical Software (Minitab 2007).

[SECTION] sexing markers
Marsupial sexing markers were tested for amplification success in the koala using Y-linked primers (IMY1 and IMY2) designed to amplify a 159-bp region of sex determining region of the Y chromosome (SRY) sequence in the northern brown bandicoot (Isoodon macrourus) (Watson et al. 1998) and X-linked primers (GpdEx12 and GpdEx13R) developed from wallaroo (Macropus robustus) sequence to amplify 175 bp of DNA within the G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) gene (Loebel et al. 1995;Loebel & Johnston 1997). Y-linked DNA was amplified in a single reaction along with the X-linked G6PD region as an internal control. Reactions comprised 5 lL of GoTaq â Green Master Mix, 1 lg of BSA, 0.2 lM each of IMY1 and IMY2, 0.3 lM each of GpdEx12 and GpdEx13R and 1 lL of DNA template, adjusted to 10 lL with water. Thermal cycling began with an initial denaturation of 3 min at 94 °C, followed by 35 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 58 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 30 s and finished with one final extension cycle at 72 °C for 4 min.

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] scat collection and storage
Exposure to weather-Where scats were exposed to all weather conditions, there was a significant decrease in both DNA concentration (from 0.50 ng/lL at week 1 to 0.05 ng/lL at week 4) and PCR amplification rates (from 62% at week 1 to 1.0% at week 4) over time of exposure. In contrast, PCR amplification rates remained steady (90 AE 4.6%) in the sheltered treatment group and mean genotyping reliability across sheltered samples was consistently high (allelic dropout: 1.0 AE 1.7%; false alleles: 2.1 AE 2.8%). GEMINI simulations indicated that three replicates would be required for reliable genotyping using scats, up to 4 weeks old, stored outside in a sheltered position (Table 1). Koala scat collection should therefore be conducted during a period of dry weather.
Storage methods-Spraying koala scats with 70% ethanol before storage in paper bags did not produce a difference in amplification success or genotyping error rates compared to storage in paper bags alone. Storage in paper bags, with or without ethanol treatment, did, however, provide less reliable genotypes compared to isolates obtained from scats left outside, protected from rain (sheltered group). Amplification success was 24% greater (P < 0.0005) and allelic dropout 17% lower (P = 0.001) for samples stored outside (sheltered group) compared to those stored in paper bags (Table 1).
Differences in DNA concentration were not significant between scats stored in paper bags and those stored in an open sheltered position. This indicates that the reduced genotyping reliability observed for samples obtained from scats stored in paper bags was not associated with the loss of cells (and thus available DNA) onto the surface of the paper bag. It may be that volatile components originating from the eucalypt leaves consumed by koalas could reach increased concentrations within the confines of the closed paper bag, potentially exerting a negative effect on surface cells and DNA and/or increasing carryover of inhibitory molecules. Collecting koala scats in bags (paper or otherwise) is therefore not ideal and should be avoided.

[SECTION] dna yield and genotyping optimization
DNA quantity-DNA concentration of isolates obtained from single scats ranged from 0.08 to 120 ng/lL ( x = 6.1 AE 1.5 ng/lL). Scats that were <30 h old provided higher DNA yields ( x = 11 AE 1.6 ng/lL) than older scats ( x = 2.2 AE 0.31 ng/lL) (P < 0.0005), see Fig. 1. The presence of koala DNA was confirmed by successful amplification of the mitochondrial control region.
A positive correlation was found to exist between scat density and DNA concentration (Fig. 1), with higher DNA yields being obtained from scats with higher densities, most likely due to the evaporation of moisture from the scat. Scats dry out rapidly; scat density is reduced by 45 AE 5.5% after 30 h, with no evidence of further reductions in density past this point. Scat density could be used to determine the freshest scats, which will likely yield higher DNA concentrations. Because scats from an individual koala differ little in size, weight alone could be used to indicate the most recent scats from one animal.
Amplification success and genotyping error-Rates of amplification success and genotyping error were calculated using 21 samples whose DNA concentrations increased incrementally from 0.25 to 20 ng/lL. Amplification success increased from 87% for isolates containing 0.25-1.0 ng total DNA per reaction, to 95% for samples with 1.0-5.0 ng DNA, to 100% in samples providing more than 5 ng total DNA per reaction. Average chromatograph peak height also significantly (P < 0.0005) increased from 4315 AE 305 where samples provided 0.25-1.0 ng total DNA per reaction, to 6050 AE 321 for samples with 1.0-5.0 ng DNA, to 9375 AE 510 in samples having more than 5 ng total DNA per reaction, indicating that koala specific PCR product increases with increasing total (koala and foreign) DNA levels. Allelic dropout and false alleles both decreased from 7.5% to 2.7%, respectively, in samples with 0.25-1.0 ng total DNA to 1.8% and 0.3%, respectively, in samples supplying more than 1.0 ng total DNA per reaction (Table 2). GEMINI simulations indicated that four replicates would be required for amplifications with 0.25-1.0 ng total DNA/reaction, while three replicates would be sufficient for samples containing more than 1.0 ng total DNA. Scat storage and genotyping reliability-DNA samples isolated from scats stored for up to 10 weeks were found to give complete genotypes, identical to genotypes  obtained from fresh scats (<30 h old at DNA isolation).
Where total DNA concentration of isolates was between 0.25 and 5.0 ng/lL, 5.5% of amplifications failed for scats <54 h old, while 28% of amplifications failed when scats were more than 54 h old. Failed reactions, however, did not increase with storage time when total DNA concentration exceeded 5 ng/lL (0.5% for isolates from scats <54 h old and 0.0% from scats >54 h old). DNA yield was, however, significantly lower from stored scats relative to scats <30 h old, so isolating DNA from fresh scats will maximize DNA yield and thus increase genotyping reliability.
Sexing markers-DNA isolated from four male koalas and five female koalas was successfully amplified using Yand X-linked sexing markers. The sex of the individual sampled was correctly designated in all cases (Fig. 2). These markers may be combined with the microsatellite suite to obtain both the sex and unique genotype of the individual sampled.

[SECTION] discussion
Genetic sampling of wild, living koalas can be used to provide data that are currently lacking for most koala populations (EaCRC 2011). We have demonstrated that DNA recovered by surface washing of a single koala scat provides a reliable individual genotype and may therefore be used to identify individual koalas and be used for population genetic studies. Obtaining DNA isolates of sufficient quantity and quality from a single scat negates the need to isolate DNA from multiple pellets, as is sometimes required (e.g. Soto-Calderon et al. 2009), thus minimizing the chance of sample contamination between different individuals. Screening DNA isolates for total DNA concentration allows inferior isolates (<0.25 ng/lL) to be discarded prior to genotyping and samples with sufficient amounts of DNA to be analysed using the minimum number of required replicates, thereby minimizing costs. A summary of the methods developed in this study for reliable DNA isolation and genotyping from a single koala scat is provided in Fig. 3; by following the recommendations determined in this study, optimal quality DNA isolates should be obtained. DNA degradation is increased when biological samples are exposed to moisture (Piggott 2004). This  study demonstrated that scats exposed to inclement weather had higher amplification failure, allelic dropout and false alleles, compared to sheltered samples. Brinkman et al. (2010) also observed high amplification rates in deer pellets protected from rain over 4 weeks, compared to those exposed to weather. In the absence of rain, or where scats are found in weather-protected positions, field collection of samples up to 4 weeks old should produce DNA isolates that can be reliably used for genotyping studies. Collection of scats within this time frame should be easily achieved. Scats <2 weeks old can be recognized in the field by the presence of a shiny coating on the scat, the absence of cracking and a distinctive eucalypt odour (Sullivan et al. 2002). A single koala can produce up to 200 scats per day (Ellis et al. 1999) and is not likely to have been residing in the same tree for more than 24 h (Ellis et al. 2009). It has also been shown that 50% of total scat production is expected to be located within 1 m of the tree base (Phillips & Callaghan 2011), making finding samples an efficient process, especially if a koala is present which would attract a searcher to a tree.
While storage of scats in paper bags has been found to be effective for the brush-tailed rock wallaby (Petrogale penicillata), the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and the northern hairy-nosed wombat (Lasiorhinus krefftii) (Piggott & Taylor 2003a;Walker et al. 2009), this study found that genotyping reliability was significantly lower for scats stored in paper bags compared to those left outside in a sheltered position. Volatile substances evaporating from the scat may be retained within the paper bag, thereby inducing cell and DNA damage. Volatile molecules, phenolics or microbial contaminants may also be carried over into the surface wash and DNA isolates, potentially inhibiting subsequent amplification and decreasing genotyping reliability.
Samples stored in the open for up to 4 weeks were shown to have low rates of genotyping error. The amount of DNA isolated was, however, significantly lower from stored scats, potentially due to decreased surface washing efficiency for dry scats. Obtaining lower DNA yields will necessitate a greater number of replicates, therefore increasing genotyping costs. DNA is therefore ideally isolated from a fresh scat sample, although this may not always be possible. Faecal samples are commonly stored at À20 °C to prevent further sample degradation (Ball et al. 2007;Spiering et al. 2009). Liquid nitrogen storage of surface washes carried out in the field for the northern hairy-nosed wombat has been found to produce DNA isolates with low levels of amplification failure and genotyping errors (Walker et al. 2009). Freezing surface washes may therefore provide an alternative storage method that could increase the yield of DNA isolated from koala scats (Fig. 3).
Genetic sampling of a koala from a single scat can provide DNA that is suitable for microsatellite genotyping and a range of ecological investigations. Obtaining genetic samples from scats will enable the collection of large sample sizes, without introducing sampling bias or interfering with the study animals. Population data may subsequently provide information that could help to prioritize and inform management strategies relating to koala conservation in Australia, aiding the long-term viability of this species.

FILE: `Video-scats’ combining camera trapping and non-invasive genotyping to assess individual identity an.grobid.tei (1).xml
