FILE: Wildlife Society Bulletin - 2015 - Miles - A paired comparison of scat‐collecting versus scat‐swabbing methods for.grobid.tei.xml
====================================================================================================
[SECTION] title
Tools and Technology

[SECTION] abstract
Noninvasive DNA sampling from scats can provide powerful tools for wildlife research depending in large part on how scats are collected in the field. Preservation of scat in 95-100% ethanol can be highly effective, but not always practical. Use of swabs to sample the mucous layer from scats is a popular alternative, but has not been adequately tested in arid environments, where the mucous layer can rapidly desiccate. We conducted a paired comparison of methods, extraction from scats stored in ethanol ("direct method") versus from swabs ("swab method"), for carnivore scats collected under typical field conditions during May-September 2013 and January-February 2015 in northern California, USA. Direct quantification of DNA indicated that the extracts from ethanol-preserved direct-method samples contained, on average, an order of magnitude (14Â) more target DNA than extracts from swab method (P < 0.03). For mitochondrial sequencing, which is typically used for species-typing, we obtained slightly higher success for the direct (81%) than the swab (73%) extracts, but not significantly so (P ¼ 0.25, n ¼ 104). Among 62 canid scats, microsatellite genotyping (typically used for individual identification) was much more successful for the direct extracts (74%) than the swab extracts (35%; P < 0.001, n ¼ 62). Together, our findings indicated a substantial advantage of ethanol preservation followed by extraction directly from scats over swabbing in our arid study area. Our results apply most specifically to canids in the arid study environment; swabbing is potentially more effective in humid environments or in other carnivore species. Nevertheless, our findings highlight the importance of conducting pilot studies before committing to swabbing as a means of fecal DNA collection.

[SECTION] (no title)
Noninvasive fecal sampling and genetic analyses of scats are used increasingly in wildlife research (e.g., Waits and Paetkau 2005, Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, Gulsby et al. 2015, Lounsberry et al. 2015). The value of this approach for estimating abundance, occupancy, individual longevity, home range, habitat use, gene flow, and social structure without the need to capture or handle individual animals presents tremendous potential, but applications are often limited by challenges in adequately preserving samples for subsequent DNA extraction and analyses (e.g., Schwartz et al. 2007).
Although many variables (e.g., diet, environmental conditions, time since deposition, DNA extraction method) can affect the success of DNA acquisition from scats (Waits and Paetkau 2005), the single most influential factor in control of most field biologists is how samples are collected and stored prior to transfer to a laboratory. A variety of storage methods have been used and tested for efficacy, including desiccation, freezing, or storage in buffers or ethanol. In most studies, pure ethanol (i.e., 95-100%) works similarly to or better than other methods for shorter storage periods and can substantially outperform them during extended storage periods (Murphy et al. 2002, Frantz et al. 2003, Piggott and Taylor 2003, Beja-Pereira et al. 2009, Panasci et al. 2011, Tende et al. 2014). However, acquiring, storing, and transporting sufficient quantities of ethanol for sample storage can be difficult in remote field conditions. Sample transport following collection and storage can also pose an issue because ethanol is volatile, highly flammable, and is subject to various shipping and travel restrictions (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). One alternative has been to use dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-based buffers such as DET (e.g., Panasci et al. 2011, Vynne et al. 2011), but this method has a limited shelf-life relative to ethanol (e.g., Murphy et al. 2002).
Another method that has become increasingly popular, and is even required by some service laboratories, involves the use of a cotton swab to collect the epithelial cells themselves from the mucous layer of scats in the field (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). The accessibility of the mucous layer, however, likely depends on time in the environment, ambient conditions, and various other factors. In general, fecal swabs are likely to be most successful when scats are sufficiently fresh that the mucous layer containing the epithelial cells remains moist, also enabling separation from the fecal matrix, which typically contains polymerase chain reaction (PCR) inhibitors (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009). Depending on the purpose of a study, however, reliance solely on freshly deposited scats may not be feasible, such as in studies of rare species (e.g., Stenglein et al. 2010, Sacks et al. 2011, Statham et al. 2012, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). Therefore, it is of interest to know how methods of fecal collection and preservation are likely to perform relative to one another under more variable field conditions. In such cases, the mucous layer may not be as readily separated from the external scat via swabbing.
Unfortunately, it is difficult to evaluate the efficacy of swabs used on nonfresh scats based on the existing literature because few studies have reported their success in terms of DNA quantity (but see Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009), which, along with PCR inhibition, ultimately determines all measures of downstream success. Comparisons based solely on the downstream success measures themselves, such as proportion of scats that yield species types, are complicated by differences among study protocols. This problem is particularly significant for nuclear DNA (nDNA) amplification, which can be highly sensitive to particular species, markers, amplification protocols, and the authors' criteria for success (e.g., number of loci amplifying, differences in numbers of replication attempts, etc.). For these reasons, paired comparisons are crucial. We are aware of only one such study (i.e., using scats of unknown and variable ages), which compared extractions from swabs of scats preserved by freezing (i.e., swabbed in the laboratory at the time of extraction) to those from subsamples of the same scats preserved in DMSO buffer (Vynne et al. 2011). The study reported a 73% success rate in mitochondrial amplification of the swab extracts, which was higher than the comparably low 53% success they achieved for the DMSO-based extracts. Nevertheless, genotyping success from those swab samples identified in the first step to be from the target species was relatively high (82%). However, this study was conducted in a semitropical climate, which potentially preserves the moisture in the mucous layer for a greater period of time. We are aware of no study that has compared swabbing directly to ethanol-preserved scats or which has explored the efficacy of swabbing in an arid environment. In the present study, we used a paired design to directly compare the performance of methods involving fecal swabs versus ethanol-preserved fecal material using mesocarnivore scats collected from an arid, Mediterranean climate zone, and ranging up to 3 weeks old. We compared approaches both in terms of mitochondrial DNA sequencing, which is commonly used for species identification, and, for a subset of scats that were shown to be canine, nuclear (e.g., microsatellite) genotyping, which is used for individual and sex identification. Importantly, we also directly quantified the amount of target-species DNA in extracts, which will facilitate future comparisons to studies in other environments.

[SECTION] study area
We collected scats for this study from California's Sacramento Valley (USA), in elevations <150 m, latitudes ranging from 39.368N to 40.408N, and longitudes ranging from 122.258W to 121.438W. The landscape was composed primarily of agricultural lands, including flooded rice agriculture, dry cropland, vineyards, and orchards. Remnant grasslands remained where livestock were grazed. The study area was hot (highs ranged from 328 C to 408 C) and experienced almost no precipitation during the summer, and mild (highs ranged from 88 C to 248 C), with very little precipitation during the particular winter during which sampling for this study was conducted.

[SECTION] methods
We collected 104 putative mesocarnivore scats for this study during May-September 2013 (n ¼ 79) and January-February 2015 (n ¼ 25). We resampled transects every 2-3 weeks, collecting all mesocarnivore scats encountered. The 104 scats used for this study excluded those collected on the first run of transects and, therefore, were presumed to have been collected 21 days since deposition. In the field, we collected scats in individually labeled paper sacks and recorded whether scats appeared fresh (<2 days old), moderate-aged (2-4 days old), or older (>4 days). Within 12 hr of collection, we transferred a portion of each scat (approx. 2 g) into >4 parts (approx. 8-12 mL) 95-100% ethanol in a 15-mL tube and swabbed the unsampled portion of the same scat. Specifically, we used Q-tips 1 cotton-tipped swabs to sample the external surface area of approximately half of each scat on all sides. We first moistened swabs with 95-100% ethanol to help free cells from the scat surface (except for 3 scats that were so fresh there was no need to premoisten swabs; Rutledge et al. 2009). We allowed swabs to air dry and then stored them in manila coin envelopes. We stored all samples at room temperature (20-258 C) until DNA extraction. The average time between collection in the field and DNA extraction was 9.3 days (SD ¼ 7.7 days). Note: we chose ethanol as the moistening agent because it evaporates quickly. However, because other studies have moistened swabs with salt solutions, such as phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; e.g., DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), we swabbed a subset of 25 scats with both PBS and ethanol; we found no significant differences (Supporting Information 1). We also used a subset of samples to test our primary storage method (i.e., dried in manila envelopes) to storage of swabs in ethanol to control for the preservation versus the celltransfer aspect of swabbing and, again, found no qualitative differences in terms of DNA yield, inhibition, or performance (Supporting Information 2).
For DNA extraction directly from the ethanol-preserved scat samples, we used a QIAmp Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) to extract DNA from approximately 200 mg of the outer surface of scats, following the manufacturer's protocol, except that DNA was eluted in 100 mL of elution buffer. For swab samples, we extracted DNA using a DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen). We transferred swabs from envelopes directly into 2-mL microcentrifuge tubes with reagents for digestion: 700 mL PBS, 200 mL of Buffer AL, and 25 mL of Proteinase K. To remove swabs from the digestion tubes, we vortexed samples for 5-10 s, centrifuged them for 1 min at 14,000 rpm, and pressed swabs against the sides of the tubes to remove any remaining liquid before discarding. All subsequent steps followed manufacturer's instructions. Hereafter, we use the terms "direct" and "swab" to differentiate the DNA extracted directly from scat preserved in ethanol versus from swabs, respectively. We first attempted to amplify and sequence a 402-bp fragment of the mammalian mitochondrial cytochrome b gene using primers (Perrine et al. 2007) and procedures (Aubry et al. 2009) described previously. Although use of a shorter fragment, such as by other studies (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011;DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), would likely have produced higher species-typing success, we chose the longer fragment for purposes specific to various ongoing research projects in our laboratory. Because the direct method typically incorporates some fecal matrix in the extraction procedure, these extracts were likely to contain PCR inhibitors. Therefore, for direct-method extracts failing to amplify in the first step, we performed 10-fold dilutions to reduce the concentration of any PCR inhibitors and attempted a second time to amplify them at the cytochrome b fragment (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009). (We did not sequence the samples that amplified after dilution, which resulted in 4 samples that amplified but which we did not species-type or, therefore, use in subsequent analyses.) We evaluated sequences to determine species using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) in the nucleotide database in Genbank.
From the scats that assigned to coyote (Canis latrans), gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), or red fox (Vulpes vulpes) for !1 of the 2 preservation methods in the previous step, we selected all but 10 samples (set aside for unrelated purposes) to attempt nDNA amplification. Specifically, we attempted to amplify 7 canine nuclear DNA microsatellite loci that amplify in all canid species in our study area (AHT137, AHT142, CXX-279, CXX-374, INU055, REN162C04, REN169O18; primer sequences provided by Moore et al. 2010). Because nuclear DNA occurs in much lower copy-number than mitochondrial DNA, we used only the undiluted (i.e., original) extracts, along with the Qiagen Multiplex PCR Kit reagents and manufacturer's protocol using Q-solution (Sacks et al. 2011). We used STRand software to call alleles (Toonen and Hughes 2001). Because we were primarily interested in gross performance, we did not attempt to quantify allelic dropout, which would have required replications, but instead report numbers of loci amplified and, for purposes of quantifying success discretely, considered genotyping successful when !6 loci were successfully amplified for at least one allele in the single attempt. Elsewhere, we have reported allelic dropout rates for the same study system using the direct-method approach (Sacks et al. 2010(Sacks et al. , 2011)).
Lastly, we performed a quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of a subset of 35 pairs of the undiluted extracts on which we attempted genotyping. The reduced subset was necessary to complete the quantitation assay on a single 96-well plate, which also included 12 internal positive control (IPC) standards, 12 extracts used in the supplementary swab-storage comparison (Supporting Information 2), and 2 blanks. We estimated concentration of canine genomic DNA based on canine Melanocortin-1 receptor gene copies and incorporated the IPC (a synthetic DNA fragment added to each sample in known concentration) for detection of PCR inhibition (Evans et al. 2007). We quantified inhibition in terms of the number of cycles required for amplification of the IPC to a predetermined threshold concentration minus the number of cycles required for amplification of the IPC to the same threshold concentration in standards containing no inhibitors; specifically, we used the average value among 12 standards. We incorporated negative controls into all procedures, including extraction, PCR amplification, sequencing, and genotyping steps. Importantly, our technique quantified canine genomic DNA only, whereas previous studies (Rutledge et al. 2009) quantified total genomic DNA, which includes up to 20Â as much nontarget (e.g., from intestinal microorganisms) as target DNA (Ball et al. 2007).
For each fecal extraction protocol, we calculated success rates in terms of species identification, genotyping success, and both processes combined. We compared methods with respect to numbers of mitochondrial DNA amplifications and failures and microsatellite successes and failures using Fisher's exact tests (Zar 1999). We compared microsatellite genotyping success across species using a x 2 test of independence (Zar 1999). Because the cutoff for genotyping success was necessarily arbitrary, we also used a 2-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate the effects of method and species on numbers of loci amplified (including zeros) in the canid scats. We used paired t-tests to compare DNA concentrations and inhibition between the direct and swab methods. We log-transformed the DNA concentration estimates prior to analysis to normalize residuals. To estimate 95% confidence intervals for proportions (or percentages), we employed a method based on the F-distribution (Zar 1999). Statistical tests were run using SYSTAT (version 9.0, SPSS Incorporated, Chicago, IL) and significance was assessed at alpha ¼ 0.05.

[SECTION] results
We amplified mitochondrial DNA successfully from 84 (80.8%, 95% CI ¼ 71.9-87.8%) of the 104 samples using the direct method compared with 76 (73.1%, 95% CI ¼ 63.5-81.3%) using the swab method (Table 1). This difference was not statistically significant (Fisher's exact test, P ¼ 0.25). We observed little difference in success rates for scats thought to be <2 days old versus those apparently 2-4 days old, but a marked decline in success in the oldest-looking scats (Fig. 1). Altogether, we obtained at least one amplification product from 91 of the 104 scats. A BLAST search indicated 72 of the 87 scats were from one of the 3 wild-canine target species (Table 1).
For microsatellite genotyping, we obtained significantly greater success using the direct-extracts (74.2%, 95% CI ¼ 61.5-84.5%) compared with the swab extracts (35.5%, 95% CI ¼ 23.7-48.7%; Fisher's exact test, P < 0.001), and significantly greater success for red fox scats than for coyote or gray fox scats for both the direct method (89.5% [95% CI ¼ 75.2-97.1%] red fox, 50.0% [95% CI ¼ 29.1-70.9%] coyote and gray fox; x 2 2 ¼ 12.0, P ¼ 0.003) and the swab method (47.4% [95% CI ¼ 31.0-64.2%] red fox, 16.7% [95% CI ¼ 4.7-37.4%] coyote and gray fox; x 2 1;2 ¼ 6.1, P ¼ 0.048). Although we considered our single attempt successful only if !6 loci amplified on the initial attempt, replicate genotyping could have increased our success for both direct and swab extracts. For example, we amplified !1 locus in 42 of the 64 canid scats from swabs, suggesting that we could have potentially increased our swab genotyping success to a maximum of 66% (i.e., if all of these produced usable genotypes after multiple attempts), albeit with significant added expense. We also amplified significantly more of the 7 microsatellite loci using the direct extracts ( x ¼ 5.7 loci, SE ¼ 0.27) compared with the swab extracts ( x ¼ 3.1 loci, SE ¼ 0.38; ANOVA: F 1,118 ¼ 27.5, P < 0.001), and obtained a significantly greater success rate for both methods, respectively, for red fox scats ( x ¼ 6.4 vs. 4.2 loci) than for coyote ( x ¼ 4.6 vs. 1.4 loci) or gray fox ( x ¼ 4.5 vs. 1.2 loci) scats (F 2,118 ¼ 14.5, P < 0.001). There was no significant interaction between method and species (F 2,118 ¼ 0.555, P ¼ 0.58), suggesting that differences in methods were qualitatively applicable to all 3 canid species investigated in this study, even though the success rates differed markedly among them. We performed qPCR on 35 of the canine samples. The DNA concentrations were much higher on average in the direct-method extracts ( x ¼ 0.85 ng/mL, SE ¼ 0.49 ng/mL) than the swab extracts ( x ¼ 0.06 ng/mL, SE ¼ 0.04 ng/mL; t 34 ¼ 2.28, P ¼ 0.029). However, inhibition also was much higher on average in the direct-method extracts ( x ¼ 2.01 cycles, SE ¼ 0.51 cycles) than the swab extracts ( x ¼ 0.07 cycles, SE ¼ 0.04 cycles; t 34 ¼ 3.63, P ¼ 0.001). To interpret inhibition values, we compared these to internal standards  (positive controls): the number of cycles required to reach threshold concentration in the absence of inhibition among these controls was 27.15 cycles (SD ¼ 0.43). Thus, relative to variation in the uninhibited controls, we identified 28.1 cycles (i.e., 27.15 þ 1.96 Â 0.43) as the lower limit for significant inhibition. We observed significant inhibition in only 1 swab extract (28.34 cycles) but in 15 of the directmethod extracts (range ¼ 28.12-38.05 cycles).

[SECTION] discussion
Previous studies have investigated the use of swabs to obtain DNA from epithelial cells on the periphery of very recently deposited scats (Ball et al. 2007, Rutledge et al. 2009) or scats from boreal regions during winter when they were immediately frozen (Wasser et al. 2011). However, in many circumstances, dependence on fresh (or frozen) scats can be overly restrictive (e.g., Stenglein et al. 2010, Sacks et al. 2011, Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b).
Studies in tropical regions have used swabs to obtain cells from older scats with some success (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011, DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b). However, we are aware of no study prior to ours that has investigated the efficacy of swabs used to sample scats in an arid climate, where the mucous layer could desiccate more rapidly and, therefore, become more difficult to separate from the scat surface. For this reason, we conducted the present study to determine the efficacy of swabs to sample scats in an arid climate zone.
Our success rates for mitochondrial amplification and red fox scat genotyping of DNA extracted directly from scats collected in 95-100% ethanol were very similar to previous results using this same method in the same study area (Sacks et al. 2011). Specifically, based on 950 putative red fox scats, we had previously experienced an 84% success rate for mitochondrial amplification and an 82% microsatellite genotyping success rate (from 690 verified red fox scats; Sacks et al. 2011). In contrast, using swabs in this study, we achieved significantly lower sequencing success and, especially, genotyping success rates. Our genotyping success rates for coyotes and gray foxes paralleled these results, with genotyping success higher in both cases for the direct approach in comparison to swabbing. Reasons for the generally higher success rate in red foxes than the other 2 canid species were unclear. One possibility relates to the markers themselves, which were previously optimized specifically for red foxes (Moore et al. 2010). Alternatively, the differential success among species could stem from differences in DNA quantity or quality associated with scat extractions, for example, related to inhibitors associated with differing dietary tendencies. Unfortunately, we quantified DNA and tested for inhibitors in too few coyote (and no gray fox) samples to determine whether there could have been a systematic difference in DNA yield or inhibition among species in this study. The question of species-specific differences in DNA yield and overall success clearly requires further study. On the other hand, our quantification of the amount of target species DNA in our extracts from direct and swab methods on each scat clearly demonstrated that our higher success in the ethanol (direct) relative to swab extracts was attributable to significantly higher (over an order of magnitude) DNA yields from the former than latter sample types. Importantly, our relatively poor swab success could not be attributed to the particulars of our protocol. There are nearly as many variations on swabbing protocols as there are studies that have used swabs. For example, some studies have swabbed previously frozen scats to transfer cells directly into digestion buffer at the time of DNA extraction (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011), stored swabs in empty vials that were subsequently frozen (DeMatteo et al. 2014a, b), or stored swabs in DET buffer at room temperature (Rutledge et al. 2009). We tried multiple approaches for preservation and handling of swabs prior to extraction, all of which produced similar results in terms of both DNA yields and amplification and genotyping success. We also found no differences related to whether we used PBS or ethanol as a swab-moistening agent. Thus, the factor that limited our swab success was simply the amount of intact DNA that we were able to recover from the periphery of scats that were collected in our study area. Vigorously rubbing a swab moistened either with ethanol or PBS over a significant portion of a scat surface was typically unable to recover as much DNA as a small portion of that surface used directly in extractions, suggesting that once the mucous layer had desiccated, swabbing was an inefficient way of removing epithelial cells from the fecal surface.
The superior performance of the direct method relative to the swab method(s) occurred despite greater transfer of PCR inhibitors in the former than latter method. In fact, the swab samples contained essentially no PCR inhibition based on the internal positive controls, whereas the direct extracts tended frequently to exhibit detectable PCR inhibition. We were eventually able to counter PCR inhibition of mitochondrial DNA sequencing by dilution of the extracts. Interestingly, nearly all of the same undiluted direct extracts that failed mitochondrial PCR were successfully genotyped with microsatellites in their undiluted form despite the presence of inhibitors confirmed in a subset of these. This success was likely due to the particular PCR chemistry we used for microsatellites. Although our mitochondrial DNA reactions utilized a standard polymerase (Amplitaq; Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, CA), our microsatellite reactions utilized a commercially available kit (Qiagen Multiplex) with a hot-start polymerase and proprietary additives (Q-solution) found previously to perform well for fecal DNA (Luikart et al. 2008).
Although it seems clear from our findings that swabs performed poorly compared with the direct use of scats stored in ethanol in our study, it is important to note that the swabs did not fail entirely. Swabs potentially could be useful in some circumstances, particularly for speciestyping from mitochondrial DNA, which is much more plentiful than nuclear DNA. Additionally, increased DNA concentration from swab extracts could be achieved by eluting DNA in a smaller quantity of buffer, such as 50 mL, rather than the 200 mL used in the present study. It is also possible that the success of swabs varied according to taxon. In particular, our findings are most applicable to canid scats.
Previous studies using swabs for canids and felids in higher humidity tropical environments experienced somewhat higher genotyping success than we did for canids in our arid study area (Vynne et al. 2011;DeMatteo et al. 2014a). Although our swab species-typing success was similar to those by Vynne et al. (2011;73%)   et al. 2014a). This difference could relate to humidity. Although humidity is thought to degrade DNA generally (e.g., Vynne et al. 2011), it is also conceivable that humidity causes the mucous layer to remain more easily separated from the scat surface for longer periods of time, potentially enhancing the relative utility of swabs in tropical or subtropical relative to Mediterranean climate zones. On the other hand, it is also possible that the higher nDNA success in the tropical studies stemmed from more sensitive downstream procedures used in those studies rather than from higher DNA quantity in extracts. For example, we only performed a single extraction attempt versus 2 by DeMatteo et al. (2014a, b); we performed a single genotyping attempt versus up to 4 by Vynne et al. (2011) and up to 6 by DeMatteo et al. (2014a), and to count as "successful," we required that all but one locus amplify, compared with a single sex marker by Vynne et al. (2011) and amplification of all but 2 or 3 loci (depending on species) by DeMatteo et al. (2014a, b). The disparity between the number of swab samples showing amplification of any loci versus 6 or more loci in this study suggests that our success rate with swabs might have been more similar to these tropical studies had we replicated extraction attempts, genotyping efforts, or used less stringent criteria for "success."
Thus, although fecal swabs appear to present an excellent alternative to ethanol fecal storage and extraction methods for very fresh samples and can be potentially useful in tropical environments, our findings suggest that studies relying to a large extent on older scat samples, particularly of canids in arid environments, can potentially obtain substantively better data sets by collecting scat pieces in ethanol and extracting DNA directly from their external surfaces. Other methods, such as those involving silica to keep samples dry, also have been shown to work well in some but not all instances (e.g., Murphy et al. 2002). Given the potentially significant time, effort, and expense required to obtain scats from rare carnivores, we suggest that swab-based collection methods should be carefully tested against others in pilot studies prior to embarking on large collections reliant on swabs or any other particular method and, if possible, to include preservation in pure ethanol as one of the comparison groups.

[SECTION] title
Non-invasive genetics can help find rare species: a case study with Rhinolophus mehelyi and R. euryale (Rhinolophidae: Chiroptera

[SECTION] abstract
The reliability of species identification is of primary importance as much of biodiversity studies, ecology, legislation, and conservation are based on this taxonomic level. Species identification problems can obscure the conservation status, especially for rare and endangered species, which are of special concern for conservation. This problem is especially significant for some taxonomic groups such as chiropterans, as many monitoring programs are run during the hibernation season when animals should not be disturbed, hence not handled. In the present study, we used Rhinolophus mehelyi as a case study to develop and propose a new monitoring strategy via the use of non-invasive genetics to reliably identify individuals to species.

[SECTION] (no title)
The International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List has become an increasingly powerful tool for conservation planning, management, monitoring, and decision making ( Rodrigues et al. 2006 ). At a regional level, a species can be classified as Regionally Extinct (RE) " when there is no reasonable doubt that the last individual potentially capable of reproduction within the region has died or disappeared from the region or, in the case of a former visiting taxon, individuals no longer visit the region. This will depend on how much effort has been devoted to searches for the taxon, which in turn will vary, both with organism and region " . One could be fairly confident in saying that a large mammal is RE if it has not been observed over the last few decades; however, this might be rather difficult with small elusive mammals such as bats. Further difficulties arise when the species of interest is morphologically very similar to another more common species ( Boston et al. 2010, Puechmaille et al. 2012 ).
Non-invasive genetic techniques, using biological material left behind by animals as a source of DNA, are becoming routinely used in conservation biology and monitoring programs, particularly for threatened and protected species ( Luikart et al. 2010 ). The DNA obtained can be used to identify the species from which the sample originated, most commonly through sequencing of a short fragment of mitochondrial DNA ( Kohn and Wayne 1997 ). Potential difficulties associated with non-invasive genetics are the low quality and/or quantity of DNA recovered and the potential presence of PCR inhibitors ( Taberlet et al. 1999 ). Nevertheless, specific improvements in the techniques to extract and amplify DNA from non-invasive genetics have been developed to overcome these difficulties in a diverse range of taxonomic groups (e.g., Eggert et al. 2005, Puechmaille et al. 2007 ).
Mehely ' s horseshoe bat, Rhinolophus mehelyi Matschie 1901, is a medium-sized rhinolophid with a discontinuous distribution from North Africa (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, and Egypt) and southern Europe (Iberia, Sardinia, Sicily, and the Balkans) through Asia Minor, Anatolia, to Transcaucasia and Iran. The species is globally classified as " vulnerable " but is thought to have gone extinct in north-eastern Spain, Mallorca, Croatia, and Israel ( Flaquer et al. 2010 , Hamidovi ć pers. com., Levin pers. com.) and is near extinction in France, Romania, and Sicily ( Rombaut andHaquart 2002 , Dragu andBorissov 2011 , Mucedda pers. com.). Most observations in France are from the period 1908 -1965, during which this species was regularly observed at several sites in the Gard, H é rault, and Bouches-du-Rh ô ne d é partements in southern France ( Mottaz 1908, Hugues 1914, 1936, Gallocher 1958, K ö nig and K ö nig 1961, Jeantet and Gory 1997 , Jeantet pers. com.) and only once in Corsica ( Kahmann and Goerner 1956 ). Species identifications have been verified by examinations of voucher specimens previously collected in southern France and deposited in the Natural History Museum in Paris ( Rode 1939 , Masson andBesson 1988 , Puechmaille pers. obs.), the Natural History Museum of N î mes (Jeantet pers. com.), the Staatliches Museum fur Naturkunde Stuttgart ( K ö nig and K ö nig 1961 ), the Natural History Museum in Geneva ( Miller 1912 , Strinati andAellen 1958 ), and the Zoological Museum in Berlin (Lange pers. com.). In the last decade, sightings of hibernating bats similar to R. mehelyi have been reported, especially in the H é rault and Gard D é partements in southern France ( Ruffray 2011 , M é dard and Derivaz pers. com.). Nevertheless, R. mehelyi is morphologically very similar to Rhinolophus euryale Blasius, 1853, another medium-sized horseshoe bat regularly observed in these regions. These two species could easily be confused (discussed in detail in Puechmaille et al. 2012 ), especially when the animals are only observed from a distance, as during the hibernation period, when the bats should not be disturbed.
Here we report on a new strategy to identify bat species in hibernation through the genetic analysis of guano collected underneath the bats of interest. Pre vious studies have shown that it is possible to extract goodquality DNA from bat guano ( Vege and McCracken 2001, Zinck et al. 2004, Puechmaille et al. 2005, 2007, Puechmaille and Petit 2007 ), although it has never been tested with guano collected at hibernation sites. In this study, we used non-invasive genetics to confirm the species of a group of hibernating bats (Gardon gorges, Gard department, France) that were suspected to be Rhinolophus mehelyi based on visual observation.
On the 20th of February 2008, a plastic sheet covered with newspaper was placed in a cave underneath a group of 18 hibernating medium-sized Rhinolophus suspected to be Rhinolophus mehelyi based on visual identification. No droppings were present on the first visit (22nd February) 2 days later, whereas six droppings were collected on the second visit (27th February) 5 days later. Each dropping was individually placed in a tube with silica gel to absorb humidity and hence preserve DNA ( Puechmaille et al. 2007 ). Droppings were then sent to the laboratory where only non-invasive DNA samples are analyzed, hence minimizing potential contamination problems. For comparison, droppings collected in a cloth holding bag from captured Spanish R. mehelyi (colony Villuercas in Salsamendi et al. 2008 ) were also included. A total of eight droppings from France (n = 6) and Spain (n = 2) were extracted following the protocol detailed in Puechmaille et al. (2007) . Given that long DNA fragments have been amplified from guano ( Boston et al. 2012, Goodman et al. 2012, Ruedi et al. 2012, Dool et al. 2013 ), we amplified the full cytochrome b and partial D-loop in two overlapping fragments. The first fragment (885 bp) was amplified using primers mtDNA-R3-F and mtDNA-F3-R, and the second fragment (1025 bp) using primers mtDNA-R2-F and mtDNA-F2-R ( Puechmaille et al. 2011 ). PCR mix and PCR conditions were as described in Thong et al. (2012) . The amplified PCR products were then purified and directly sequenced by Macrogen Inc. (Seoul, South Korea) using the same primers as mentioned above. The forward and reverse sequences per fragment were edited and assembled for each individual using the program CodonCode Aligner 4.0.1 (CodonCode Corporation, Dedham, MA, USA).
Of the six French samples extracted, two did not amplify whereas four amplified for both fragments. We combined these six sequences obtained (GenBank accession number KF031265 -KF031268) with another five sequences retrieved from GenBank and belonging to Rhinolophus mehelyi (n = 1), R. euryale (n = 3), and R. ferrumequinum (n = 1, used as the outgroup) to perform a maximum likelihood tree reconstruction in PAUP* ( Swofford 2003 ) using HKY models as selected by the hierarchical likelihood ratio test in Modeltest 3.7 ( Posada and Crandall 1998 ).
The phylogenetic reconstruction clearly indicated the presence of two strongly supported clades (bootstrap supports of 100%), which could be identified as being Rhinolophus euryale and R. mehelyi based on the sequences of known identity from GenBank and the Spanish R. mehelyi samples ( Figure 1 ). Whereas the two non-invasive samples from Spain grouped with R. mehelyi , all the French sequences from the hibernation site grouped with R. euryale , and hence belong to this latter species.
These results highlight the limitations of visual identification of hibernating bats and advocate for the use of non-invasive genetics to confirm species identity for rare bats, especially for those that are difficult to identify on the basis of morphological criteria. Recently, Puechmaille et al. (2012) reviewed morphological criteria to differentiate both species and showed that some of these criteria vary geographically, further complicating the correct identification of these species. Although our study revealed unambiguously that the suspected animals in the gorges du Gardon were Rhinolophus euryale and not R. mehelyi ; these results on their own are not enough to confirm that the species is extinct in France. Further field surveys combined with non-invasive genetic analyses are urgently needed to clarify the status of the species in the sites where the species was present until the 1960s ( Jeantet andGory 1997 , Gory andJeantet 1999 ).
In terms of climatic conditions, hibernating sites generally have low temperatures and high humidity ( Webb et al. 1996, Vi š ň ovsk á et al. 2006 ). DNA degradation decreases at low temperatures but increases at higher humidity; therefore, equipment should be placed in the driest locations available where the subject bats are present. We also recommend that samples only a few days old should be preferentially collected. Previous work has demonstrated that ca. 90% of samples kept in dry conditions provide adequate quality and amount of DNA for species identification ( Puechmaille et al. 2007, Boston et al. 2012 ). In the present study, we amplified large fragments ( > 800 bp) to maximize the amount of information obtained from the sequences to gain information on population differentiation between the French and Spanish samples. If species identification is the only target, shorter fragments allowing species discrimination should be used (usually ca. 100 -200 bp), which would likely increase amplification success ( Broquet et al. 2007 ). DNA extraction protocols that efficiently remove PCR inhibitors should preferentially be used ( Puechmaille et al. 2007 ); however, if some inhibitors remain after extraction, more diluted DNA extracts should be used and/or amplified along with bovine serum albumin that binds to inhibitors during the PCR. As seen with the group of hibernating bats in the Gardon gorges, bats are unlikely to produce large numbers of droppings during their hibernation period but might produce a few droppings when they wake up from torpor, allowing their genetic identification based on mitochondrial DNA. Identification to the species level might not be possible if two species cannot be differentiated using mitochondrial DNA, either because of current or past hybridization (e.g., Myotis myotis/Myotis blythii ; Berthier et al. 2006 ). In such situations, species identification could be obtained through microsatellite genotyping using reference species datasets.
Studies based on droppings have demonstrated that individuals could be identified by their unique genetic multilocus genotype ( Puechmaille et al. 2007 , Puechmaille andPetit 2007 ) and although here we only used mitochondrial DNA, it should be possible to also amplify nuclear DNA from these droppings from hibernation sites. DNA fingerprints obtained at hibernation sites could then be compared with fingerprints obtained at maternity colonies and would allow the identification of connections between maternity colonies and hibernation sites, still a grand challenge in bat biology. These techniques, although probably very costly if used at large scale ( Boston et al. 2012 ), could nevertheless be used for smaller sample sizes to inform movements of rare and endangered species that cannot be marked with more conventional techniques (e.g., ringing or passive integrated transponder tagging). The genetic information obtained non-invasively can also be used to investigate the fidelity of individuals to a particular site or survival rates if the sampling is carried out in multiple years. Additionally, these data can also inform about population structure and genetic diversity.
With the increasing legal requirement of countries to monitor and preserve their biodiversity, new methods such as non-invasive genetic tools presented herein are necessary to study species, particularly those critically endangered and elusive.

[SECTION] title
Multipronged strategy including genetic analysis for assessing conservation options for the snow leopard in the central Himalaya

[SECTION] abstract
The snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is an endangered carnivore of southern and central Asia. Approximate 10% of the global population occurs in the Himalayan region of Nepal. The snow leopard is thought to be in decline because of human-snow leopard conflicts, poaching, habitat loss and fragmentation, decreasing prey populations, and a lack of awareness and enforcement of conservation legislation. In this study, we used habitat surveys and genetic analyses of putative snow leopard scats to estimate the abundance, habitat preferences, and diet profile of the snow leopard in the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal. Cliffs, grassland, and shrubland at high elevation (3,000-5,000 m) were the preferred habitats of snow leopards. Eighty-three percent of collected scats collected were verified to be from snow leopards using mitochondrial DNA cytochrome-b species-specific polymerase chain reaction assays. Sixty-two percent of the scats were successfully genotyped using 6 microsatellite markers, and identified as having originated from 5 different individuals. The dispersion of multiple scats from the same individual suggested minimum movement ranges of 89.4 km 2 for males and 59.3 km 2 for females. Estimated population density was 1.9 individuals/100 km 2 and 22 snow leopards were estimated to inhabit the upper Mustang region. Microhistological analysis of scats (n ¼ 248) revealed that blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur) was the primary wild prey (63%), and livestock also contributed significantly (18%) to snow leopard diet. We used a multipronged strategy for assessing conservation options for this rare carnivore and compared our findings with those pertaining to other predators of the region that share similar habitats and resources. The findings from this study will be helpful in managing snow leopards and similar carnivore populations across the snow leopard's entire geographic range.

[SECTION] (no title)
The snow leopard is one of the top predators in the Himalayan ecosystem (Fox 1994;Oli 1997;Ale 2007;Jackson et al. 2008;Lovari et al. 2009). Snow leopard numbers in Nepal are declining, primarily due to human-wildlife conflicts (including retaliatory killing for livestock depredation and poaching), loss of habitat due to high densities of livestock, habitat fragmentation, decreasing prey populations, and a lack of conservation awareness and conservation legislation enforcement (Oli 1997;McCarthy et al. 2005;Jackson et al. 2006;Ale 2007;Lovari et al. 2009;Aryal et al. 2010aAryal et al. , 2010c)). However, our knowledge of the distribution and ecology of snow leopards in Nepal is lacking, and the snow leopard's secretive habits and distribution in inaccessible habitats make it challenging to gather critical information (Fox 1994;Oli 1997; Jackson et al. 2006Jackson et al. , 2008;;Ale and Brown 2009;Lovari et al. 2009;Shehzad et al. 2012;Aryal et al. 2013b).
Published studies on the snow leopard in Nepal (Oli 1997;Ale 2007;Lovari et al. 2009;Karmacharya et al. 2011) mainly focus on presence-absence, diet, home range, and habitat in the Dolpa, Manang, and Sagarmatha regions. Lacking, however, is information for the upper Mustang region. The Mustang region has a cold desert climate, low human density, and low prey and predator densities, and lacks forest (Aryal et al. 2012a(Aryal et al. , 2012b(Aryal et al. , 2014b)). These environmental variables are known to influence snow leopard density, abundance, home-range area, and feeding ecology (Aryal et al. 2012a). Furthermore, the Snow Leopard Information Management System (SLIMS) methodology (Jackson and Hunter 1996) has been widely used in previous studies for estimating snow leopard status within its geographic range (Jackson and Hunter 1996;Ale 2007). The SLIMS methodology has reported bias (Janecka et al. 2008;McCarthy et al. 2008); however, it is cost effective and easy to implement for monitoring of this species (Jackson and Hunter 1996;Ale 2007;McCarthy et al. 2008;Lovari et al. 2009). Recently, genetic analysis of DNA from fecal samples and camera trapping have been recognized as more reliable methods to identify individuals and estimate population sizes (Janecka et al. 2008;McCarthy et al. 2008;Karmacharya et al. 2011;Shehzad et al. 2012).
We report the results of a population survey based on genetic analysis of putative snow leopard scats in the upper Mustang region of Nepal. This technique has recently been used for snow leopard studies throughout its range, and appears reliable for identifying field-collected scats for use in diet analysis, landscape connectivity, gene flow, distribution, and population density analyses (DeYoung and Honeycutt 2005;McCarthy et al. 2008;Lovari et al. 2009;Karmacharya et al. 2011;Shehzad et al. 2012). The objectives of our study were to estimate snow leopard abundance in the upper Mustang region, compare feeding ecology between snow leopards in Manang and Mustang districts, and estimate potential habitats for snow leopards in the Annapurna Conservation Area.

[SECTION] materials and methods
Study area.-The study was conducted in the upper regions of the districts of Mustang and Manang in the Annapurna Conservation Area in Nepal. Habitat surveys were conducted in the upper Mustang region, where putative snow leopard scats were collected. However, only known snow leopard scats were collected from the Manang district. The Manang district covers an area of 2,246 km 2 and its elevation ranges from 1,600 to 8,156 m (Mt. Manaslu-Aryal et al. 2010b, 2010c, 2012a). Further details about the study area are described in Aryal et al. (2012bAryal et al. ( , 2014b)). The climate of the districts was subalpine, with temperatures ranging from 258C to À38C (Aryal et al. 2014a). Agricultural production was very limited and animal husbandry and tourism were the major sources of income (Aryal et al. 2013a). The vegetation of the area was primarily high-altitude grassland and included species such as Caragana spp., Carex spp., and Kobresia spp. (Aryal et al. 2012a(Aryal et al. , 2014a(Aryal et al. , 2014b)). The Mustang and Manang districts both provided good pastureland for livestock and also supported a large number of rare and endangered fauna, including blue sheep (Pseudois nayaur), gray wolf (Canis lupus), brown bear (Ursus arctos), lynx (Lynx lynx), and snow leopard (Aryal et al. 2012a(Aryal et al. , 2014b) ) Habitat survey.-In May 2010, we visited the 6 Village Development Committees in upper Mustang and met with local people and herders (n ¼ 241). We conducted a workshop in upper Mustang to explain the threats faced by the snow leopard and prepare a participatory map for quantifying the distribution of the snow leopard. We divided upper Mustang into grids with a cell size of 4.5 3 4.5 km, based on an average snow leopard home-range size of approximately 20 km 2 (11-37 km 2 [Jackson 1996], and 13.9-22.3 km 2 [Oli 1997]). These participatory maps were georeferenced using a topographic map of the region. We surveyed the grids of upper Mustang using a single-season (one-time) survey to estimate actual snow leopard population density and distribution in participatorymapped region. If we found sign or had a direct observation of the target species in a grid, we recorded that grid as an area of habitat use and snow leopard presence, stopped the survey in that grid, and started in another grid (Hall et al. 1997;MacKenzie et al. 2006). Based on the survey with local people and herders, we first visited grids that contained the most probable snow leopard habitat, including riverbeds, ridges, and gullies, on horseback to search for snow leopard sign. If we found no sign of snow leopards after travelling all possible sites of the grid, we noted the area as an absence, and then moved to another grid. For remote and inaccessible areas, we used information from local people to determine snow leopard presence or absence. The main purpose of this survey was to understand habitat use and availability for snow leopards in the region.
We entered all presence and absence data into ArcGIS 10 (Environmental Systems Research Institute 2011) to create a presence-absence grid, and then overlapped this with the study area using Hawth's Analysis Tools for ArcGIS 9.x (Beyer 2004). We characterized presence areas as habitat areas currently in use and absence areas might be potential habitat for snow leopard. We calculated elevation, slope, aspect, and land use for each presence and absence grid as well as the distance to water sources and villages. Slope was reclassified into 7 categories using 108 intervals (1 108 to 7 ! 608). Aspect was reclassified into 8 classes (north, northeast, east, southeast, south, southwest, west, and northwest). Vector layers (contours of 20-m intervals, land-use layer, and ecological layers) were obtained from the Department of Survey, Government of Nepal, and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development 2011). We took 20-m interval contour layers and created a 500-m interval elevation model (digital elevation model) using 3-dimensional analysis, and prepared slope and aspect layers for further analysis. Overlapping the presence-absence grid with the layers allowed for further analysis of habitat use and availability for snow leopards in the upper Mustang region.
We used Ivlev's electivity index (IEI) to understand habitat preference of snow leopards (Ivlev 1961;Krebs 1989;Hall et al. 1997;Ale and Brown 2009;Aryal et al. 2010b) The IEI is calculated as U% À A%/U% þ A%, where U represents use area (presence area) and A represents availability area (absence area -Ivlev 1961;Krebs 1989). A 1-way analysis of variance was performed to evaluate habitats, with the null hypothesis being that all habitats were used in proportion to their availability. ''Use area'' as a dependent variable and ''available area'' as an independent variable were used for the analysis. Spearman's correlation was used to test for significance between various ''use'' and ''available'' areas of snow leopard habitats.
Snow Leopard Information Management System habitat surveys and scat collection.-The SLIMS surveys of snow leopard sign were conducted from January to June 2010 in the upper Mustang region (Jackson and Hunter 1996). Putative snow leopard scat samples were identified based on size, pugmarks, scrapes, and scent spray (Aryal and Kreigenhofer 2009). Scat samples were collected from ridges, riverbeds, and cliffs, with the SLIMS method (Jackson and Hunter 1996). We only collected scats for diet analysis if we found signs of snow leopard scraping or scent spray (Jackson and Hunter 1996;Ale 2007); however, noninvasive genetic work on scats from India, China, and Mongolia suggested that up to 54% of scats collected as snow leopard scats were actually from other species, such as red fox (Vulpes vulpes- Janecka et al. 2008). Snow leopard scats were collected from both study areas for 3 seasons (winter: November 2009, January-February 2010; spring: March-April 2010; summer: June-July 2010). Additional scats were collected during April-July 2011 and March-April 2012 for noninvasive genetic analysis. This detailed survey methodology was adopted in the upper Mustang region to collect putative scats. However, from the Manang district, we only collected scats of snow leopards from January 2010 to April 2010, and did not conduct habitat surveys.
DNA extraction.-Putative scats of snow leopards (n ¼ 34) collected from upper Mustang during April-July 2011 and March-April 2012 were analyzed using SLIMS recommended protocols for genetic analysis. Scats were preserved in silica gel and transported to the genetic laboratory of the Center for Molecular Dynamics, Nepal, for analysis. DNA was extracted using the Qiagen QIAamp DNA Stool kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the recommended protocol.
Species identification.-A cytochrome-b segment of mitochondrial DNA specific for snow leopard was amplified using a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) primer set (CYTB-SCT-PUN F and CYTB-SCT-PUN R) for species identification (Janecka et al. 2008). A 7-ll PCR was prepared containing 3.5 ll of 53 Qiagen Master Mix, 0.7 ll of 53 Qiagen Solution, 0.07 ll of each primer, 1.16 ll of distilled water, and 1.5 ll of extracted undiluted DNA. The PCR was carried out at the following thermocycling conditions: 958C for 15 min followed by 50 cycles of 948C for 30 s, 608C for 15 s, and 728C for 1 min. One known snow leopard sample was incorporated as positive control. The amplified PCR products were visualized in 1.8% agarose gel.
Sex identification.-Sex identification was accomplished using PCR on snow leopard species PCR-positive samples with felid sex-specific PCR primers (AMELY F and AMELY R- Murphy et al. 1999). A 7-ll PCR was prepared containing 3.5 ll of 23 Qiagen Master Mix, 0.7 ll of 53 Qiagen Solution, 0.07 ll of each primer, 1.16 ll of distilled water, and 1.5 ll of extracted undiluted DNA. PCR thermocycling conditions were: 958C for 15 min followed by 50 cycles of each: 948C for 15 s, 558C for 30 s, and 728C for 1 min. The PCR products, with incorporated male and female snow leopard positive controls, were visualized in 2% agarose gel.
Individual identification by PCR.-Six microsatellite loci located at 6 different chromosomes of the snow leopard genome were targeted using sets of 6 primers with tagged fluorescent dyes (see detail for 6 microsatellite primer sequences in Janecka et al. [2008] and Karmacharya et al. [2011]). Six polymorphic microsatellite loci chosen were sufficient to give the value of probability of identity that was adequate to characterize individuals in a population sharing the same genotype (Janecka et al. 2008).
Genotyping for individual identification was optimized for multiplex PCR. Six microsatellite primers were divided into 2 combinations each containing 3 of the primer pairs. One combination of primer pairs included tagged forward and untagged reverse primers for loci PUN124, PUN229, and PUN1157 (Janecka et al. 2008). The 2nd combination consisted of primer pairs, tagged forward and untagged reverse primer, for loci PUN132, PUN894, and PUN935 (Janecka et al. 2008). For each sample, multiplex PCR was performed for both combinations in a 7-ll reaction volume. For the 1st multiplex PCR combination, a total of 7-ll reaction volume contained 3.5 ll of Qiagen Master Mix (23), 0.7 ll of Qsolution (53; Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), primers for PUN124 at 0.5 lM, primers for PUN229 at 0.4 lM, primers for PUN1157 at 0.2 lM, and 1.5 ll of DNA. Similarly for the 2nd multiplex PCR combination, a total of 7-ll reaction volume contained 3.5 ll of Qiagen Master Mix (23), 0.7 ll of Qsolution (53), primers for PUN132 at 0.5 lM, primers for PUN894 at 0.4 lM, primers for PUN935 at 0.2 lM, and 1.5 ll of DNA.
The PCR was carried out at the following thermocycling conditions: 958C for 15 min followed by 40 cycles at 948C for 30 s, 558C for 90 s and 728C for 90 s, and a final extension of 728C for 10 min. The PCR product was diluted to 1:60 by adding 118 ll of distilled water to 2 ll of the PCR product. One microliter of the diluted PCR product was then mixed with 9 ll of Hi-Di formamide (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, New York) and 0.25 ll of GeneScan 500-Liz DNA size standard (Applied Biosystems, Warrington, United Kingdom). The mixture was denatured at 948C for 5 min and immediately cooled. The samples were then injected into a capillary tube (36 cm, POP4 polymer) by applying an injection voltage of 1 kV for 5 s in an ABI310 Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, New York). The capillary electrophoresis was performed at a voltage of 15 kV at 608C. We determined the size of alleles using the software Genemapper 4.0 (Applied Biosystems 2009). Individuals were identified using unique composite genotypes.
Movement pattern analysis.-The locations of scats from genetically identified snow leopard individuals were plotted in the ''land use'' layer of the region. Minimum convex polygons were created to calculate the home ranges and understand the movement pattern and area covered by the individual. We used Hawth's Analysis Tools for ArcGIS 9.x (Beyer 2004) for the calculation of area of coverage by all individuals and by each individual. Once the home-range area was calculated it was used to estimate the potential number of snow leopards living in the region by dividing the area of suitable habitat in the upper Mustang region by the average home-range size of snow leopards.
Diet analysis.-Standard microhistological methodology was used to identify prey species from hair samples found in scats by comparing them to reference hair samples from all potential prey species (Oli 1993;Oli et al. 1993;Mukherjee et al. 1994;Aryal and Kreigenhofer 2009;Aryal et al. 2012b). Snow leopard scats were collected via SLIMS; therefore, we collected scats only if we found snow leopard sign around the scats, such as scent spray, scrapes, pugmarks, or a combination of these. There were no other cat species in the area; however, we made careful observations in order to distinguish snow leopard scats from those of other carnivores, such as red fox, jackal (Canis aureus), wolf, and domestic dog (Aryal and Kreigenhofer 2009;Aryal et al. 2014b). The microscopic structure of the medulla and cuticular structure of hair were observed to identify prey items in the scats (Oli 1993;Bahuguna et al. 2010;Aryal et al. 2014b).
Hair samples from the scat were first washed in hot water. Items other than hair such as mud, bones, and vegetation were recorded and then removed; only hair samples were processed further. Hairs were thoroughly air-dried and then cleaned in ether for 1 h to remove wax and any traces of moisture. Finally, the hairs were passed through xylol for 24 h. A gelatin solution was used to prepare slides to show the cuticular structure of hairs and examine the medulla structure of the hair; cuticular scales were observed by the impression technique (Oli 1993;Bahuguna et al. 2010). Slides were observed under a light microscope (1003 and 4003). At least 20 hair samples were analyzed from each scat sample and we calculated the frequency of occurrence of each prey item in the snow leopard scats (Oli 1993;Mukherjee et al. 1994;Aryal and Kreigenhofer 2009;Bahuguna et al. 2010;Aryal et al. 2014b). A chi-square test was used to determine significant differences between prey frequencies within each season and between seasons.

[SECTION] results
Snow leopard status.-Snow leopard surveys were conducted in 6 Village Development Committees (Lomangthnag, Chhunup, Chhoser, Charang, Ghami, and Surkhang) of the upper Mustang region (Fig. 2). An occupancy survey revealed the presence of snow leopards in 41 grids covering an area of 846.0 km 2 , whereas snow leopards were absent in 77 grids covering 1,211 km 2 (Fig. 2).
One hundred thirty-eight transect lines were surveyed in potential snow leopard habitats, including ridgelines, riverbanks, and gullies in the upper Mustang region. Transect line lengths varied from 100 to 1,000 m and covered 59.9 km. Altogether, 283 instances of snow leopard sign were recorded along the transects. Scrapes were the most common type of sign (62%) observed, followed by scats (35%), pugmarks (1%), and urine spray (1%; Table 1). Chhoser and Surkhang Village Development Committees contained most of the snow leopard sign-34% and 33%, respectively-followed by the Ghami,   1). However, there was no significant difference in the distribution or density of sign throughout the study area (v 2 5 ¼ 2.25, P ¼ 0.09; Table 1). Habitat types.-Snow leopards preferred cliffs (IEI ¼ 0.80), grassland (IEI ¼ 0.29), shrubland (IEI ¼ 0.67), and areas near water bodies (IEI ¼ 0.41), whereas they avoided agricultural areas and glaciers (IEI , 0; Table 2A). Snow leopards primarily used barren land (55%), followed by grassland (39.5%), but did not frequent sand (2%) or glaciers (, 1%).
Snow leopards also used , 1% of land near human settlements, a habitat type that compromised approximately 2% of available land in the upper Mustang region.
Elevation.-Snow leopards preferred elevations ranged between 3,500 and 5,000 m, especially elevation ranges of 4,000-4,500 m (IEI ¼ 0.59) and 4,500-5,000 m (IEI ¼ 0.44). Snow leopards avoided elevations . 6,000 m and , 3,000 m (Table 2B). Elevations utilized were significantly correlated with utilized habitat types (r s ¼ 0.720, d.f. ¼ 9, P ¼ 0.02), but their use by snow leopards was not correlated with aspect (r s ¼ À0.234, d.f. ¼ 9, P ¼ 0.54) or slope (r s ¼ 0.661, d.f. ¼ 9, P ¼ 0.53).
Aspect and slope.-Although the IEI was positive for southern (IEI ¼ 0.05), southwestern (IEI ¼ 0.01), western (IEI ¼ 0.08), and northwestern aspects (IEI ¼ 0.04), and negative for the other aspects (IEI À0.02; Table 2C), there were no significant differences in the use of different aspects by snow leopards (v 2 7 ¼ 0.78, P ¼ 0.99; Table 2C). Snow leopards had positive IEI for slopes of 418-518 (IEI ¼ 0.03) and 518-648 (IEI ¼ 0.19), but there were no significant differences in the use of different slopes by snow leopards (v 2 8 ¼ 0.0001, P ¼ 1; Table 2D).
Species identification.-Out of 34 putative scat samples, 85% (29) were identified as originating from snow leopards (Supporting Information S1, DOI: 10.1644/13-MAMM-A-243. S1). Of these, 27.6% were identified as originating from a male and 72.4% from a female (Supporting Information S2, DOI: 10.1644/13-MAMM-A-243.S2). Out of the 29 snow leopardpositive PCR samples, 62% were successfully genotyped using 6 microsatellite markers. Five unique individuals (3 males and 2 females) were identified (Fig. 3; Table 3).
Movement pattern and population density.-The 5 snow leopards ranged over an area of 264.7 km 2 during the study periods in which we collected scats (Fig. 3). The minimum convex polygon area of Female 3 was 59.3 km 2 and the area of Male 1 was 89.4 km 2 for the year; the average of polygons was 52.9 km 2 (Fig. 3). Male 1 and Females 2 and 3 had overlapping movement areas. The single data points for Male 2 and Female 1 fell outside of the movement areas of all other individuals (Fig. 3). Population density was 1.9 individuals/100 km 2 , estimating an average 22 snow leopards (snow leopard suitable area [1,162.5 km 2 ] divided by average movement area [52.9 km 2 ]) in the upper Mustang region.
Diet composition of snow leopards.-A total of 248 snow leopard scats were collected from the study area (157 from upper Mustang in 2009-2012 and 97 from Manang in 2009-2010) and subjected to microhistological diet analysis to identify the prey of snow leopards.
Blue sheep represented most of the snow leopards' diet (63%) in the Annapurna Conservation Area (v 2 15 ¼ 1.3, P ¼ 0.01; Table 4), with the 2nd-most commonly consumed prey item being livestock (18.4%), followed by the Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana; 7%).
Upper Mustang region.-Overall, blue sheep contributed a significant majority (65%) of the diet content for snow leopards in the upper Mustang region (v 2 12 ¼ 14.3, P ¼ 0.0001). This was uniform across all seasons, with blue sheep comproing the highest percentage of prey species in snow leopard scats in winter (65%; v 2 10 ¼ 9.9, P ¼ 0.01), spring (61%; v 2 11 ¼ 12.24, P ¼ 0.0001), and summer (54%; v 2 10 ¼ 9.12, P ¼ 0.0001; Table 4). Livestock contributed an average of 17.4% to the snow leopard diet throughout all seasons in the upper Mustang region, with slightly more livestock contributing in winter (21%), followed by spring (15%) and summer (13%; Table 4).
Manang region.-In the Manang region blue sheep also represented a significant majority of the diet of snow leopards (59%, v 2 15 ¼ 2.39, P ¼ 0.001). This predominance of blue sheep as the main prey of the snow leopard occurred throughout all seasons, with 58% in spring-summer (v 2 15 ¼ 16, P ¼ 0.008) and 61.7% in winter (v 2 15 ¼ 1.4, P ¼ 0.23; Table 4). Livestock composed an average of 23.5% of the overall diet of snow leopards in the Manang region (v 2 15 ¼ 1.7, P ¼ 0.3), but again slightly more livestock were found in winter (25.6%) than in spring (20.7%; Table 4).

[SECTION] discussion
Occupancy and SLIMS.-In our occupancy survey, we used a 4.5 3 4.5-km grid, which represented the assumed average home-range size for snow leopards in Nepal (Jackson 1996;Oli 1997). The home range of snow leopards depends on prey availability and the landscape pattern (McCarthy 2000), with home ranges expected to be smaller in regions of high density of prey (MacArthur 1972;McCarthy 2000), as was the case in our study area. Our small sample sizes did not allow us to estimate actual home ranges, but rather minimum home ranges of the snow leopards for which we collected multiple scats. Our estimates of minimum home-range size were nonetheless larger than previous estimates of 37 km 2 obtained by radiotracking (Jackson 1996).
Site occupancy modelling is used to estimate population density, occupied habitats, and species richness (MacKenzie et al. 2002(MacKenzie et al. , 2006)). We used a single-season occupancy habitat survey and did not find snow leopard sign in 77 grid plots; however, this does not mean snow leopards were not present in  these grids. Therefore, occupancy surveys lasting 2 or more seasons are recommended to understand seasonal habitat use and occurrence of the species across the landscape. Therefore, had we relied on the SLIMS method, which uses sign density to estimate snow leopard numbers, we would have concluded that 8-25 snow leopards existed in the upper Mustang region.
The SLIMS methodology has several weaknesses, including observer bias, misidentification of sign, effects of varying environmental conditions, and site-selection bias. It is, nonetheless, a useful method for obtaining preliminary presence and absence data for snow leopards in a region (McCarthy et al. 2008). McCarthy et al. (2008) suggested a more reliable and lower-cost method to determine snow leopard population and distribution estimates via fecal DNA analysis. However, multiseason presence-absence site occupancy surveys may be the best option when DNA analysis is prohibitively expensive (MacKenzie et al. 2002(MacKenzie et al. , 2006)). ). Our results showed that noninvasive genetic analysis was more appropriate method to estimate snow leopard density. These methods can be implemented for other species (e.g., brown bear, red fox, wolf, blue sheep, and marmot) at the regional level to explore their status. These species coexisted and shared similar habitat with snow leopards at the regional level (Aryal et al. 2010b(Aryal et al. , 2010c(Aryal et al. , 2012a(Aryal et al. , 2013b)).
Habitat use and availability.-Our results showed snow leopards avoided areas associated with agriculture and human settlement in the upper Mustang region, where they used only about 0.4% of these areas, similar to results of previous studies (Schaller 1977;Jackson and Hunter 1996). However, a lack of wild prey species often causes snow leopards to approach human settlement in search of livestock. Most of the upper Mustang pastureland was utilized seasonally by livestock. Similarly, snow leopard habitats in Sagarmatha National Park were significantly used by tourists, porters, guides, and livestock, which disturbed and harassed snow leopards in the region (Wolf and Ale 2009). In upper Mustang, habitat preference by the snow leopard depended on prey availability. Cliffs, grasslands, shrubland, ridges, and gullies were preferred by snow leopards where more livestock and wild prey were observed grazing regularly. Barren land and glaciers were avoided by snow leopards, although they might be used by leopards opportunistically while hunting, mating, and marking territory borders (Lovari et al. 2009;Wolf and Ale 2009). Similar habitat features were used by brown bears (Aryal et al. 2012b) and blue sheep (Aryal et al. 2012a(Aryal et al. , 2013b) ) in the region.
Our study showed that in upper Mustang and Manang, snow leopards preferred the 3,000-to 5,000-m elevation range, but not higher than 5,000 m. Other studies suggested that snow leopards preferred higher elevations (Schaller et al. 1988;Fox et al. 1991;Schaller 1998), whereas Wolf and Ale (2009) recorded a preference for lower elevations.
Genetic-based estimates of movement areas and density.-Our study estimated snow leopard home ranges to vary from 59 to 89 km 2 , which was greater than reported in previous studies in this region (Jackson and Ahlborn 1984;Jackson 1996;Oli 1997), but much smaller than the home range of . 300 km 2 reported for snow leopards in Mongolia (McCarthy et al.  Sunquist 1981;Smith 1993;Majumder et al. 2012).
Diet and noninvasive analysis.-In recent studies (Karmacharya et al. 2011), only 27% of putative snow leopard scats were found to actually be from the target species. Similarly, Lovari et al. (2009) reported that only 44% of field-collected scats belonged to snow leopards. Shehdaz et al. (2012) reported that only 43.3% of scats belonged to snow leopards out of all collected samples (n ¼ 203). However, in our study about 85% of scat samples were from snow leopards, most likely because we only collected scat associated with snow leopard scrapes, leading to a low level of misidentification.
Our analyses suggested that the snow leopard's primary wild prey species was the blue sheep followed by the Himalayan marmot in upper Mustang, and musk deer (Moschus spp.) in the Manang region, where Himalayan marmots were absent. Significantly, livestock was the 2nd most consumed item, which may be of concern to both the local farmers and the snow leopards. Predation of livestock was particularly severe in winter, when marmots are unavailable. We analyzed indigestible hair samples from snow leopard scats collected in upper Mustang and Manang. It is important to recognize that by only studying hair samples from scat, we cannot determine whether the prey was killed or scavenged, and it is impossible to predict how many individuals of the identified prey species were consumed, especially with small mammals such as pikas (Ochotona roylei) and marmots commonly found in the scats (Floyd et al. 1978;Oli et al. 1993;Aryal and Kreigenhofer 2009). Earlier studies in Nepal also documented conflicts between people and snow leopards due to snow leopard depredation of livestock; these data were collected through interviews with local people and diet analysis (Schaller et al. 1987;Fox et al. 1991;Oli 1993;Oli et al. 1993;Aryal and Kreigenhofer 2009).
Blue sheep was the main prey species of snow leopards in Manang and upper Mustang, whereas Himalayan tahr (Hemitragus jemlahicus) was the primary prey species in Sagarmatha National Park (Lovari et al. 2009). Microhistological-based diet analysis gives lower estimates for small mammals and the method relies on the proportion of hairs or animal remains in the scats (Ackerman et al. 1984). Therefore, our results estimated the minimum proportion of small mammals, such as pikas and marmots. Our diet analyses indicated that there was no marmot in the snow leopard diet from the Manang district; however, Oli et al. (1993) reported that about 20% of the overall diet consisted of marmots in the same area 2 decades ago. Field surveys for marmots and interviews with local people (n ¼ 279) over the past 3 years have indicated that the marmot is only found in the Mustang region and is not found in the Manang region. Therefore, marmots found in snow leopard scats in Manang district (Oli et al. 1993) might be due to snow leopards travelling from upper Mustang to Manang, even though there was a 7-km 2 area composed of high mountains, barren land with no grasses, and an absence of prey species representing a barrier between Manang and upper Mustang in terms of connectivity of habitat (Fig. 2). Further genetic-based studies should be conducted to examine the connectivity of snow leopard populations between the Manang and upper Mustang regions.
There were other predators in the region such as brown bears, red fox, and wolf that depend upon similar habitat and prey species (Aryal et al. 2012a). Because snow leopards and brown bears have overlap of diet and habitat in the region, there may be competition between them. Our research can be a model that can be replicated with other species at the regional level to understand interactions among species. Finally, we believe the findings may be useful in the preparation of a conservation strategy for snow leopards and its associate prey at a regional level.
