[SECTION] title
Real-time assessment of hybridization between wolves and dogs: combining noninvasive samples with ancestry informative markers

[SECTION] abstract
Wolves and dogs provide a paradigmatic example of the ecological and conservation implications of hybridization events between wild and domesticated forms. However, our understanding of such implications has been traditionally hampered by both high genetic similarity and the difficulties in obtaining tissue samples (TS), which limit our ability to assess ongoing hybridization events. To assess the occurrence and extension of hybridization in a pack of wolf-dog hybrids in northwestern Iberia, we compared the power of 52 nuclear markers implemented on TS with a subset of 13 ancestry informative markers (AIMs) typed in noninvasive samples (NIS). We demonstrate that the 13 AIMs are as accurate as the 52 markers that were chosen without regard to the power to differentiate between wolves and dogs, also having the advantage of being rapidly screened on NIS. The efficiency of AIMs significantly outperformed ten random sets of similar size and an additional commercial set of 18 markers. Bayesian clustering analysis implemented on AIMs and NIS identified nine hybrids, two wolves and two dogs. Four hybrids were unambiguously assigned to F1xWolf backcrosses. Our approach (AIMs + NIS) overcomes previous difficulties related to sample availability and informative power of markers, allowing a quick identification of wolf-dog hybrids in the first phases of hybridization episodes. This provides managers with a reliable tool to evaluate hybridization and estimate the success of their actions. This approach may be easily adapted for other pairs of wild/domesticated species, thus improving our understanding of the introgression of domestication genes into natural populations.

[SECTION] introduction
Hybridization is increasingly recognized as a powerful evolutionary force promoting speciation (Soltis & Soltis 2009), shaping adaptation through introgressive hybridization (Kays et al. 2010) or yielding evolutionary novelties (Godinho et al. 2008). However, hybridization can also pose a risk to species, particularly non-natural hybridization (Rhymer & Simberloff 1996;Allendorf et al. 2001), turning this process into the focus of attention within conservation and management disciplines and leading to an intense and controversial debate in recent times (e.g. Wolf et al. 2001;Haig et al. 2004;Fitzpatrick et al. 2010;Stronen & Paquet 2013).
Climate change (Garroway et al. 2010), species translocation, introduction or invasion (Kidd et al. 2009), and habitat transformation (Mullen et al. 2012) or human pressure (Rutledge et al. 2012) are increasing the chances for hybridization and genetic introgression between closely related species, including between wild and domestic forms (Randi 2008). The latter is considered a very worrying type of hybridization for wild species due to the consequences of intensive artificial selection in domestic stocks to conform to human interests and is expected to increase the probability for accumulation of deleterious alleles, as well as to disrupt co-adapted gene complexes or local adaptations in wild populations (Allendorf et al. 2001;Randi 2008).
A classic example of the conservation implications of this process is the hybridization between wolves (Canis lupus) and its domestic form, the dog (Canis l. familiaris).
In particular, the idea that the spread of domestication genes into wolf populations could disrupt local adaptation or increase genetic homogenization through introgressive hybridization soon became a major conservation issue for this charismatic species (Vil a & Wayne 1999;Boitani 2000) and is today the focus of research and conservation interest, especially in Europe (Randi 2011). Several cases of hybridization with dogs have been reported throughout the entire range of the species (Randi 2011), but to date, results appear to suggest that its frequency in the wild is low and few instances of significant introgression of dog genes into wolf populations were described (Randi & Lucchini 2002;Vil a et al. 2003;Verardi et al. 2006;Godinho et al. 2011;Hindrikson et al. 2012; but see Anderson et al. 2009).
However, the extremely high genetic similarity between wolves and dogs (Wayne & vonHoldt 2012) makes the detection of hybrids a difficult task, which is exacerbated by the fact that wolf-dog hybrids can exhibit typical dog or wolf phenotypes. This problem could be partially solved using biparental molecular markers, but their effectiveness appears to be strongly dependent on both the number (see V€ ah€ a & Primmer 2006) and availability of accurate allelic and genotypic frequencies in reference populations (e.g. 'pure' wolves and dogs), a crucial issue when applying Bayesian clustering to detect hybridization (Anderson & Thompson 2002;Falush et al. 2003).
A major conservation concern is the low chance of detecting hybridization events, which, to date, have been essentially anecdotal reports (e.g. casual observations, roadkills, poaching or hunting of suspected individuals). For a correct assessment of these cases, obtaining tissue samples (TS) from the animals is usually needed (but see Bohling & Waits 2011;and Caniglia et al. 2013). Consequently, because obtaining TS from wolves is often difficult, our ability to assess the occurrence of wolf-dog hybridizations in real time and its extension at a population level is still very limited. This is unfortunate because repercussions on our understanding of the ecological, evolutionary and conservation implications of this process are substantial. For example, from a management point of view, the invasive nature and difficulty of collecting TS from a representative number of individuals limit our ability to evaluate the occurrence and extent of hybridization in real time, which can lead to significant delays in management efforts to mitigate their potential effects. In this respect, ecologists must provide managers with reliable, quick and efficient tools to evaluate the occurrence of hybridization and its importance at a population level.
The alternative to address this task is the use of noninvasive samples (NIS). Although the use of NIS has grown extraordinarily in recent years (Long et al. 2008), their application to detect hybridization is still rare (Bohling & Waits 2011;Rutledge et al. 2012;Caniglia et al. 2013), and the optimization of results for detecting wolfdog hybrids is far from achieved. Here, we test the utility of NIS to assist conservation practitioners in the management of wolf-dog hybridization. To do so, we use already available NIS and TS samples from a canid pack composed of wolves and hybrids in northwestern Iberia. Our main objectives are to evaluate the utility of NIS (i) for a quick detection of hybridization at both individual and population levels and (ii) to estimate the genetic composition of individuals and identify their respective hybrid classes. To do this, we compare the power of a set of 52 nuclear markers, including those described in Godinho et al. (2011) for TS, with a second one of 13 markers we selected for NIS. Our panel of 13 markers is based on their ancestry informative power, and offers a fast and inexpensive solution to study ongoing hybridization events.

[SECTION] material and methods

[SECTION] the canid pack of barbanza
We used as case study a canid pack located in the Sierra del Barbanza (42°42 0 N-8°56 0 W), a mountainous area (ca. 416 km 2 ; 0-600 m.a.s.l) in northwestern Iberia (Galicia; Fig. 1b,c), where wolves have been present at least during the last four decades in a human-dominated landscape (Llaneza et al. 2012a), feeding mainly on livestock, particularly cattle and horses (Guiti an et al. 1979;L opez-Bao et al. 2013). In this area, feral dogs are thought to be numerous although no population estimates exist. In 2011, field observations (A. Perez, personal communication) and a subsequent study funded by the Regional Government of Galicia showed the pack included both wolves and wolf-dog hybrids (Godinho et al. 2012;Fig. 1a). As a consequence, in the same year, based on general management recommendations of wolf-dog hybridization events (Boitani 2000), stakeholders decided for the removal of putative hybrids from the field (two in July and two in September 2011, a male and a female each time; Godinho et al. 2012).
Between August and September 2011, we collected 38 wolf-like scats along existing paths, forest trails and firebreaks, where the probability of territorial marks detection is maximized (Llaneza et al. 2014). Samples were collected during four different surveys (at least 1 week interval between surveys, 2 days per survey) corresponding to a total sampled distance of about 35 km per sampling (ca. 105 km in total). All scats compatible with wolf-like canids were collected, which increased the chance of collecting scats from red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) and dogs. Both TS from the four putative hybrids and NIS were stored at room temperature in sterile tubes containing approximately four parts of 96% ethanol.

[SECTION] laboratory procedures
DNA from TS was extracted using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA) according to manufacturer's instructions. The same extraction procedure was used for reference samples (242 wolves and 237 dogs). Reference wolves were obtained from dead animals (mainly roadkills and legal hunting) collected between 1996 and 2012 and were selected to allow a maximum of two wolves per pack/generation across the Iberian range (Fig. 1b). All wolf samples carried an Iberian mtDNA haplotype (Vil a et al. 1999;Godinho et al. 2011) and were classified according to the Euclidean distance to Barbanza in three groups: <10 km (n = 17), 10-50 km (n = 19) and >50 km (n = 206). Reference dogs were comprised of stray dogs (n = 45) and a random selection of samples including (i) six Iberian herding breeds (Serra da Estrela, n = 28; Castro Laboreiro, n = 24; Cão de Gado Transmontano, n = 22; Rafeiro do Alentejo, n = 25; Fila de São Miguel, n = 15; Serra de Aires, n = 13), (ii) three hound breeds (Portuguese Water Dog, n = 8; Podengo Português, n = 25; Perdigueiro Português, n = 26) and (iii) German Shepherd (n = 6). Reference dogs carried dog mtDNA haplotypes (Vil a et al. 1999;Godinho et al. 2011).
DNA was extracted from faecal samples following Frantz et al. (2003) protocol after applying the GuSCN⁄silica method (Boom et al. 1990). Subsequently, PCR inhibitors were removed from samples using the Microcon â YM-30 centrifugal Filter System (Millipore, Billerica, MA). All pre-PCR procedures were carried out in a dedicated laboratory used only for the manipulation of lowquality DNA under sterile conditions and positive air pressure. Negative controls were included throughout the entire process to test for DNA contamination. The quality of noninvasive DNA was assessed based on the amplification of one high-copy DNA target (420 bp of the mtDNA HVI region; Vil a et al. 1999) and four amplification replicates of three low-copy DNA targets (microsatellites). Samples exhibiting dog or Iberian wolf mitochondrial haplotypes (n = 25) and successful amplification of the four markers were analysed further.

[SECTION] markers selection and genotyping
Individual multilocus genotypes were determined for TS using a set of 52 nuclear loci selected across the genome without regard to the degree to which they differentiate wolves and dogs, and for NIS using a subset of 13 ancestry informative markers (AIMs) of the initial 52 loci. The 13 markers were specifically selected based on (i) the magnitude of F ST values between wolf and dog for 11 markers and (ii) the probability of identity (PID) for two additional loci to ensure unequivocal individual identification.
Fourty-two of the 52 loci matched to the panel screened by Godinho et al. (2011), and the same methodology was applied. The remaining 10 loci include eight microsatellites, one single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in intron 2 of solute carrier family 24 member 5 gene (SLC24A5) and a 5 bp deletion at intron 3 of the KIT ligand gene (KITLG) (see Appendix S1 for a complete description of new markers and primers). Additionally, scats were screened for a molecular sexing test following Seddon (2005).
For each TS, 50 microsatellites were amplified in five multiplex reactions, while for NIS, 11 microsatellites and the 5 bp deletion of KITLG were amplified in two multiplex reactions (see Appendix S2 for markers description, multiplex sets and PCR conditions). Each locus was amplified and genotyped four different times for each scat sample to minimize errors. Amplifications were performed using the QIAGEN Multiplex PCR Kit (except for Finnzymes Canine Genotypes Panel 1.1) following the manufacturer's instructions and using a 10 ll final volume and negative controls to monitor possible contaminants. Fluorescent labelling of PCR fragments was accomplished following Blacket et al. (2002). PCR products were separated by size on an ABI3130xl DNA analyzer. Alleles were determined using GENEMAPPER 4.1 (Applied Biosystems) and checked manually by two observers. For scat samples, the consensus genotypes over the four replicas were determined following three rules: (i) heterozygous genotypes were accepted if the same genotype was observed in two independent PCRs; (ii) homozygous genotypes were accepted if the genotype was observed in three independent PCRs; and (iii) samples that failed to amplify at four or more loci were removed from further analysis.
Successful amplifications for the SLC24A5 and mtDNA fragments were sequenced in both directions following the BigDye chemistry (Applied Biosystems), and sequencing products were separated in the same DNA analyzer. Sequences were aligned and compared in the software SEQSCAPE 2.0 (Applied Biosystems), and any discrepancies re-assessed. Data were deposited in Gen-Bank (see Data Accessibility for Accession numbers).

[SECTION] data analysis
Data sets with 52 and 13 markers were analysed in parallel for all procedures in order to evaluate the power of the subset selected for NIS. Genetic diversity was evaluated for wolves and dogs (Barbanza individuals were excluded) based on allele frequencies and observed (Ho) and expected (He) heterozygosities for each locus at each population using ARLEQUIN 3.5.1.2 (Excoffier et al. 2005).
The same software was used to test for deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and significance of association between genotypes at pairs of loci in each population (LD). The level of statistical significance was adjusted using strict Bonferroni corrections (Rice 1989). Allelic richness (AR) and private allelic richness (PrAR) per population were estimated using the rarefaction algorithm implemented in ADZE 1.0 (Szpiech et al. 2008) after standardizing to the smallest sample size (N = 224).
ARLEQUIN was also used to estimate genetic differentiation between wolves and dogs through a hierarchical analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) using h analogues of Wright's F-statistics. Significance of genetic differentiation was tested by random permutations, under the null hypothesis that all individuals belong to a single population.
Multiple identical genotypes from NIS were identified and excluded from analysis as they are likely from the same individual. The mean allelic dropout and false allele amplification values across loci for the 13-loci data set were evaluated using GIMLET (Vali ere 2002). Individual genotypes of 242 reference wolves and 237 reference dogs were analysed using the Bayesian clustering procedure implemented in STRUCTURE 2.3.3 (Falush et al. 2003) assuming two populations (K = 2) and including a set of previously validated wolf and dog samples (Godinho et al. 2011). The STRUCTURE analysis was performed independently 20 times for 10 6 permutations after a burn-in period of 10 5 permutations using the admixture model with correlated allele frequencies among populations and no priors for individual identification (POPFLAG=0). The average membership proportion (Qi) for wolf and dog reference samples and the individual membership proportions (q i ) to the inferred clusters and their 90% probability intervals (CI) were assessed in each run of STRUCTURE. The same analysis was repeated including Barbanza individuals, but this time considering each parental class as a separate entity (POPFLAG=1) and turning on the option PFROMPOPFLAGONLY to update allele frequencies throughout the run using only reference individuals, causing the qi estimate for each unknown individual dependent only on the reference set and not on other unknown individuals in the sample (Pritchard et al. 2010).
The power of admixture analyses to distinguish parental from hybrid classes and to establish the range of expected q-values for admixed generations was assessed for both the 52 loci and the 13 AIMs by simulating both parental and hybrid genotypes in HYBRIDLAB v.1.0 (Nielsen et al. 2006; named STRUCTURE-training by Latch et al. (2011). Genotypes of 100 wolves and 100 dogs with q-values greater than 0.98 (training data set) were used to generate 1000 of each parental genotypes.
The results were then used to simulate 1000 of each F 1 and first and second backcross genotypes to both wolves and dogs. Simulated genotypes were then submitted to admixture analyses with STRUCTURE using the same model and settings described above (10 5 burn-in, 10 6 iterations, admixture model, correlated allele frequencies, POPFLAG=0). In addition, we compared the results obtained for our set of AIMs with 10 subsets of 13 randomly selected markers from the initial set of 52 to test its performance. We also carried out a comparison with the set of 18 microsatellites available as a single multiplex on the Finnzymes commercial kit. These subsets were checked for genetic diversity, probability of identity (PID), probability of identity between siblings (PIDsibs; using GIMLET) and differentiation between 1000 simulated wolves and 1000 simulated dogs. All subsets were also run on STRUCTURE (10 5 burnin, 10 6 iterations, admixture model, correlated allele frequencies, POPFLAG=0) for estimation of the average population assignment (Qi), range of individual assignments (qi range) and 90% probability intervals (CI) for both wolves and dogs. As an indicator of effectiveness, we also calculated the proportion of wolves with qi wolf below 0.95 and the proportion of dogs with qi Dog below 0.90. Statistical differences between the Qi Wolf obtained using the selected AIMs and each of the Qi Wolf generated by each randomly selected subset of 13 markers, as well as the Finnzymes set, were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests. We further tested for differences in the proportion of wolves with qi < 0.95 between the selected AIMs and the 11 subsets of markers using a two-samples proportion test.
A detailed analysis of hybrid ancestry was conducted using NEWHYBRIDS 1.1 (Anderson & Thompson 2002). The posterior probability of assignment (qi) to seven genotype frequency classes (wolf, dog, F 1 , and first and second-generation backcrosses to wolves and dogs) was estimated for each Barbanza individual using prior population information for reference samples. Settings used were 10 6 MCMC permutations following 10 5 burn-in steps, no information for allele frequencies and Jeffreystype priors for both mixing proportions and allele frequencies.
To evaluate the proportion of individuals studied at Barbanza, we also estimated the number of individuals in the area using the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) implemented in the 'capwire' R package (Pennell et al. 2013). This is a capture-recapture method that accounts for the fact that individuals can be 'captured' more than once per sampling session using NIS. We used the equal capture model (ECM) and performed a parametric bootstrap (1000 bootstraps) to estimate 95% CI for the MLE.

[SECTION] results
Individual identification at the Barbanza pack using NIS MtDNA sequences were obtained from 35 wolf-like scats (92.1%), from which 25 (71.4%) were assigned to the Iberian wolf haplotype W7 (Vali ere et al. 2003), four to the dog (11.4%) and six to the red fox (17.2%). Individual identifications of scat samples resulted in 62.1% success, representing 18 of the 29 wolf or dog mtDNA identifications. Mean values of allelic dropout and false alleles amplification across loci (12.3% and 1.0%, respectively) and across samples (13.0% and 0.8%) were under the average expected values for noninvasive genetic studies (Broquet et al. 2007).
Overall, between July and September 2011, we identified 13 individuals, 10 of them using NIS (individual TS4 was identified using both methods; Table 2). We could determine the sex in eight NIS, identifying in total (including TS) eight females and four males (Table 2). The MLE-estimated census size in Barbanza area was 14 (95% bootstrap CI: 11-20 individuals; dogs were excluded from the analysis), suggesting that we sampled a significant fraction of the estimated population (80%).

[SECTION] comparing diversity and differentiation for 52 and 13 loci
The comparison between 52-and 13-loci data sets for genetic diversity of Iberian wolves and dogs showed contrasting results. The 52-loci data set showed higher genetic diversity for all measured statistics, for both wolves and dogs, including mean number of alleles per locus, allelic richness and expected heterozygosity (Table 1). Nonetheless, values achieved with 13 loci for the private allelic richness were very similar, for both wolves and dogs, conforming the expectations of retaining loci that maximize differentiation (Table 1). Regardless of the data set, Iberian wolves exhibited lower genetic diversity values for all parameters when compared to dogs (see Appendix S3 for individual diversity and differentiation measures for the 13 AIMs). When analysing wolves and dogs separately, we did not observe any significant LD pairwise combinations (significance probability level P < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for 132 comparisons) or deviations from Hardy-Weinberg expectations (P < 0.01) for any loci. This observation likely results from the selection of wolf reference samples avoiding familiar relationships, and the same applies to both stray and purebred dogs.
Population pairwise F ST-52 (0.193) and F ST-13 (0.341) over loci revealed a highly significant genetic differentiation between wolves and dogs (P < 0.0001; Table 1) for both data sets. Nonetheless, the larger F ST value exhibited by the selected 13 loci shows a greater effectiveness to differentiate the two gene pools. Our AMOVA results also showed that a high proportion of genetic diversity was explained by variation between populations in both data sets (19.90% for 52 loci, 35.86% for 13 loci).

[SECTION] detecting hybridization with 52 and 13 loci
Bayesian clustering analyses performed with reference samples showed concordant results for both 52 and 13 sets of loci and a similar power to sharply differentiate wolves from dogs (Table 2; Figs 2 and3). The average proportion of membership to the wolf cluster was similar for both data sets (Qi 52 = 0.998 and Qi 13 = 0.997; Table 2), with qi-values ranging between 0.977 < qi 52 < 1.000 and 0.965 < qi 13 < 0.998. Only three and six out of 242 reference wolves presented the minimum value of the 90% CI below 0.90 for 52-and 13-loci data sets, respectively (minimum CI 52 = 0.879 and minimum CI 13 = 0.818). Notably, the 37 wolves collected <50 km to Barbanza evidenced qi > 0.98 and narrow CIs, reflecting a nonadmixed genetic background for the wolf population in the area. All reference dogs were probabilistically assigned to the dog cluster with very similar performance in both data sets, showing an average proportion of membership of Qi 52 = 0.997 and Qi 13 = 0.993, but larger CI for 13 loci (CI = 0.669-1.000) than for 52 loci (CI = 0.864-1.000; Table 2 and Fig. 2).
The effectiveness of the 13-loci data set was further evaluated using 1000 simulated genotypes from each parental and hybrid class. This STRUCTURE-training procedure revealed average assignments to the correct parental class of qi wolf = 0.967 (minimum qi wolf = 0.910) and qi dog = 0.945 (minimum qi dog = 0.809). Furthermore, only 5% among the 1000 simulated wolf genotypes exhibited a qi wolf < 0.95, while 10% of dog simulated genotypes presented qi dog < 0.90. These Bayesian clustering results obtained with the use of selected AIMs on simulated genotypes of parental classes allowed two different threshold values to be defined for wolves and dogs, respectively, 0.90 and 0.80. Average qi of simulated F 1 genotypes was 0.495 (highest qi F1 = 0.757), and the average qi BxWolf and qi BxDog to their respective clusters was 0.740 and 0.749. For second-generation backcrosses, our battery of loci revealed an average of qi Bx2Wolf and qi Bx2Dog of 0.854 and 0.860, respectively. Based on  defined thresholds, these results suggest that our set of 13 AIMs detect 100% of F 1 individuals, and 96.3% and 66.4% of first-generation backcross individuals to wolf and dog, respectively. For the second-generation backcrosses, the power achieved by this set of loci was 68.2% and 22.8%, respectively, to wolf and dog.

[SECTION] hybrid identification at barbanza
Based on 0.90 and 0.80 thresholds for wolf and dog assignments, respectively, as established using simulated individuals, the clustering assignment of the 13 wolf-like Barbanza individuals clearly showed our data set contained two wolves (qi NIS3 = 0.998 and qi NIS7 = 0.984) and two dogs (qi NIS4 = 0.943 and qi NIS9 = 0.981). The remaining individuals exhibited varying assignments to the wolf cluster equal or below 0.90 (0.905 < qi < 0.670) and wide CI (Table 2). The two wolves and the nine wolf-like individuals exhibited a wolf mitochondrial haplotype, while the two dogs presented dog mtDNA haplotypes. The four analysed TS showed very similar results on clustering analysis with either 52 or 13 loci, although the use of a reduced number of loci slightly shifts the qi-values towards hybridization (Table 2). Analysis of recent ancestry using NEWHYBRIDS for the 13-loci data set confirmed the assignment to parental classes of the two wolves and two dogs previously identified by clustering analysis and further identified one other individual with a high posterior probability of being a wolf (NIS1 = 95.3%; Table 3). Four individuals had a high probability assignment (>80%) of being firstgeneration backcrosses to wolf, while the remaining four were assigned ambiguously to both parental and hybrid classes (Table 3). However, while the use of both sets of nuclear markers showed high agreement at population level, there were slight disagreements at individual level: the four individuals genotyped using TS were undoubtedly identified as second-generation backcrosses to wolf using the 52 loci, while the analysis with the smaller data set assigned two individuals to first-generation backcross to wolf, and the other two were not assigned to any particular hybrid class.

[SECTION] discussion
Worldwide, millions of free-ranging dogs coexist with a few tens of thousands of wolves. Consequently, despite biological constraints, there are many opportunities for wolves and dogs hybridize, and cumulative data suggest Fig. 4 Relationship between F ST values and the proportion of wolves with individual assignment (qi) <0.95 (circles) for the selected set of 13 AIMs, the whole set of 52 markers, a commercial panel of 18 markers (Finnzymes) and 10 randomly selected subsets of 13 markers. For each set of markers, proportions were calculated based on 1000 simulated wolves and dogs, respectively. For each set of markers, the observed range in the qi-values is also shown (grey bars).
Table 3 Inferred ancestry for wolves and dogs, and for the 13 Barbanza pack individuals. Ancestry was calculated in NEWHYBRIDS using seven genotype classes [wolf, dog, F 1 , BxWolf (backcross to wolf), BxDog (backcross to dog), Bx2Wolf (second-generation backcross to wolf) and Bx2Dog (second-generation backcross to dog)]. Values in bold indicate probabilities higher than 10% of belonging to a hybrid class 52-loci 13-loci that hybridization may be more frequent than previously suspected (Godinho et al. 2011). Traditionally, hybridization studies have required the slow and generally expensive use of TS collected from dead or trapped animals, thus limiting population-level assessments. Furthermore, difficulties have been reported in correctly identifying wolf-dog backcrosses using simulated individuals and sets of 16-18 microsatellites (Randi 2008), typically resulting in a large threshold implemented in clustering analyses. In contrast, our method avoids these difficulties and is both innovative and easily applicable for hybridization studies. This is because we actively searched for the most informative markers among a previously wellknown extensive set and demonstrate that a small subset of carefully selected 13 AIMs is as accurate as an extensive set of 52 markers, additionally showing a major advantage of being rapidly screened on NIS.
Current studies on wolf-dog hybridization typically consider a set of 11-18 markers (Randi & Lucchini 2002;Vil a et al. 2003;Hindrikson et al. 2012; but see Verardi et al. 2006 for a set of 16 markers arranged in four different linkage groups) to achieve high differentiation values between wolves and dogs (average F ST = 0.28 using Randi &Lucchini 2002 andVerardi et al. 2006). Nonetheless, these studies fail to achieve reliable assignments to recent hybrid classes further than F 1 s using threshold values of 0.80 (but see Caniglia et al. 2013 for a threshold of 0.95 although no available data for the reliability of hybrid classes). In a recent study, Godinho et al. (2011) combined the use of a much larger panel of microsatellites with an assignment study of simulated individuals to reduce the uncertainty on probability intervals, increasing the threshold value to 0.85 and achieving, for the first time, high confidence on identifying first-generation backcross individuals (84% of successful identification). In a similar approach with a panel of 100 unlinked SNP markers, vonHoldt et al. (2013) could detect mixed ancestry within up to four generations of wolf-dog hybridization, although using a threshold of 0.80 and having only 72% of correct identifications of first-generation backcrosses to wolf. Nevertheless, approaches like those, using large numbers of markers, are not currently feasible for low-quality DNA samples, which are often the only ones available for rapid evaluation of a local hybridization event.
Our methods of using 13 nuclear markers specifically selected to have a high differentiation power between Iberian wolves and dogs (F ST of 0.341 for the empirical data and 0.408 for the simulated data) allowed not only a great accuracy in assigning individuals to parental classes (Qi wolf = 0.997) with a threshold that could be safely brought to 90% for assignments to the wolf cluster, but also a high probability of detecting hybrids in empirical cases, including first-generation backcrosses to the wild population. The establishment of a sharp threshold of 90% for this data set, assuming that values below that threshold indicate admixture to the wild population, includes all qi-values for the 242 wolf reference samples and all 1000 simulated wolves, fully supporting our approach. The larger threshold established for assignment to the dog cluster has no consequences on detecting continuous hybridization to wolf and is not a managing concern.
The efficiency of our methodology using 13 AIMs significantly outperformed the ten random sets established for the same number of markers, as well as the set of 18 markers included in the commercial kit, both when using traditional differentiation measures (F ST ) and for Bayesian assignment analysis. However, our AIMs were not more efficient than the whole set of 52 markers for Bayesian assignment analysis (although being more efficient to differentiate populations based on F ST ), confirming expectations that a high number of markers is preferable to a small selected panel. In any case, these results clearly show that selecting informative markers is important when two biological entities involved in hybridization events are very closely related helping on the dilemma of accomplishing this kind of projects with noninvasive samples.
One drawback of our approach is that the use of a small panel of AIMs leads to lower estimates of genetic diversity and, therefore, may not be suitable for some population genetic analyses. On the other hand, allele frequencies may change over time, especially in small populations (e.g. stochastic events, genetic drift, Allee effects, nonrandom mating or selection), which could affect assignment accuracy when studying hybridization. In such cases, selection of molecular markers should be revised over time. Furthermore, the method we propose requires that an extensive list of markers be available for which differences in allele frequencies among the populations under investigation have been estimated. This applies to any species in which our approach would be used and constitutes an additional cost that should be considered before starting a study of hybridization with noninvasive samples.

[SECTION] the barbanza pack
The Bayesian clustering analysis based on the 13-loci data set identified nine hybrids at Barbanza, together with two wolves and two dogs. Hybrids were assigned to first backcrosses to wolf or were ambiguously assigned to different hybrid classes (Table 3). While the discrepancies on recent ancestry analysis for the Barbanza TS using 13 or 52 loci should be further investigated using simulations, it remains clear that our methods can correctly identify hybrids, which is essential for the effective management of suspicious cases of hybridization. The hybridization event at Barbanza started with a cross between a female wolf and a male dog, as inferred by the presence of an Iberian wolf mtDNA haplotype in all hybrids, corresponding to the typical direction of wolf-dog hybridization (but see Hindrikson et al. 2012). Despite the uncertainty of the impact of these crosses in the genetic composition of wolf populations (for example, due to difficulties of hybrid integration in packs), our results do suggest that the Barbanza pack has quickly evolved towards a hybrid swarm, with a minimum of two generations of backcrossing to wolves. These findings are alarming because wolf packs in nonexpanding populations generally consist of related individuals (Lehman et al. 1992), and thus, other unobserved individuals in the area may also exhibit admixed ancestries.

[SECTION] management implications
Efficient identification of wolf-dog hybrids is crucial for the implementation of conservation and management strategies, particularly in the first phases of an episode of hybridization, as well as to evaluate the success of the strategies that have been implemented. Despite the recent increase in the number of studies focusing on this topic, no efficient and effective method for assessing real-time grey wolf-dog hybridization events at the population level has been proposed (although methods have been suggested for other systems like the red wolfcoyote; Bohling et al. 2013). In this regard, our approach of using a small set of AIMs provides managers with a reliable, quick and efficient tool for an intensive and extensive evaluation of hybridization at both individual and population levels. For example, assuming a minimum territory size of 100 km 2 centred in the rendezvous site of the Barbanza pack, the area sampled here covered a substantial portion of that territory (40%; Fig. 1c). Moreover, we identified 11 wolf-like canids (80% of the estimated population), which is fully compatible with the values reported in Iberia for pack size after reproduction (7-9 individuals; Llaneza et al. 2012b) plus some floater animals, suggesting that our method allows a comprehensive evaluation of hybridization in a given area. Our goal to obtain a quick method to identify hybridization events was achieved. Once there is the suspicion of a hybridization event, we estimate that a maximum of 2 months would be required to know the extent of the problem in an area equivalent to a pack territory. Finally, we note that the logistic and economic investment to evaluate hybridization in this area was feasible (ca. 1500€ for the fieldworkone person working 8 daysplus ca. 5000€ for laboratory workone person working 3 weeks).
Current management guidelines state that every practical measure should be implemented to remove obvious hybrids from the wild once an event of hybridization has been detected (Boitani 2000). This implies mainly lethal control, although keeping hybrids in captivity and sterilization have also been suggested (Ciucci 2012). Nevertheless, the efficiency of removing hybrids from the wild remains very uncertain. Therefore, the methods shown here constitute a step forward towards the effective management of wolf-dog hybridization. In our case study, due to the use of NIS coupled with a panel of AIMs, we now know that implemented management actions removed only 44% (four of nine identified hybrids) of wolf-dog hybrids in the region of Barbanza. Thus, we suggest that the combination of NIS and AIMs may offer a great opportunity to better understand the extension and persistence of hybridization between wolves and dogs at a global scale and its ecological, evolutionary and conservation consequences. This approach also brings up the opportunity to evaluate and improve the few existing management guidelines about wolf-dog hybridization.
Finally, our methods may be easily adapted for other pairs of wild/domesticated species, eventually making this an important tool to evaluate the impact of the introgression of domestication genes into natural populations. We believe this is both relevant and timely to examine many situations that have been documented in nature for a variety of species, especially because we now have the genomic and computational tools available which may facilitate this task. For example, the rock pigeon genome has very recently been made available, but the occurrence of true natural populations is questionable (Shapiro et al. 2013), eventually making this the first species to become extinct in the wild through introgressive hybridization with domestic/feral populations (Rhymer & Simberloff 1996). Another remarkable and intriguing example has been described for the wildcat (Felis silvestris) in both Scotland and Hungary, where the extent of introgressive hybridization from domestic breeds may preclude their recovery (Randi 2008). In summary, we suggest that the development and generalized application of the approach described here for the management of wolf-dog hybridization events may offer a very useful tool for conservation biologists in general.

[SECTION] title
A non-invasive tool for assessing pathogen prevalence in koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) populations: detection of Chlamydia pecorum and koala retrovirus (KoRV) DNA in genetic material sourced from scats

[SECTION] abstract
Pathogenic diseases may threaten the viability of wild animal populations, especially when already vulnerable. The mitigation of risks associated with pathogenic infections in populations is an important factor in conservation strategies. Koalas are of conservation concern across the north of their range and are affected by two main pathogens; Chlamydia pecorum and the koala retrovirus (KoRV). This study tested whether DNA from C. pecorum and KoRV could be detected in genetic material isolated from koala scats. Detection of C. pecorum in scat isolated DNA samples was compared with results obtained from urogenital swabs collected from the same individuals as part of an independent study. The ability to detect KoRV in scats from both northern and southern regions of the koala's range was also assessed. There was a high level of concordance (5/6) between the detection of C. pecorum in DNA isolated from scats and urogenital swabs from the same individual. In positive samples, C. pecorum ompA genotypes were identical between DNA from scats and urogenital swabs in two out of three cases. In samples from the south of the koala's range, KoRV copy number was higher in DNA isolated from scats compared to DNA isolated from ear tissue, potentially indicating the detection of horizontally acquired infections. Our results demonstrate the ability to detect C. pecorum and KoRV in DNA isolated from koala scats. This method will be useful for studying the prevalence, transmission and impact of these pathogens in wild populations which may subsequently inform conservation management strategies.

[SECTION] introduction
Pathogens infecting wild animal populations can affect the health of individuals and may lead to reduced fitness and mortality. Pathogenic diseases can reduce species viability and have been implicated in wild population declines (Tompkins et al. 2015). Consequently, pathogens may have a negative impact on biodiversity and their role as a potential driver of extinctions is becoming increasingly apparent (Smith et al. 2009). Greater data collection may facilitate characterisation and understanding of pathogen prevalence, transmission and impacts, and has the potential to inform and enhance management and conservation strategies.
Endemic to Australia, the koala (Phascolarctos cinereus) is an arboreal marsupial inhabiting the country's east coast, from Queensland to South Australia (Fig. 1), that has suffered dramatic population declines over the past two decades (Department of the Environment 2015). While the causes of decline are likely multifactorial, two pathogens have potential contributory roles: the obligate intracellular bacterium, Chlamydia pecorum, and the koala retrovirus (KoRV), both of which infect koalas throughout their range. C. pecorum commonly infects the eyes and/or urogenital tract of koalas (Markey et al. 2007). Ocular infection with C. pecorum may lead to severe keratoconjunctivitis (Cockram and Jackson 1981), while urogenital infections are known to result in cystitis and reproductive disease, which may lead to decreased fecundity or sterility (Martin and Handasyde 1990a;Obendorf and Handasyde 1990). A second species of Chlamydia, C. pneumoniae, also infects koalas but is usually associated with mild symptoms of disease (Jackson et al. 1999). There is evidence that different strains of C. pecorum have varying pathogenic potential (Mohamad et al. 2008(Mohamad et al. , 2014) ) and that apparently asymptomatic chlamydial infections may have hidden impacts. In cattle, for example, reduced calf growth rates have been associated with asymptomatic C. pecorum infection (Poudel et al. 2012). The potential impacts of C. pecorum on individual koalas and koala populations highlight the need for better characterisation and understanding of the prevalence of C. pecorum infection.
KoRV is a retrovirus that is considered to be endogenous in northern koala populations and in the process of becoming endogenous in southern populations (Simmons et al. 2012). Although numerous strains of KoRV have been reported to date (Xu et al. 2013(Xu et al. , 2015)), KoRV-A is most commonly detected. Unlike most known endogenous viruses, proviral KoRV (viral DNA inserted into the host genome) is capable of producing active virus (Tarlinton et al. 2005); KoRV may therefore be transmitted vertically, from parent to offspring, or horizontally via contact transmission. Modes of KoRV horizontal transmission are not clear, however KoRVs closest known relative, the gibbon ape leukaemia virus (GALV) can also be transmitted both vertically, in the germline, and horizontally, via exposure to faeces or urine (Kawakami et al. 1977(Kawakami et al. , 1978)). Though not definitive, links have been made between KoRV infection and the incidence of lymphoma and leukaemia in koalas, as well as with clinical chlamydial infections (Tarlinton et al. 2005;Xu et al. 2013). In the north of the koala's range (from Port Macquarie northwards; Fig. 1), 100 % of koalas tested were found to be infected with KoRV. However, in the south-eastern state of Victoria, there is evidence that endogenous KoRV is less common, with virus integrated only into infected cells (exogenous infection) and a significant number of Victorian koalas tested are found to be KoRV negative (Simmons et al. 2012).
Knowledge of the epidemiology of C. pecorum and KoRV across the koala's range could identify pathogen free populations and/or populations at high risk of increased mortality due to infection. Detecting pathogenic organisms in wild animals is often challenging, as sampling typically involves animal capture which can be difficult, especially where the species is elusive or when population densities are low. Once located, site factors and an animal's position, often, in the case of koalas, in the tops of trees exceeding 30 metres in height within rugged terrain, may also limit accessibility and make capture difficult or impossible. Animal capture is usually followed by invasive procedures such as anaesthesia and the collection of urogenital or ocular swabs, tissue biopsies or blood extraction. These methods require veterinarians and/or specialist expertise, making widespread sampling costly and time consuming. Due to difficulties in sampling wild animals, the prevalence of pathogens is often determined using samples of convenience such as deceased individuals (e.g. roadkill) or those admitted to veterinary clinics or wildlife shelters. Though a subset of the wild population, the prevalence of infectious agents may be greater in the portion of the population that has met with misadventure or is unwell (entering shelters or clinics) compared to the overall wild population. Therefore, this type of sampling has the potential to lead to a biased result, which may not be indicative of the true prevalence of the pathogen within the wider population.
As in other marsupials, both male and female koalas have a cloaca, a common external opening to the urogenital and gastrointestinal tracts (Archer et al. 1987). It therefore seems probable that dead Chlamydia infected cells and shed infectious particles (elementary bodies) may be detected in genetic material sourced from koala scats. The ability to carry out microsatellite genotyping using koala DNA isolated from scats (Wedrowicz et al. 2013) suggests that it should also be possible to detect KoRV in infected epithelial cells. In koalas originating from Queensland, the ability to detect endogenous KoRV (where all cells will contain at least one KoRV copy) in DNA isolated from koala scats has been demonstrated by Miyazawa et al. (2011). However, the ability to detect exogenous KoRV infections (in scat isolated DNA), where all somatic cells are not infected, is less certain. Given evidence that a large proportion of Victorian koalas may only carry horizontally acquired, exogenous KoRV infections (Simmons et al. 2012), this is important to determine.
The detection of koala pathogens in non-invasively sourced DNA could provide a viable alternative to invasive sampling. The ability to detect C. pecorum and KoRV in DNA isolated from koala scats would be a valuable tool with the potential to facilitate and expedite the collection of prevalence data for these infections across the koala's range. The objective of this study, therefore, is to determine whether C. pecorum and KoRV-A DNA can be detected in genetic material non-invasively sourced from koala scats, providing a tool that can assess the presence of these pathogens in wild koala populations.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] chlamydia pecorum

[SECTION] sample collection and dna isolation
Scat samples were collected from six koalas in the Strzelecki Ranges, Victoria during March 2015. The six individual koalas from which scats were collected were also captured as part of an independent study carried out by the NSW Office of Environment and Heritage (Allen 2015). The purpose of the study carried out by Allen (2015) was to determine the prevalence of chlamydial infections in the Strzelecki Ranges koala population by capturing and collecting ocular and urogenital swabs from koalas. Results obtained from DNA isolated from urogenital swabs (six koalas: K01-K06) collected for the Allen (2015) study allowed direct comparison of C. pecorum presence detected by both methods. Scats located on the ground beneath each koala captured by Allen (2015) were collected for the isolation of DNA according to the methods described by Wedrowicz et al. (2013). To assess detection reproducibility in DNA isolated from scats from the same individual, DNA was isolated from three different scats collected beneath each koala, resulting in three DNA isolates per individual. The concentration of total DNA isolated from scats was determined using the Qubit Ò 2.0 Fluorometer following the manufacturer's instructions.
Presence/absence assay for C. pecorum Real time assays for C. pecorum targeting a 76 bp region of the ompA gene were carried out as per Pantchev et al. (2010). Reactions also incorporated TaqMan Ò Exogenous Internal Positive Control (IPC) Reagents in order to differentiate failed reactions, due to PCR inhibition, from true negative results. Amplification was carried out using the Applied Biosystems Step One Plus instrument using a presence absence protocol. PCR product using primers amplifying 1140 bp of the ompA gene (details below: ompA gene sequencing) was used to prepare 1:10 serial dilutions for standards ranging from 8 9 10 0 -8 9 10 6 copies per reaction. Standards were used to assess reaction sensitivity including an IPC, as well as to estimate the number of chlamydial DNA copies in different samples. A standard PCR to determine the gender of the sampled individual was also carried out using DNA isolated from scats as outlined in Wedrowicz et al. (2013).

[SECTION] ompa gene sequencing
The presence of C. pecorum in samples which tested positive via real time PCR was confirmed by amplification of 1140 bp of the ompA gene. Amplification of ompA was carried out using BIO-X-ACT TM Short DNA Polymerase  (Bioline). Reactions consisted of 19 OptiBuffer, 19 Hi-Spec additive, 2 mM MgCl 2 , 0.5 mM each dNTP, 1 unit of BIO-X-ACT Short DNA Polymerase and 0.25 lM of each primer (ompAfor and ompArev; Kollipara et al. 2013) made up to 20 lL with water. DNA was initially denatured for 5 min at 95 °C, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 54 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 1 min each and ending with a single final extension of 7 min at 72 °C. PCR products were purified using the Wizard Ò SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System (Promega) and sequencing was carried out by the Australian Genome Research Facility (AGRF), Melbourne, Victoria. Resulting sequences were trimmed using Sequence Scanner V2 (Applied Biosystems) and nucleotide BLAST (NCBI 2016) used to determine the similarity of sequences to those previously reported. Genotypes were classified according to Kollipara et al. (2013), where ompA sequences with less than 1 % nucleotide differences to previously reported sequences were designated by the same genotype letter followed by a prime symbol and a number to differentiate multiple variants with minimal base pair differences.

[SECTION] comparison of scat and urogenital results
Results of C. pecorum presence in DNA isolated from scats were compared to C. pecorum presence in urogenital swabs obtained by Allen (2015). Results reported by Allen (2015) were determined independently by the Koala Health Hub (KHH) at The University of Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. DNA isolated from swabs testing positive for C. pecorum were provided for this study by the KHH allowing amplification and sequencing of the ompA gene to be carried out for swab isolated DNA as described above.

[SECTION] koala retrovirus (korv)

[SECTION] sample collection and dna isolation
Koala scat samples were collected from wild individuals in the Strzelecki Ranges, South Gippsland (n = 17), Raymond Island (n = 2) and from koalas at the Koala Conservation Centre (n = 6) on Phillip Island, all in Victoria (total VIC samples; n = 25) (Fig. 1). Koala scats were also obtained from the Port Macquarie Koala Hospital in New South Wales (NSW, n = 15). Scats were collected and DNA isolated according to the methods outlined in Wedrowicz et al. (2013). To compare the results from scat samples with those from a commonly utilised invasive DNA source, DNA was also isolated from ear tissue samples (n = 50) from deceased individuals, collected by staff at the Southern Ash Wildlife Shelter (SAWS), Rawson, Victoria. Approximately 3 mm square was excised from ear samples and cut into small pieces. DNA was then isolated using the DNeasy Ò Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer's protocol.

[SECTION] korv-a pcr
Standard PCRs utilised KoRV-A specific primers published in Xu et al. (2013) alongside koala b-actin primers (Markey et al. 2007) to confirm the presence of koala DNA. Standard PCRs for KoRV-A were made up of 5 lL GoTaq Ò Green Master Mix (Promega), 1.0 lM of each KoRV-A primer, 0.1 lg bovine serum albumin (BSA), 1 lL of DNA template and water to give a final volume of 10 lL. PCR cycling parameters were 95 °C for 2 min followed by 35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 64 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 30 s followed by a final extension of 72 °C for 5 min. Standard PCR for koala b-actin consisted of 5 lL GoTaq Ò Green Master Mix, 1.0 lM of each KoRV-A primer, 0.1 lg BSA, 1 lL of DNA template and water to bring the final volume to 10 lL. PCR cycling parameters were 95 °C for 2 min followed by 35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, 60 °C for 30 s and 72 C for 30 s and finished with a final extension of 72 °C for 5 min. To ensure the lower sensitivity of standard PCR assays was not resulting in an increased number of false negatives, real time PCR assays, using the same primers specific for KoRV-A (Xu et al. 2013), were carried out by the KHH on the same set of samples (VIC and NSW, n = 40) tested by standard PCR to independently validate results. Real time PCRs were carried out on both undiluted and 1:10 dilutions of DNA isolates.
KoRV-A copy number DNA from tissues (n = 50) and additional scat samples (n = 117) collected in the South Gippsland region were also screened for KoRV (data not shown). Using a subset of randomly selected positive samples, KoRV copy number was compared between Victorian scat samples (VIC, n = 13) and ear tissue samples (TISS, n = 13) along with scat samples collected from New South Wales (NSW, n = 8). This was carried out using real time PCR with KoRV-A primers (Xu et al. 2013) and b-actin primers (Markey et al. 2007) to standardise copy number. Standards were produced for the KoRV-A and b-actin assays by amplifying the two targets using standard PCR. KoRV-A and b-actin PCR product was then purified using the Wizard Ò SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System (Promega). Serial 1:10 dilutions ranging approximately from 10 0 to 10 6 copies of KoRV-A or b-actin PCR product were then used as standards for the estimation of copy number. Both PCRs were carried out using 10 lL of SYBR Ò Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems), 0.25 lM of each primer and 2 lL of DNA template made up to a total of 20 lL with water and cycling parameters consisting of 50 °C for 2 min (UDG activation), 95 °C for 2 min (polymerase activation) followed by 50 cycles of 95 °C for 3 s and 60 °C for 30 s. A melt curve was produced to check for non-specific products. All standards, controls and samples were tested in duplicate.

[SECTION] korv-a sequencing
A subset of PCRs positive for KoRV (n = 6) were sequenced to confirm the detection of KoRV-A. Primers were designed using published KoRV-A sequence (Genbank AF151794.2; Hanger et al. 2000) and Primer-BLAST (Ye et al. 2012) to target a 1115 bp region of the KoRV env gene; primers were designated KoRV-env1-F (5 0 -AGACG GGAAGTGTCGTTTGG-3 0 ) and KoRV-env1-R (5 0 -GGG GGTGAGGCCAGAATTAC-3 0 ). Positive samples were amplified using 10 lL GoTaq Ò Green Master Mix, 0.5 lM of each primer and 0.1 lg BSA made up to a final volume of 20 lL. PCR products were purified using the ISOLATE PCR and Gel Kit (Bioline) and sequencing was carried out by AGRF.

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] chlamydia pecorum

[SECTION] assay sensitivity and reproducibility
The detection limit for the C. pecorum assay, with the addition of an internal positive control, was consistent with the limits reported by Pantchev et al. (2010) at eight copies of chlamydial DNA per PCR (Online resource 1, Fig. S1). C. pecorum DNA was detected in all three scats from each positive individual indicating that, when present, C. pecorum is consistently found in DNA isolated from koala scats. The total number of C. pecorum copies detected in DNA isolated from urogenital swabs was much higher compared to scats (Table 1). Results obtained from scat or urogenital swab isolated DNA were generally concordant (Table 2), but, one of the six scat DNA isolates was positive for C. pecorum while the urogenital swab was negative (K06).

[SECTION] c. pecorum copy number and dna concentration
DNA isolated from scats ranged in concentration from 1.4 ng/lL up to 42 ng/lL (Table 1; Fig. 2). The estimated copy number of C. pecorum increased with increasing DNA concentration (Fig. 2). Different scats from the same individual were consistently either positive or negative, though there was variation in the number of C. pecorum copies detected for independent scats from the same individual (Table 1). Of the fifteen DNA samples isolated from scats positive for C. pecorum, twelve had less than 10 C. pecorum copies per ng of DNA isolated while the remaining three samples had somewhat higher copy numbers; 15, 37 and 74 C. pecorum copies per ng of DNA (Table 1). Compared to DNA isolated from scats for each individual, C. pecorum copy number was on average, three (K02), ten (K01 and K04), and 3000 (K05) times greater in DNA isolated from swabs. ompA genotypes detected using DNA isolated from scats and swabs
Of the five Chlamydia positive samples detected using DNA isolated from scats, four were successfully sequenced at ompA with two different genotypes being detected (Table 2). Referring to the types reported by Kollipara et al. (2013), genotypes were most closely related to ompA types F (K01, K02 and K06; F 0 3, n = 3, two bases difference to genotype F, both non-synonymous) and C (K04; C 0 1, n = 1, one base difference, synonymous). Each of the four positive urogenital swab samples produced different ompA sequences to one another (Table 2). These included F 0 3 (K01) and C 0 1 (K04), both of which matched the sequences obtained from counterpart scat samples. An ompA sequence 100 % identical to genotype F described by Kollipara et al. (2013) was detected in the swab sample of koala K05, but the ompA sequence obtained for K05 using scat isolated DNA could not be read, possibly due to the presence of multiple strains. The remaining swab sample (K02) was identified as genotype M (Legione et al. 2016) and differed to the corresponding ompA sequence from the paired scat isolated DNA (F 0 3). The ompA sequence (genotype M) obtained from swab DNA for individual K02 was noted to have some level background sequence while all other sequences were completely free of any background noise.

[SECTION] koala retrovirus (korv)

[SECTION] comparison between standard and real time pcr results
The DNA concentration isolated from the 40 scat samples tested for KoRV presence ranged from undetectable (\0.10 ng/lL, n = 3 NSW samples) to 41 ng/lL with a mean of 4.2 ng/lL and median of 1.2 ng/lL (Online resource 1: Table S2). Standard PCR results (undiluted template) were identical to the real time PCR results (undiluted template), except for three (12.5 %) South Gippsland positives which tested negative by real time PCR when isolates were diluted 1:10 (Online resource 1: Table S2). KoRV-A was detected in 24 of the 40 samples tested (60 %). Using both standard and real time PCR all six Phillip Island samples tested in this study were negative for KoRV while all 15 NSW samples tested positive. As expected, b-actin and KoRV-A cycle thresholds decreased with increasing amounts of total DNA concentration obtained from koala scats (Fig. 3), indicating greater amounts of koala and KoRV DNA present in DNA isolates with higher DNA concentration.

[SECTION] confirmation of korv-a presence by sequencing
A 1115 bp segment of the KoRV env gene was sequenced for a subset of positive samples to confirm the detection of KoRV DNA. Sequences of samples from NSW koalas (n = 2) were 100 % identical to KoRV-A sequence (AF151794.2; Hanger et al. 2000). All samples from Victorian koalas that were sequenced (n = 4) had six identical nucleotide base changes in the env segment. The six polymorphisms in the Victorian samples were all synonymous, not having an effect on the amino acid sequence of the env gene.

[SECTION] differences in korv-a copy number between sample groups
Quantitative PCR revealed significant differences in copy number between scat samples from NSW and Victoria. On average, more than four KoRV-A copies per genomic unit were detected in scats sampled in NSW, whereas less than one copy per genomic unit was detected in Victorian scat samples (Fig. 3; p = 0.01). This is concordant with results reported by Simmons et al. (2012) further supporting the hypothesis that most infections in Victoria are exogenous, as endogenous proviral DNA would be expected to be present in every cell if acquired vertically via the germline. Simmons et al. (2012) showed that KoRV is endogenous in northern koala populations, and is inserted into the genome multiple times, with an average of 165 KoRV copies per cell reported for Queensland individuals; the mean of four KoRV copies per genomic unit value reported for NSW koalas in this study is substantially lower. KoRV-A copy number also differed significantly between scat and ear tissue samples collected in South Gippsland, with scats having on average, 30 times as many KoRV-A copies per ) while the KoRV-A PCR had a regression fit of C T = 31.6-2.9 log 10 DNA (R 2 = 26 %, p = 1.9 9 10 -4 ) genomic unit than tissue samples (Fig. 4; p \ 0.0005). KoRV-A in DNA isolated from ear tissue averaged 0.003 ± 0.002 copies per genomic unit while DNA isolated from scats had a mean of 0.09 ± 0.01 KoRV-A copies per genomic unit.

[SECTION] discussion
Pathogenic organisms can impact wild animal populations by reducing animal health, longevity and the ability to successfully reproduce. Impacts such as these may result in decreased population size causing losses in genetic diversity (Frankham et al. 2012) which, together with other threatening processes such as habitat loss and fragmentation, may greatly increase the risk of inbreeding, deleterious genes and extirpation. Given declines in koala numbers and the 2012 listing of northern koala populations as vulnerable under the Environmental Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (Department of the Environment 2015) it is imperative that the prevalence of C. pecorum and KoRV within the koala population is determined. Obtaining such data via swabs however, can be costly and time consuming, especially for species such as the koala, which are difficult to capture. DNA isolated from a single scat can provide information on the presence and characteristics of C. pecorum and KoRV. Both C.
pecorum and KoRV were detected in DNA isolated from koala scats. The non-invasive collection of samples therefore has potential to greatly increase sample size in studies of koala pathogens, without the requirements of capturing, handling or even observing an animal. This allows for the collection of more samples from wider and more diverse geographic areas, increasing both the spatial distribution and number of samples obtained for studies of pathogens in wildlife. Such data is critical for effective species management, especially in the case of inter-population translocations or releases proposed by wildlife managers or carers.
In Australia, the translocation of wild animals is common, with 54 species (*14 %) of Australian mammals having at least one documented translocation (Short 2010). Additional undocumented movements of animals carried out by wildlife carers releasing individuals after rehabilitation are also commonplace in Australia (Guy and Banks 2012;Reid 2014). Translocations are often carried out for conservation reasons, however the risk of transferring pathogens between endemic and introduced individuals is an important consideration that requires prior assessment (Leighton 2002) and post translocation surveillance (Mathews et al. 2006). Severe Chlamydia infections are more likely in individual koalas not previously exposed to these bacterial infections (Martin and Handasyde 1990b). The inadvertent introduction of C. pecorum to populations that have historically been free of infection, therefore, has the potential to result in devastating consequences. The effects of exposure to novel strains are also important considerations due to possible differences in strain pathogenicity (Mohamad et al. 2008(Mohamad et al. , 2014)). Although the pathogenic effects of KoRV are not entirely clear at present, preventing transmission of the virus to KoRV free populations is important. Obtaining baseline data on KoRV prevalence in wild populations will enable monitoring of infection rates and future changes that may occur.
C. pecorum has also been found to infect other Australian marsupials such as the greater glider (Petauroides volans), the short-eared brushtail possum (Trichosurus caninus) and the western barred bandicoot (Perameles bougainville) (Bodetti et al. 2003). Other than the koala, limited research into the effects of this pathogen on marsupial populations has been carried out. Given that urogenital infections with Chlamydia may be subclinical, yet affect reproduction, the presence of this bacteria in marsupial populations may potentially be an under recognised cause of population declines. The use of scat sourced DNA could provide a simple and useful method for screening and characterising Chlamydia infections in a range of marsupial species. Similarly, a retrovirus similar to KoRV and GALV has been detected in an Australian rodent, Melomys burtoni (Simmons et al. 2014). Using DNA sourced non-invasively from scats, sampling power and the ability to identify other potential retroviral hosts and/or cross species transmissions may be greatly increased. This method could therefore also be of value to the study of these bacterial and viral pathogens in other Australian marsupials. Screening for potential pathogens, utilising non-invasive genetic sampling techniques as described here, may be a useful addition to studies of other mammals. This study demonstrates that C. pecorum strains, also found to cause urogenital infection in koalas (Kollipara et al. 2013;Legione et al. 2016), can be detected in DNA isolated from koala scats. It is important to recognise that infection with C. pecorum does not mean that an individual will have symptoms of chlamydiosis. The presence of C. pecorum does, however, provide an indication that the individual carries the pathogen and is probably capable of transmitting the bacteria to other individuals. Conversely, a negative result does not necessarily show that the individual is free of infection, since latent infections or low level shedding of infectious particles could result in too few C. pecorum particles present on koala scats for detection.
Results of the C. pecorum assay were largely concordant between scat and swab samples, although some differences were also noted. One individual (K06) tested positive for C. pecorum in DNA isolated from scats and negative using DNA isolated from the urogenital swab. This may indicate that insufficient biological material was obtained during swabbing or that infected cells detected in scat DNA were located at other reported sites of chlamydial infection such as the gastrointestinal tract (Burach et al. 2014). Another explanation is that scats were from another koala having visited the same tree rather than the koala captured; genotyping of both the scat and swab DNA isolates would be required to confirm or exclude this possibility. The ompA genotype obtained for one individual (K02) differed between scat and swab samples; the scat sample providing the F 0 3 genotype and the swab sample the M genotype. The M genotype sequence obtained from this swab was however the only sequence with a substantial amount of background, potentially indicating the presence of multiple strains or alternatively, sample contamination. Further investigation is needed to determine whether differences in the ompA type detected using different sample types from the same individual is due to the collection of scats from unintended individuals, as described above, or to multiple strain infections, potentially located at different anatomical sites (Burach et al. 2014). For example, infections of the gastrointestinal tract may be present in scat samples, but absent from urogenital swab samples.
Compared to DNA isolated from swabs, the number of C. pecorum copies detected in scat DNA was much lower and the number of estimated C. pecorum copies varied between DNA samples isolated from independent scats from the same individual. Although positive samples were consistently positive across the three separate scats, it is possible that the bacteria may not be detected when the rate of shedding of infectious particles is low. Copy number variability was at least, in part, related to the concentration of DNA obtained from scats. Further work to determine the minimum quantity of total DNA needed for reliable detection of C. pecorum in DNA isolated from scats, from individuals with various infectious loads, would be appropriate. Testing multiple independent scats from the same individual may increase confidence in results obtained. The only male koala included in this study (individual K05) was estimated to have a C. pecorum copy number that was between 2200 and 4500 times lower in DNA sourced from scats compared to DNA sourced from swabs, while the females in the study had copy numbers in scats that were between one and fifty times lower. Differences in the anatomy of female and male koalas could potentially affect the ability to detect C. pecorum in males and female scats; this requires further investigation.
Compared to Victorian tissue samples, significantly greater amounts of KoRV-A were detected in DNA isolated from Victorian scat samples (Fig. 4). This difference suggests the possible detection of infection acquired horizontally (exogenous infection) in Victorian koalas. All northern NSW samples in this study tested positive for KoRV, while no samples were KoRV positive in the Phillip Island group of samples. This is consistent with results previously reported by Simmons et al. (2012), who found all Phillip Island (Victoria) samples tested to be KoRV negative and all samples tested in the Port Macquarie (NSW) area to be KoRV positive. Apart from one sample, standard and real time PCR assays of the samples tested here produced equivalent results. Where presence or absence of KoRV is all that is required for a study, standard PCR can also provide useful data. The small number of diluted positive samples that tested negative by real time PCR indicates that KoRV may not be detected when DNA concentration is quite low. One way to address this may be to screen DNA samples for quantity and quality in order to ascertain the suitability of samples for testing. Additionally, if KoRV detected in scat isolated DNA originates from exogenous infections, the number of cells in which KoRV DNA has integrated may be highly variable, resulting in low copy numbers in some samples. Consequently, until further information is obtained, presence only studies are likely to be most suitable using these methods. In Victorian samples, higher KoRV-A copy number was found in DNA isolated from scats compared to ear tissue, suggesting that koala scats provide a practical source of DNA for detecting the presence of KoRV infections acquired both vertically and horizontally.
Koala conservation research will benefit from the use of an integrated approach, employing the relatively simple method for detecting C. pecorum and KoRV described here. Genetic material isolated from koala scats has been shown to provide DNA that can be reliably used to obtain genotypic data, DNA sequence information and to identify gender (Wedrowicz et al. 2013). DNA isolated from scats can provide information on population substructure, relatedness between individuals, gene flow, migration and hybridisation using genotyping (Czarnomska et al. 2013;Piggott et al. 2006;Stenglein et al. 2011). The gender of the individual sampled can be determined by PCR (Wedrowicz et al. 2013), while sequencing of mitochondrial DNA can provide phylogenetic information suitable for evolutionary analyses (Houlden et al. 1999). Genotypic data can also be paired with habitat and environmental models to look for factors that may impede or facilitate gene flow across the landscape using landscape genetics (Storfer et al. 2006).
The ability to detect pathogens in DNA isolated from koala scats may supply critical information that can be combined with genetic data to provide a multidimensional picture of koala biology. Since pathogen DNA sequences can be obtained using this method, non-invasive sampling may also permit studies of pathogen diversity, transmission and spread throughout wild populations. In the case of C. pecorum, the likelihood of particular C. pecorum strains having high or low virulence could also be investigated using ompA markers along with additional C. pecorum DNA markers such as incA and ORF663 (Mohamad et al. 2014). A general trend of increased C. pecorum shedding has been shown for individuals with increasing severity of chlamydial disease (Wan et al. 2011) and there is also evidence of differing infectious load between C. pecorum strains (Legione et al. 2016). It may, therefore, also be useful to differentiate individuals with high or low loads of C. pecorum using DNA isolated from scats. However, further comparisons of copy number between swabs and scats would be required in order to more accurately gauge the variability of C. pecorum copy number in scat isolated DNA and the number of scats needed to give a reliable estimate of infectious load. Pathogen detection from scats could be paired with ecological studies, thereby revealing whether infection might have an effect on behaviour or movement. This information has the potential to provide increased knowledge of many aspects of C. pecorum and KoRV infection in koala populations including transmission, pathogenicity and host effects. Together, the plethora of information that is able to be gained from a single koala scat can be used to promote a holistic approach to koala conservation and management.
