[SECTION] title
A Protocol for DNA Extraction from Feces of the Wild Pygmy Lorises, Nycticebus pygmaeus

[SECTION] abstract
We developed a new method to isolate DNA from wild pygmy lorises' feces. The feces were washed two or three times with precooled acetone, which removed numerous potential PCR inhibitors. The DNA was purified with phenol/chloroform after incubation with proteinase K. D-loop region and cytochrome b were amplified and sequenced successfully from the extracted DNA. Comparison with the PCR products demonstrated the fecal DNA extracted by the improved protocol was better than the fecal DNA extracted without acetone preprocessing.

[SECTION] introduction
Two families of Lorises, Nycticebus (Primates: Prosimii: Loridae) are currently recognized -slow lorises (Nycticebus coucang and Nycticebus bengalensis) and pygmy lorises (Nycticebus pygmaeus). N. pygmaeus has a much more limited distribution range than the slow lorises (Wolfhein, 1983). Its current diversity is in mainland Southeast Asia, from China to Vietnam. These are found only in Pingbian, Hekou, Maguan, Jinping and Luchun of Yunnan, near the Sino-Vietnamese border (Wang, 1998;Zhang et al., 2002;Fooden, 1996;Duckworth, 1994). N. pygmaeus is a nocturnal and almost entirely arboreal primate. It typically lives in semi-evergreen and secondary forests (Wolfhein, 1983;Polet et al., 2004;Groves, 1970). The pygmy lorises' food diversity include gums, fruits, birds' eggs, chicks, geckos and arboreal small mammals (Ratajszczak, 1998;Tan, 1994), but it is an insectivorous species. N. pygmaeus is one of the least studied species of all prosimians (Fitch-Snyder and Jurke, 2003). The Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) included pygmy lorises (Wang, 1998). In its latest assessment in 2006 the IUCN classified the pygmy lorises as ________________________ ''vulnerable" (IUCN). It is also listed as one of the first protected animals in China. Therefore, new field research methods appropriate for these primates are urgently required for the study of the pygmy loris.
Noninvasive samples of animals such as feces, hair and feathers are commonly collected for studies of wildlife population (Dalèn et al., 2004;Hogan et al., 2008). The DNA extracted from noninvasive sources has been developed and tested on a wide range of species. The noninvasive genetic surveys found broad application for conservation genetics and wildlife management, in especial as species that are endangered, elusive, or exist at low densities over vast areas (Kohn et al., 1999;Adams et al., 2003;Eggert et al., 2003;Wilson et al., 2003;Bellemain et al., 2005;Prugh et al., 2005;Smith et al., 2005). Pygmy lorises, the risk species.
The fecal DNA genotyping of is more advantageous than the traditional live-trapping survey technique (Taberlet and Luikart, 1999;Fernando et al., 2003;Smith et al., 2005). The objective of this study was to establish an extraction method for DNA from fecal samples, for conducting non-invasive surveys.

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] fecal samples
Fecal samples from seven individuals of pygmy loris were collected from the Daweishan Nature Reserve of Pingbian, Yunnan Province, China. Samples of fresh fecal material were transported to the laboratory in an icebox, and stored at -70 º C. The procedure in this study followed protocols approved by China Wildlife Conservation Association, American Society of Primatologists Principles for the Ethical Treatment of Non-Human Primates, and also legal requirements of China.

[SECTION] total dna isolation
DNA was extracted by three different methods viz., alcohol extraction method (Zhang et al., 2004), PBS extraction (Sambrook and Russell, 2002) and acetone extraction method (Zhong et al., 2003). The method ultimately developed is described below: 1)
The fecal sample (0.05-0.10 g) was placed in a 2.0 ml centrifuge tube, to which double distilled water was added. The sample was mixed thoroughly and then kept at room temperature for 2 min.

[SECTION] 2)
The supernatant was poured in a 2.0 ml centrifuge tube, and centrifuged at 4,500x g at 4°C for 4 min; 3)
The supernatant solution was once again poured in another 2.0 ml centrifuge tube, and centrifuged at 5,040 g at 4°C for 6 min to pellet down the cells. 4) Supernatant was discarded and 500µl precooled (at -20°C) acetone was added in the cells, swirled and then after one minute centrifuged at 5,040 g at 4°C for 5 min. The cell pellet was washed with acetone, twice or three times.

[SECTION] 5)
The acetone was poured out and then the cells were treated with 500µl lytic buffer (200 mM NaCl, 100 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 2.0% SDS, 50 mM EDTA, 1.0% Triton X-100) at 55°C for 3 h or 24 h. Then added 1.25 µl RNase (10mg/ml) at 37 °C for 30 min.

[SECTION] 6)
To the above lysate equal volume of mixture of phenol: chloroform: isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1 volume), was added then mixed and kept for 1 min, and centrifuged at 16,000 g at 4°C for 10 min, The supernatant was collected and the pellet was wash by phenol: chloroform: isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1) 2 to 3 times.

[SECTION] 7)
The above supernatant containing DNA was treated with equal volume of isoamyl alcohol at -20°C for 12 h 8)
The DNA was centrifuged at 16,000 g at 4°C for 2 min. The supernatant was discarded while the pellet was washed with 70% ethanol and then with 20µl double distilled water twice. The DNA was stored at -20 º C.
Conventional electrophoresis was then performed to verify that DNA had remained intact (0.8% agarose gel, 100 volts, 0.5X TBE buffer) (Suau et al., 1999).

[SECTION] pcr
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of Cyt b and D-loop was performed using primers shown below. Reactions were performed in 50 µl volume containing 1.0 µl DNA template, 5.0 µl 10  PCR buffer (containing 25 mmol/l Mg 2+ ), 1.0 µl of dNTPs (10 10 -3 mmol/ml), 2.0 µl primer (10  10 -6 mmol/ml), 0.5µl Taq DNA polymerase, and 40.5 µl ddH 2 O. Amplification conditions were as follows: 94°C initial denaturation for 5min; 30 cycles each of 94°C for 1min, 48 to 55°C for 1min, and 72°C for 1min; 72°C extension for 10min. PCR products were visualized on an agarose gel electrophoresis.

sense antisense AGA CTC ATG ACT AAC ATT CGA TAG GGC TGT GTC TTC ATT TGA G D-loop (Chen et al., 2006) sense antisense CCT GAA GTA GGA ACC AGA TG CTC CAC CAT GAG TAG CAC CCA AAG C
Sequencing and sequence analysis PCR product was sequenced at the Beijing Genomics Institute (BGI). All the sequences was compared with the sequences in the Gen-Bank database using BLAST program available for the NCBI internet website (http://www.ncbi.nlm. nih.gov.).

The DNA sequences from this study were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers: Cyt b HQ842857-HQ842862 and D-loop HQ842864-HQ842879.

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] faecal dna quality
There was the tailing phenomenon in DNA by the different extract methods; all were different degree of degradation (Fig. 1); especially, the alcohol extract method and the PBS extract method; the products of the alcohol extract method and the PBS extract method were more segments, which were less than 100bp; however, the product of the acetone extract method were long fragments more than 2000bp and less degradation. The A260/A280 was about 1.8-2.0 of the fecal DNA.

[SECTION] amplificative quality from faecal dna
The PCR products of D-loop and Cyt b with pygmy loris' fecal DNA extracted by different extract methods, the D-loop was about 400 bp (Fig. 2A), and the Cyt b was near 1140 bp (Fig. 2B).
The amplification success rates of Cyt b with fecal DNA obtained by alcohol extraction method, PBS extraction method and acetone extraction method, were 20.98±0.83%, 22.94±0.72% and 32.51±0.55%, respectively. (Fig. 3A). The amplification success rates of D-loop with fecal DNA obtained by alcohol extraction method, PBS extraction method and acetone extraction method were 20.47±0.81%, 25.17±0.53% and 40.06±0.62%, respectively (Fig. 3B). The amplification success rates of Cyt b or D-loop with fecal DNA obtained by acetone extraction method was higher than that by alcohol extraction method and PBS extraction method. It is suggested that we can obtain high quality and quantity of fecal DNA by acetone extraction method.

[SECTION] discussion
A wide size range of host mitochondrial, microsatellite and even protein encoding nuclear DNA can be amplified from fecal extracts (Wasser et al., 1997). The feces are a plenty of resource for noninvasive sampling (Zhong et al., 2003). The DNA extraction from feces can be used for genetic analysis of population, species and/or individual identification. It can also help the field ecological studies for determination of population estimates and delimiting of territory (Wang, 2001).
The component of feces is complex. It not only contains the animal intestinal cell DNA, but also DNA of parasites (bacteria, viruses) and the undigested food. The process of eluted feces by pro-cool acetone with 2 or 3 times, will wipe off many PCR inhibitors (Schneiderbauer et al., 1991, Wang andWang, 2012). We obtained an average of 23.14 µg/g of fecal DNA.

[SECTION] title
Genetic Structure Among Hibernacula of the Endangered Gray Bat (Myotis grisescens)

[SECTION] abstract
In an attempt to fill knowledge gaps relating to genetic structure in the endangered gray bat (Myotis grisescens), we investigated geographic patterns in multilocus microsatellite DNA (msDNA) genotypes and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) haplotype frequencies across eight primary hibernacula. Isolation-by-distance (IBD) was absent in the msDNA data and no bottlenecks were detected, with genotypic diversity (A R = 6.52, H o = 0.64) and overall genetic differentiation (F ST = 0.024, P < 0.001) being comparable to other Myotis and North American vespertilionids. Genetic structure (Φ CT = 0.063, P < 0.001) among groups of populations (K = 2) was observed. We also identified a pattern of slight east-west regional genetic structure, likely attributable to the natural barrier of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain, in the haplotype data (Φ CT = 0.086, P < 0.05), along with moderate IBD (r = 0.486, P < 0.05). Though genetic differentiation among populations was generally low, significant interpopulation genetic structure, likely arising from some degree of philopatric behavior and a lack of hibernacula-associated mating sites within the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain, was observed.

[SECTION] introduction
The endangered gray bat (Myotis grisescens), listed by the U.S. Fish and Widlife Service (USFWS) in 1976 (Brady et al., 1982), inhabits karst regions of the southeastern United States (Harvey et al., 1999). The species experienced a 25% population decline prior to its listing (Tuttle, 1979;Harvey, 1992) that was largely attributed to the loss of suitable hibernacula due to anthropogenic disturbance to hibernating bats and modification of critical cave microclimate conditions (Barbour and Davis, 1969;Tuttle, 1979;Brady et al., 1982;Martin, 2007). Gray bats require specific conditions for hibernation, with winter roosts that maintain temperatures across a narrow range of 5-11°C (Harvey et al., 1999). Individuals are typically philopatric to both summer ranges and winter caves (Tuttle, 2003), but may use as many as six different caves in the summer. Because there are a limited number of caves that meet the required hibernacula conditions, gray bats often travel hundreds of kilometers between summer and winter sites (Tuttle, 1976). However, the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain represents a major disjunction between eastern and western karst regions, and because it is an area of limited cave availability, it may significantly influence gray bat migratory patterns and genetic structure.
While population sizes in gray bats have in recent years increased dramatically due to careful management, approximately 95% of the overall pop ulation still hibernates in only 17 caves (Tuttle, 1979;Harvey et al., 2006). Because a large portion of the species' overall population is confined to such a small number of critical sites, gray bats are particularly vulnerable to impacts of natural or anthropogenic stressors. Over the past few years, the fungal infection White-nose Syndrome (WNS) has killed over six million hibernating bats in the United States, effectively destroying entire populations at some hibernacula (Foley et al., 2011;USFWS, 2011;WNS Cooperative Partners, unpublished data). The fungus responsible for WNS, Pseudogymnoascus destructans, has been detected in gray bats (Foley et al., 2011;USFWS, 2011), but no subsequent mass mortality has been observed.
Traditionally, bat migratory movements have been determined through wing-banding studies (Barclay and Bell, 1988;O'Shea et al., 2004). Tens of thousands of gray bats were banded from the 1930s to 1970s and many existing summer colonyhibernacula associations were determined. Since that time, there have been significant changes in census sizes of hibernacula populations and perhaps large-scale movements of gray bats among hibernacula (Grigsby et al., 1993;Harvey, 1996;Sasse et al., 2007). Although banding still occurs, determinations of existing and future summer colony-hibernacula associations via traditional banding studies can be limited by poor recovery of bands or loss/ effacing of identifying markings (Barclay and Bell, 1988), as well as by the labor required for such studies.
A potential alternative approach for determining associations between summer colonies and hibernacula populations is a combination of noninvasive or minimally-stressful genetic sampling with DNAbased assignment approaches. Noninvasive or minimally-stressful sampling of genetic material from bats can take various forms, including wing tissue (Worthington Wilmer and Barratt, 1996), blood, fur, guano (Zinck et al., 2004), and buccal samples (R. F. Lance, personal observation). Because guano is the least invasive genetic sampling method (as samples can be collected without capturing bats or disturbing colonies), its use is preferred when working with endangered or sensitive bat species. Guano can be collected at any time of the day or year if sample age is not an issue, or by using strategically placed tarps during outflights if fresh samples are required. Use of noninvasive sampling has become especially important over the past few years as WNS has spread rapidly among caves of various species, as handling of bats has been discouraged and is highly regulated. Using this combination of methods, networks of cave roosts linked through bat migratory movements might be discernible, significantly improving our understanding of cave bat population dynamics and genetics. Additionally, this approach might provide a means for predicting the intercolony spread of diseases like WNS.
A key prerequisite to employing genetic assignment approaches is the determination of genetic structure within species. Therefore, our main goals in this study were to estimate the extent of popula tion genetic differentiation among and genetic diversity within gray bat hibernacula, while assessing the use of guano to detect patterns of population structure. In many temperate bat species, there is often very little overall population differentiation (Wey andt et al., 2005;Arnold, 2007;Bilgin et al., 2008;Floyd et al., 2010), despite high philopatry and mating that often occurs at autumn swarming sites associated with hibernacula. These patterns are also seen in gray bats (Tuttle, 1976;Brady et al., 1982), however, the potential divide of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain may limit interpopulation gene flow, allowing for geographic structuring of genetic variance. Under this scenario, we would expect to find interpopulation genetic differentiation with some genetic clustering of geographically proximate populations and a pattern of isolation-bydistance (IBD).

[SECTION] materials and methods

[SECTION] sample collection
We sampled eight populations at cave locations known to house major gray bat hibernacula (Fig. 1 and Table 1) from throughout the species' geographic range. Geo graph ic distance between cave locations ranged from 0.5 km (Coach Cave and Jesse James Cave in Kentucky, thought to house a single interbreeding population and treated as such in this study;  and Barratt, 1996). Tissue samples were stored in microcentrifuge tubes containing 95% ethanol and kept at room temperature for short-term storage, followed by long-term storage at -20°C.
To ensure guano samples were from gray bats and not from other species, a species-specific diagnostic DNA marker was sequenced and identified prior to further analyses (methods described below). We collected between 30-100 guano samples per cave. We assumed, considering the very large populations (tens to hundreds of thousands of bats) at each cave, that any two guano samples were highly unlikely to correspond to the same individual. Tissue samples were limited to a maximum of 50 samples per cave, per our federal permit.
We also sampled a single maternity colony, Salt Peter No. 3 Cave on Fort Leonard Wood, MO (Fig. 1 and Table 1). Maternity colony bats were captured via harp traps placed at the cave entrance and sampled following wing tissue procedures described for the other sampling locales. Trapping at the maternity colony was conducted in mid-July of 2006, after parturition and prior to juvenile emergence, to minimize negative impacts on pregnant and juvenile bats.

[SECTION] dna extraction and sample identification
For those sampling locales where only guano was collected, we randomly selected 30-40 samples for inclusion in the study. DNA was extracted from guano samples using the Qiagen DNeasy Kit (Qiagen Inc., Germantown, MD) and from tissue samples using QuickExtract Solution (Epicentre, Madison, WI). Genomic DNA concentrations (ng/µL) were calculated using the NanoDrop® ND-1000 UV-Vis Spectrophotometer (Nanodrop Technologies, Wilmington, DE) and DNA quality was assessed using the 260:280 ratio, which is the primary measure of DNA purity, with a ratio of 1.80 being considered pure (Nano Drop Spectrophotometers Technical Bulletin T042). PROC GLM (SAS, 2005) was used to compare differences in DNA quantity and quality, as well as genotyping success, among sample types (fresh and age-unknown guano, and wing tissue).
In order to confirm species identity for each sample (guano and wing tissue alike) we generated mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences (GenBank accession numbers KP986448-KP986462) for a species-level barcode marker described by Zinck et al. (2004). The marker sequence consists of 190 bp and partially overlaps (3'-5') the Valine tRNA and 16S rRNA (3') genes. As noted by Zinck et al. (2004), this same mtDNA marker region contains intraspecific sequence variation that could be informative for population genetic studies. We therefore applied the sequence data we generated for these markers to our study of gray bat population structure.
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) was conducted with 1X PCR buffer, 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.2 mM dNTPs, 10 pmol primers, 0.02 µg/uL T4, 2.5 units of Platinum Taq DNA polymerase (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY), and 20 ng of DNA via 40 cycles of 95°C for 1 min, 55°C for 1 min, and 72°C for 1.5 min, with an initial denaturation cycle of 95°C for 2 min and a final incubation of 72°C for 7 min. PCR products were purified with the Montage PCR Cleanup Kit (EMD Millipore, Billerica, MA) and sequenced on a 3130 Genetic Analyzer (Perkin Elmer, Bridgeville, PA) using the Big Dye Terminator Reaction and subsequent cleanup. Sequence data were aligned using SeqMan 1.4.1 (Kleywegt, 2005) and CodonCode Aligner 3.5 (Codon -Code Corporation, Centerville, MA) software. Mitochondrial haplotypes were identified for each individual. All sequences were compared to reference sequences amplified by the Mysp1/ Mysp2 primer set (J. Zinck, personal communication), as well as to sequences amplified from the wing tissue of individuals positively identified as M. grisescens during capture and sampling. We visually identified a 185 bp region of the target locus for which most of the samples exhibited quality sequence data and used DNAcollapser in the FaBox (Villesen, 2007) online software toolbox to identify all unique haplotypes in the dataset and the samples belonging to each haplotype. To be conservative, we eliminated any sample associated with a haplotype that failed to exhibit a minimum of 95% nucleotide sequence identity to the most common confirmed haplotype (BLAST2seq; http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Of the other bats that might co-occur in caves with gray bats, sequence matches were no higher than 88% identity (other Myotis spp.). CLUSTALW2 (Larkin et al., 2007;Goujon et al., 2010) was used to align all gray bat haplotypes that met our criteria for inclusion in the dataset.
In the course of compiling haplotype data for our sampled populations, we noted the presence of several nucleotide sites within the marker region that had the potential to be informative for population genetic analysis. This region included a short microsatellite-type domain in the 5' region of the 16S rDNA. One drawback of using this atypical VAL/16S marker for population genetic assessment is that there is a lack of comparative population data from other bat studies. Nonetheless, the benefit of adding a marker that would provide a different perspective, relative to conventional microsatellite DNA markers, to our overall analysis of gray bat populations argued for the inclusion of these data to the study.

[SECTION] genotype characterization
Using DNA extracted from a set of gray bat tissue samples (muscle and viscera, obtained through L. Muller, University of Tennessee, Knoxville), we evaluated 36 microsatellite loci previously developed for the greater mouse-eared bat (Myotis myotis - Castella and Ruedi, 2000) and four microsatellite loci pre viously developed for the Indiana bat (Myotis sodalis - Trujillo and Amelon, 2009). Of these 40 loci, eight loci successfully amplified gray bat DNA and were found to be polymorphic, including A2, C112, D9, E24, F14, and G9 from the M. myotis set, and MS4C09 and MS3D02 from the M. sodalis set. All loci contained dinucleotide repeat motifs. Primers were redesigned for the A2 and C112 loci and are henceforth referred to as A2L (forward primer CCAAAGTCCTGTCCACCTGT, reverse primer GATCCGTTGTCTCCCTCTCC) and C112L (forward primer AGGTGTGTGCCTGTGCG, reverse primer GTCAGCATGAAGAGAAA).
We conducted PCR following Zinck et al. (2004) with 10 pmol primer concentrations, 20 ng of DNA, and puReTaq TM Ready-To-Go TM PCR Beads (GE Healthcare, Pittsburgh, PA) for the M. myotis primers, and following Trujillo and Amelon (2009) for the M. sodalis primers, modified to add 0.02 µg/µL T4 protein. Amplification with msDNA primers was conducted using the same cycling conditions as for sequencing, except with annealing temperatures optimized for gray bats, at 52°C for D9, 54°C for A2L, E24, F14 and G9, 58°C for MS4C09 and MS3D02, and 63°C for C112L. Negative controls were included in all amplifications and reactions were prepared in a laminar flow PCR hood in a separate room from the extractions.
Fragment analysis was carried out on a 3100 Genetic Analyzer with GENEMAPPER software (Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, NY) and ROX 500 size standard. Fragment analysis reactions consisted of 2 μL PCR product, 0.5 μL size standard, and 10 μL HiDi Formamide (Applied Biosystems). All guano samples and putative homozygotes, and a subset of wing tissue samples, were amplified and genotyped at each locus a minimum of three times to confirm their status. MICRO -CHECKER (van Oosterhout et al., 2004) was used to estimate null allele frequencies and large allele dropout.

[SECTION] msdna genetic diversity
We characterized multilocus microsatellite genotypes by calculating the mean number of alleles per locus, and expected and observed heterozygosity in MSA 4.05 (Dieringer and Schlotterer, 2003), and F IS values in GENEPOP 4.0.10 (Raymond and Rousset, 1995). We then calculated rarefactioncorrected allelic richness in MSA 4.05 (Dieringer and Schlotterer, 2003). We conducted an analysis of variance using PROC GLM (SAS Institute, 2005) to determine whether differences in observed heterozygosity or allelic richness existed among populations, treating each locus as a randomized block to control for interlocus variation (Leberg, 1992). We also used PROC GLM to test for differences between sample types (guano versus wing tissue). Probability tests for Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) and linkage disequilibrium were conducted in GENEPOP, then corrected for multiple comparisons using the sequential Bon ferroni method (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
To evaluate whether individuals from sampled sites were from a population that had experienced a recent bottleneck, we used 1,000 replicates of the two-phased model (TPM) with 70% of the mutations following a step-wise mutation model (SMM) and 30% following an infinite alleles model (IAM) in the program BOTTLENECK (Cornuet and Luikart, 1996). The Wilcoxon sign-rank test was used to determine whether the number of loci with heterozygote excess was significantly different than expected if no bottleneck had occurred.

[SECTION] mtdna genetic diversity
The mean number of mtDNA haplotypes and mean gene diversity (Nei, 1987) were calculated from intrapopulation genetic diversity measures output by ARLEQUIN 3.5.1.3 (Excoffier and Lischer, 2010). The mean number of pairwise nucleotide differences among haplotypes was also calculated from ARLE-QUIN outputs. A minimum spanning network among haplotypes, with equal weightings for transitions, transversions, and deletions, was calculated in ARLEQUIN and converted to a haplotype network using HAPSTAR 0.6 (Teacher and Griffiths, 2011).

[SECTION] msdna population genetic structure
Overall F ST and G' ST were calculated in MSA. We used GENEPOP to calculate an overall R ST , which is an F ST analog that takes into account evolutionary distances between alleles, and based the estimate on a simple stepping stone model of microsatellite mutation. We evaluated population structure within the msDNA dataset using several approaches. We estimated pairwise F ST (Weir and Cockerham, 1984) among hibernacula and assessed allele frequency differentiation using GENEPOP. We also incorporated estimates of pairwise R ST as implemented in ARLEQUIN ('R ST -like' option -Slatkin, 1995;Excoffier and Lischer, 2010). In both cases, the critical value used for determining statistical significance was adjusted using a Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (Jaccard and Wan, 1996). The Bayesian clustering method of STRUCTURE 2.3.1 (Prit chard et al., 2000;Hubisz et al., 2009) was used to estimate the number of genetically divergent groups. Based on recommendations from Hubisz et al. (2009) for data sets with relatively low genetic differentiation and sampling locations with allelic pools that were likely largely independent of each other (we assume that with 30 or so samples from very large populations that were separated by considerable geographic distances that the likelihood of even a small number of recent immigrants in our samples would be very low), we analyzed our data using a no admixture model with correlated alleles and informative population priors. STRUCTURE run parameters included a 50,000 step burn-in stage and 50,000 Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) steps for each of 100 iterative runs for each K model within the range of K = 1-8. STRUCTURE results were processed using STRUCTURE HARVESTER (Web v0.6.93 -Earl and vonHoldt, 2012) and assessed following Evanno et al. (2005). Data from STRUCTURE HARVESTER relative to the optimal number of clusters (K) was entered into CLUMPP v1.1.2 (Jakobsson and Rosenberg, 2007) in order to optimize the assignment of populations to clusters (CLUMPP parameters included DATATYPE = 1, R = 100, GREEDY_ OPTION = 2, M = 2 algorithm options, and REPEATS = 10,000). We then performed a series of analyses of molecular variance (AMOVA) using ARLEQUIN 3.5.1.3 (Excoffier and Lischer, 2010) with significance determined from five loci (A2L, C112L, E24, F14, and G9) with 10% or less missing data via 10,000 permutations of the msDNA genotypes under three different putative population groups: 1) no regional structure, 2) populations west of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain vs. populations east of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain, and 3) populations grouped according to the msDNA STRUCTURE results.
We used GENEPOP to evaluate the association of genetic and geographic distances among populations. We ran the Isolation by Distance suboption with 1,000 permutations and the Spearman Rank correlation coefficient, after converting genetic differentiation values to F ST /(1 -F ST ) (Rousset, 1997), and evaluated the relationship with both linear distance and the logarithm of distance, which has been shown to perform better when testing for IBD in 2-dimensional space (Rousset, 1997). Pair wise F ST /(1 -F ST ) data from GENEPOP was then plotted in Excel against both pairwise distance and logarithm distance, separately, to obtain r-values.

[SECTION] mtdna population genetic structure
ARLEQUIN was used to perform AMOVA (Excoffier et al., 1992;Michalakis and Excoffier, 1996) on the mtDNA haplotype data under the same conditions as for the msDNA data, including putative groupings of: 1) no structure, 2) populations west vs. east of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain, and 3) populations grouped according to msDNA STRUCTURE analysis. We also used ARLEQUIN to perform analyses of pairwise population differentiation and exact tests of population structure (Raymond and Rousset, 1995;Goudet et al., 1996), with statistical significance set at P ≤ 0.011 as described by Narum (2006). ARLEQUIN was also employed in testing for IBD via partial MANTEL correlations (Mantel, 1967;Smouse et al., 1986) among matrices of pairwise Φ ST , geographic distance, and region al association. A matrix of geographic distances (km) between colonies was generated with Geographic Distance Matrix Gen erator version 1.2.3 (Ersts, 2011). A second approach, iterative simulated annealing of populations into clusters to identify a structure maximizing the proportion of total genetic variation associated with intercluster genetic differentiation, was employed using the program SAMOVA 2.0 (Dupanloup et al., 2002). The program was used to assess structure, including K = 2, K = 3, and K = 4 clusters of populations, with and without constraints associated with geographic proximity between populations, and incorporated percent sequence divergence as a measure of between-haplotype genetic distance. For each K, 1,000 iterations of simulated annealing with randomized starting partitions were used. All other run parameters were set at default values.

[SECTION] multilocus assignment tests
In order to assess the potential utility of msDNA-based individual assignment tests in determining associations between summer colonies and winter hibernacula, we conducted assignment tests with the eight hibernacula populations and for the maternity colony on Fort Leonard Wood, MO (FLW-MO). For these tests we utilized conventional likelihood-based and k-nearest neighbors (k = 1, 3, 5, 10) assignment approaches, with 'pessim istic' cross-validation (leave-one-out; L1O) of accuracy rates, in the program MLC 1.0 (Topchy et al., 2004). Also, an exhaustive genetic algorithm search, employing L1O accuracy estimates, was implemented in the program GAFS 1.1 (default parameters - Guinand et al., 2004;Topchy et al., 2004) to determine the suite of available microsatellite markers (n = 1-8) that maximizes accurate reassignment of individuals to populations of origin.

[SECTION] animal care and use guidelines
All field methodologies followed the guidelines approved by the American Society of Mammalogists (Sikes et al., 2011).
Sample collection was permitted by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (Permit # TE108962-0), The Nature Conser vancy, Arkansas Game and Fish Commission, Missouri Depart ment of Conservation, and Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency.

[SECTION] results

[SECTION] genetic diversity
DNA used in our analyses (positively identified as gray bat) was extracted from 96 age-unknown guano samples (average yield 21.95 ng/µL ± 16.51; average 260:280 ratio 1.65 ± 0.44), 92 fresh guano samples (average yield 15.57 ng/µL ± 16.10; average 260:280 ratio 1.61 ± 0.54), and 150 wing tissue samples (average yield 11.83 ng/µL ± 12.75; average 260:280 ratio 1.90 ± 1.20). Less than 5% of sample extractions provided > 100 ng/ µL DNA; those that did were considered outliers and not representative of typical sample yields.
Success of msDNA genotyping among samples ranged from three to eight loci (0 = 6.94 ± 1.06); any sample for which at least three loci were not resolved was discarded from the study. Genotyping success differed by sample type (F 2, 335 = 72.51, P < 0.001), with wing tissue samples having a higher average number of successfully amplified loci (7.88 ± 0.36) than guano samples (6.59 ± 1.38 for age-unknown and 6.35 ± 1.43 for fresh samples). Significant evidence for null alleles was identified for locus D9, with an Oosterhout frequency of 0.245. Because removal of D9 from our suite of microsatellites resulted in negligible differences in F ST , we concluded that any bias associated with this locus would be conservative and, therefore, included it in all subsequent analyses. Additionally, because using genotypes corrected for null alleles did not change the outcome of our analyses, we have reported data from the uncorrected genotypes.
Tests for linkage disequilibrium were not significant when the false discovery rate was adjusted for multiple comparisons. With the exception of CMC-AR, allele frequencies in hibernacula populations did not meet HWE expectations. There was signif icant variation in observed heterozygosity (F 7, 49 = 2.96, P = 0.011), but not allelic richness (F 7, 49 = 0.43, P = 0.880) among hibernacula (Fig. 2), and no population had significant heterozygote excess under mutation-drift equilibrium. Levels of We sequenced 307 samples for the target mtDNA locus. The target locus was comprised of 178 nucleotides, with 13 polymorphic positions, including six transitions and nine insertions/deletions (Table 2). Much of the haplotypic divergence (Fig. 3) was associated with a dinucleotide microsatellite (AT n ) located near the 5' origin of the 16S rDNA gene. Thirteen haplotypes (MG01-08, MG11-15) were identified within the hibernacula populations (Table 2), with a mean number of pairwise nucleotide differences among haplotypes of 4.2 (SD = 2.1). An additional two haplotypes (MG09-10) were identified from the maternity colony (FLW-MO), which also shared several haplotypes (MG01, MG04, MG06) with the hibernacula populations. The mean number of haplotypes within hibernacula was 3.875 (SD = 1.727) and the mean gene diversity was 0.241 (SD = 0.172). In terms of relative frequencies of haplotypes within hibernacula (Table 3 and Fig. 4), haplotype MG01 was dominant with a mean relative frequency of 0.865 (SD = 0.106). The next most common haplotypes, MG04 and MG03, had frequencies of 0.036 (SD = 0.068) and 0.029 (SD = 0.039), respectively. Haplotype MG01 also comprised 84.8% of the haplotypes found in the FLW-MO population (with the next most common haplotype, MG04, at 6.5%). In the minimum spanning network of all haplotypes (Fig. 3) MG01 is a central node for the radiation of several other haplotypes.

[SECTION] population genetic structure
With the nuclear msDNA loci, we found statistically significant overall genetic differentiation among hibernacula (F ST = 0.024, P < 0.001; G' ST = 0.121, P < 0.001; R ST = 0.060) and significant pairwise differentiation among a majority of populations (Table 4). No test for a pattern of IBD was statistically significant (P < 0.05), regardless of whether pairwise F ST or R ST estimates were used, or whether untransformed or log-transformed geographic distances were used.
For population clustering results from STRUC-TURE, K = 2 had the highest value of ΔK (= 95.067) by a wide-margin (the next highest value was for K = 3, ΔK = 3.164). The Evanno et al. (2005) method for selecting the most likely cluster model cannot identify the correct model when K = 1 is the best fit. In our case, the K = 1 model did not exhibit the highest mean LnP(K) as would be expected if K = 1 were the best fit, so we accepted K = 2 as the most probable population genetic structuring. Six of the eight hibernacula exhibited strong associations to one or the other putative genetic clusters (Fig. 4), but the associations of CC-MO and FC-AL were fairly weak. Cluster 1 included BSC-AR, CMC-AR, HC-TN, and PC-TN, and Cluster 2 included BC/ MPC-MO and CC/JJC-KY. AMOVA of the groupings derived from the msDNA structural analyses identified significant genetic structure among the K = 2 groups (Φ CT = 0.063, P < 0.001), as well as between three groups (Φ CT = 0.044, P < 0.001; when CC-MO and FC-AL were included as a separate group), accounting for 6.3% and 4.4% of the variation, respectively. There was no significant interregional differentiation between the two putative clusters of populations east and west of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain (Φ CT = 0.000, P = 0.850), AMOVA of mtDNA haplotype data exhibited statistically significant genetic differentiation among all hibernacula (Φ ST = 0.061, P < 0.001; 6% of overall genetic variance). Differences between eastern vs. western hibernacula groups were likewise statistically significant (Φ CT = 0.086, P = 0.027; 9% of overall genetic variance). No significant interpopulation genetic differentiation was found within eastern and western clusters (Φ SC = 0.010, P = 0.250). The exact test of population structure within the mtDNA data also found significant overall differentiation (P < 0.001), with the same population pairings showing significant differentiation as with the pairwise Φ ST test (Table 5). AMOVA of the population clusters suggested by STRUCTURE analysis of the msDNA data did not yield statistically significant regional differentiation. SAMOVA also failed to detect statistically significant differentiation between clusters of populations, though PC-TN clustered away from all other populations in nearly all simulated cases.
IBD among all hibernacula was weak to mod erate, explaining 23% of the interpopulation differentiation (r = 0.486, P < 0.05). The extent of IBD was largely unchanged (r = 0.477, P < 0.05) by taking into account regional groupings of populations east and west of the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain.

[SECTION] multilocus assignment tests
The best accuracy level for correct reassignment of individuals to a regional autumn breeding site using our suite of eight microsatellite loci was only 31.4%. An optimized suite of five loci (A2L, C112L, D9, G9, and 4C09) was found to be only mar ginally superior (36.4%) to using all loci.

[SECTION] discussion
In order to understand the biological or evolutionary significance of the observed population genetic pattern in gray bats, we compare our results to similar studies on confamilial species with natural histories similar to gray bats. In particular, we identified colonial species from temperate regions that mate autumn breeding swarms. We found that levels of msDNA genetic diversity within hibernacula populations of the gray bat were lower than those observed for fall breeding (swarming) sites in Myotis nattereri (Rivers et al., 2005) and Plecotus auritus (Furmankiewicz and Altringham, 2007), though higher than those reported for Corynorhinus townsendii (Weyandt et al., 2005;Smith et al., 2008). FLW-MO genetic diversity was also lower compared to maternity colonies of several temperate bats, such as Myotis myotis (Castella et al., 2001;Ruedi et al., 2008) and Myotis daubentonii (Ngamprasertwong et al., 2008). Levels of genetic diversity in the gray bat are also generally lower or roughly equivalent to reported values from several studies characterized by mixed samplings of summer populations, nursery colonies, swarming sites, unspecified colony types, or from populations not obviously corresponding to distinct breeding pools. While the gray bat appears to have generally lower allelic richness and heterozygosity than other vespertilionid species with similar natural histories, we are somewhat cautious in interpreting our data, as the presence of null alleles in our dataset may depress these estimates. However, levels of allelic diversity and observed heterozygosity detected in our data set were similar to those observed by other gray bat researchers (Trujilo and Amelon, 2009). At the interpopulation scale, we did not find significantly different levels of allelic richness and did not detect statistically significant signatures of recent bottlenecks. This result is not surprising considering that, although surveys have noted a past decline of overall gray bat numbers, large remnant pop u lations have remained at some hibernacula (Table 1).
Although there has been some debate over which measurements of genetic differentiation are most appropriate for microsatellite data, F-statistics may be the most reliable measure of genetic structure in our data set as they are less biased when the number of loci and samples analyzed are small, and when gene flow is high (Gaggiotti et al., 1999), a characteristic common in genetic studies of temperate bat species. Additionally, Meirmans and Hedrick (2011) recommend the use of F-statistics as a standard for comparisons among different population genetic studies. Therefore, in comparing measures of interpopulation genetic differentiation, we focused on the F ST estimates reported in those studies of other temperate bats. Relative to these other species we found a higher proportion of population pairs to be significantly differentiated (Table 4) and a similar or slightly elevated degree of overall genetic differentiation (F ST = 0.0236) in gray bats (F ST = 0.017 and 0.029 for M. nattereri and Myotis lucifugus, respectively - Rivers et al., 2005;Dixon, 2011). Population genetic differentiation was also similar to that found among breeding populations in temperate bats that mate on summer ranges (M. myotis, F ST = 0.022 - Castella et al., 2001), and greater than values reported in studies for which the correspondence of samples to breeding populations was unclear (C. townsendii, no significant differentiation -Wey andt et al., 2005 andSmith et al., 2008; Myotis vi vesi, F ST = 0.002 -Floyd et al., 2010; Myotis se pten trio nalis, F ST = 0.002 -Arnold, 2007; M. dau ben tonii, F ST = 0.017 - Ngam prasertwong et al., 2008 andAtterby et al., 2010).
We hypothesized that the Mississippi River Alluvial Plain that separates the Ouachita-Ozark Mountains from the Appalachian Range would be a source of genetic divergence among gray bat populations. This alluvial plain is a major discontinuity in the availability of the karst-associated caves, which are critical to gray bat populations as roost sites. In our gray bat mtDNA dataset, the strongest degree of differentiation was found between regional groups on either side of the alluvial plain, indicating that the alluvial plain has indeed, to some degree, been a barrier to gene flow. However, the relatively weak differentiation value (Φ CT = 0.086) between the regions indicates that dispersal (and gene flow) across this barrier does occur.
Based on the aforementioned comparisons, our hypothesis that the gray bat would exhibit stronger genetic structuring than other similar bat species is generally supported by comparable or somewhat greater estimates of F ST and Φ ST in the msDNA data, and by significant structure in the mtDNA data, including within region IBD. However, like many other volant or highly vagile animals, the degree of interpopulation genetic differentiation in gray bats is not large.
Although IBD was not detected in the msDNA dataset (a trend also documented in other Myotis spp.), genetic clustering, with the exception of FC-AL, did trend toward geographically proximal hibernacula (Fig. 4). The hibernacula pairs that were not genetically distinct from each other (pairwise F ST values were not significant) include FC-AL & CC-MO (unexpected, as these caves span 683 km and are located on opposite sides of the Mississippi River Alluvial Valley) and HC-TN & PC-TN (as expected, as these are more proximal caves, only 264 km apart). With STRUCTURE (Pritchard et al., 2000), we detected two genetic clusters among the 295 individuals sampled. Our hypothesis that gray bat hibernacula would genetically cluster within regions was, again with the exception of FC-AL, some what supported by the data we collected.  (Narum, 2006) Genotyping success rates in our study were likely slightly depressed by the use of microsatellite primers developed for Myotis congeners, as opposed to primers optimized for M. grisescens (Barbará et al., 2007), a trend also observed by Trujillo and Amelon (2009). The use of microsatellite loci primers developed for other species could also account for the presence of some null alleles in our data set (see Küpper et al., 2008 for example of increased occurrence of null alleles associated with cross-species utilization of microsatel lites). Null alleles are indicated in a data set when there is an excess of observed homozygous allelic states within a population that results from unobserved (null) alleles that fail to factor into calculations of expected homozygosity under expectations of HWE. Rivers et al. (2005) utilized six M. myotis microsatellite loci for their study of M. nattereri, including two loci that we used in our study. In their case, these loci (D9 and E24) both exhibited null alleles (with frequencies of 0.081 and 0.022, respectively). Because the frequencies of null alleles for A2L and D9 in our study were relatively low, we did not remove these loci from our analyses, nor adjust genotypes to account for potentially unscored alleles.
The use of guano as a source of DNA for bats has many positive aspects (e.g., eliminates the need for capture and handling, reduces constraints on collecting schedule due to daily and seasonal activity periods) and has been demonstrated to provide results for frequency-based population genetic analyses comparable to DNA from tissue samples (Boston et al., 2012). The use of degraded DNA (which is common in fecal samples), however, can result in relatively high genotyping error (Taberlet et al., 1996). In addition to degradation, genotyping success from small fecal sources can also be reduced due to PCR inhibitors or cross contamination (Judy et al., 2010), and not always yielding adequate amounts of nuclear DNA for the replicate PCR amplifications required for robust genotype characterization. Regardless, Vege and McCracken (2001) achieved 100% genotyping accuracy with bat guano samples at five microsatellite loci, and Zinck et al. (2004) had considerable success with sequencing mitochondrial DNA derived from bat guano of unknown age and weathering. Due to multiple replicate efforts to genotype each of our fecal samples we believe that our results have yielded similar success.
